item.title: Dementia care can cost a fortune. Families pay in more ways than one.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.84
When Angela Davis discovered that her mother with dementia had changed the locks, she knew she had to intervene. After a standard care facility didn't cut it, Davis, 65, moved her mother into her own home. Davis now manages her medications, assists with her hygiene, and monitors her at night. She sleeps on a love seat near her mom's room in case anything happens. Her mom's care, plus home maintenance, has cost about $7,000 a month. Her mom receives $3,200 monthly in retirement income, and Davis covers the rest. The stress has weighed her down; last week, she took what she thought would be a short evening nap. Next thing she knew, it was 7 a.m. the next morning and time to go to work. "It's death by 1,000 cuts, and in this case, you could say death by 1,000 memories every day," Davis said. Seven million Americans have Alzheimer's, leaving families to navigate rising costs for memory care facilities or home care. One estimate shows that lifetime costs for dementia can exceed $400,000. Two dozen families navigating dementia care told Business Insider that costs add up for frequent hospitalizations and physician visits, expensive medications, transportation costs, and round-the-clock home care. Those who can afford it spend five figures on monthly memory care facility costs. Other costs included home modifications, power-of-attorney legal fees, and technologies for aging in place. A report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that in 2025, one in four family caregivers cared for someone 50 and over with memory issues or dementia. While an estimated 7 million Americans aged 65 and over have Alzheimer's, that is expected to surge. Wendy Rowland, 53, has cared for her husband with early onset Lewy body dementia for years. To manage his treatment, they spent through his 401(k) and sold their house of 20 years, then put him into a memory care facility two years ago that now costs $6,750 a month. "I hope nothing like that happens with me, and if it does, I don't know if I would want anybody else to go through the same thing of having to figure out what to do," Rowland said. The cost of memory care can be steep It pained Keith Pavlick, 53, to witness his father slowly forget his family members' names and lose track of his surroundings. He hadn't fully anticipated the financial hit that came with it. Pavlick, a real estate agent in Orlando, has helped his mother, 79, and his father, 80, since his dementia diagnosis in March 2025. His parents moved into an assisted living facility for $9,000 a month. The $9,000 is just the start, Pavlick told Business Insider earlier this year. He knows his dad will need a heightened level of care, and memory care facilities in his area cost $14,000 monthly. "Unless you're starting out investing or bought SpaceX at the IPO, then you're probably not going to be able to take care of your parents when they're that age by yourself," Pavlick said. "I'm probably going to be selling real estate until I'm dead." Memory care costs a median of about $8,000 monthly, according to data from SeniorLiving.org. They're more expensive than standard assisted living centers because dementia patients require 24/7 supervision by specialized caregivers. They also have high security and maintenance costs. Medicare generally doesn't fund long-term memory care. Medicaid chips in for eligible families, though many said they have paid out of pocket or used long-term care insurance. Sharon Winterton, 53, has juggled working a tech sales job, raising a 14-year-old daughter, and caring for her 90-year-old mother with vascular dementia. Winterton moved her mom into an independent living facility as her memory declined. Her mom had invested in long-term care insurance, which she's used to cover her $7,000 monthly assisted living costs. Winterton said they're fortunate to avoid the high out-of-pocket cost, though she's splurged on technologies that allow her to change TV channels and monitor her mom remotely. "Thankfully, I don't have to worry a lot about her long-term care," Winterton said. There are many costs beyond direct care itself Jenn Verser, 45, hadn't anticipated moving into her childhood home in New Jersey to help care for her dad with Alzheimer's. Verser is selling her home and planning to build a two-story, roughly 1,000-square-foot addition to her parents' house. She expects it will cost at least $600,000, which they're planning to cover with a home equity line of credit, her parents' investment accounts, and the sale of her home. She said it's important to get started as quickly as possible, so that her dad can get familiar and comfortable with the addition as his Alzheimer's progresses and confusion increases. Her parents will be moving into the addition, which is "elder-friendly," with the goal of aging in place. Verser, her husband, and her child will move into the main area. Though some families told Business Insider they avoided memory care in favor of at-home care, the costs are often comparable. Tatyana Zlotsky, CEO of A Place for Mom, a platform connecting senior care providers and families, said that with home care costing about $30 an hour, based on the platform's internal data, this can end up being over $250,000 a year for 24/7 care. An early retirement or remote job can help caregivers minimize costs. Families have invested thousands of dollars in age-tech designed for dementia care, such as motion-sensor cameras, medication monitoring, and smart home devices like stove shut-off devices. Others have spent five figures on home renovations for their loved ones. Ann Gynn, 55, had cared for her mom until September, when she moved into memory care. In 2024, the content marketer in Cleveland started using JubileeTV, a remote caregiving platform allowing for remote monitoring through the TV, after many frustrating back-and-forth phone calls with her mom. Gynn created a schedule of her mom's favorite shows, and she sometimes uses the drop-in feature to see which nursing aides are in the room. "It gives me peace of mind that I have ways to get in touch with her and ways to help her that I don't physically have to be there for," Gynn said. Emotional costs can be a heavy burden too For many families, the greatest cost of dementia care isn't financial. For Michelle Keller, 59, caring for her dad has meant sacrificing going out for her 35th wedding anniversary, and, at times, forcing herself to feel optimistic. She said caregiving can be tiring and involve a lot of acting. "To be able to put on that happy face, it helps to get things done," Keller said. "If they're happier, they'll listen and follow instructions a little better. There's a lot of work involved that honestly doesn't allow you to take time to think about the mess you're in." Dementia caregivers said they've quit their jobs, gone part-time, or taken on less time-consuming roles to be more present as caregivers. The stress of worrying about falls, wandering, or medication takes a toll on caregivers' physical health, too. They don't always have the time or energy to prepare for their own long-term care. "Asking individual people to find the Goldilocks solution of how much to save for a future even that may or may not occur is unfortunately the wrong question," said Alan Weil, senior vice president of public policy at AARP. Laura Ehrlich, 54, knew her aunt's health was declining when, a few years back, she caught her giving her Social Security number to a scammer. With help from an aide, she handled her day-to-day needs, but after her aunt fell at the mall, her family decided to place her in an assisted living facility nearby. Ehrlich, who also cares part-time for her mother-in-law, stays afloat by living on a stipend from her aunt's trust. "I still haven't dealt with the loss of my parents, my husband, or my father-in-law," said Ehrlich, who has worked on and off in between caregiving. "It's just been putting up a wall and going on to the next person who needs help."

item.title: Warren Buffett has stepped down as Berkshire chairman. Here are 5 leadership lessons he leaves behind.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.78
If you want to be a high-mileage leader like Warren Buffett, it pays to be humble. The Oracle of Omaha this week gave up the job as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, after more than half a century spent building and then running the conglomerate. Buffett said his son Howard would succeed him as chairman. In that role, his son will guard Berkshire's culture and values, which the elder Buffett said are "worth more than anything on our balance sheet." That belief in the importance of organizational culture is nothing new for Buffett who has, over the years, offered a steady stream of advice on investing and leadership. Last year, in his final Thanksgiving letter to shareholders as CEO, he shared insights on the virtues of stewardship, honesty, and what he described as "good intentions" gone awry in attempts to rein in CEO pay. One broad takeaway was his call to continue learning and growing. "Choose your heroes very carefully and then emulate them. You will never be perfect, but you can always be better," Buffett wrote. Here are five other lessons Buffett shared: Stay humble The 96-year-old famously ran Berkshire with an unfussy, meat-and-potatoes sensibility. Buffett wrote about the role luck played in his life and work, and how that experience continually honed his sense of humility. "Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman," Buffett said. He also grounded some of his humble inclinations in the luck he had, being a man — compared with his sisters, whom he described as having "equal intelligence and better personalities," though they faced a much different outlook. "I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck," he said. Learn from your errors Buffett said that while he's made many mistakes, he's tried to use them as springboards for growth. "Learn at least a little from them and move on," Buffett wrote. One misstep, he said, was not intervening more forcefully when he saw indications that a "wonderful and loyal CEO" of a parent or subsidiary company would "succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease." "Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake," Buffett wrote, referring to Charlie Munger, his longtime friend and colleague, who died in 2023. Buffett said that while it's often not easy, boards need to keep watch for signs of such conditions in chiefs, and that CEOs themselves need to do the same at the units they oversee. "Directors should be alert and speak up is all that I can advise," Buffett said in the letter, which ran about seven pages. Choose the right leaders Part of Buffett's call for humility extended to how future Berkshire leaders should expect to conduct themselves — and what they should aspire to. He said that the company should only require five or six CEOs over the next century. In the shareholder letter released Friday, Buffett reiterated his confidence in Greg Abel, who succeeded him as CEO. "He has been making the decisions that matter for some time now, and I have not had to think twice about any of them," Buffett wrote. Buffett wrote last fall that he wanted Berkshire Hathaway, which was a New England textile producer when he began buying up its stock in the early 1960s, to avoid hiring top leaders who are there for the wrong reasons: "It should particularly avoid those whose goal is to retire at 65, to become look-at-me rich or to initiate a dynasty," Buffett said of the company. Think about your obit One recurring theme in his letter centered on Buffett's assertion that it's "never too late to improve." Another bit of advice: Work backward from what you want your obituary to say and then "live the life to deserve it." The release of Buffett's third annual Thanksgiving letter to Berkshire shareholders had become something of an event because of his status as one of the world's most famous investors. He said at the time that he planned to continue to address shareholders in an annual letter, though not as CEO. "As the British would say, I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of." Don't rule from the grave Buffett's decision to become chairman emeritus appeared in line with his advice against of trying to retain influence for too long. In his Thanksgiving letter, Buffett applauded the abilities of Abel, who is some three decades younger and took over as CEO at the start of 2026. "He is a great manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator," Buffett said. He also wrote about his three children, whom he said possess the "maturity, brains, energy and instincts" to disburse the family's large fortune. Earlier this year, Buffett's net worth was nearing $150 billion. After he dies, Buffett wrote last year, his children will be free to adapt to changes in tax policy and other factors as needed to continue the family's philanthropic work. "Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so," he said. An earlier version of this story appeared on November 10, 2025.

item.title: Get ready for higher holiday airfares as airlines cut flights over high fuel costs
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.74
If you haven't booked your holiday flights yet, you may want to brace your wallet: Airlines are cutting options and potentially raising fares as oil prices reach new highs. After surging in the spring following the start of the war in Iran, oil prices surged yet again this summer and surpassed $100 a barrel this month; jet fuel is $4.53 a gallon as of Thursday. Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' latest consumer price index show airfares rose more than 23% year-over-year in August. Speaking at Morgan Stanley's Laguna Conference on Wednesday, major airline executives said they are cutting flights planned this holiday season and are likely to raise fares to offset oil spikes. Mike Leskinen, CFO of United Airlines, said the company is seeing strong demand and that its customers are "incredibly, incredibly resilient," but United has already cut some routes that are on the low end of profitability and "don't make sense in a higher fuel environment." "As you look into the fourth quarter, there'll be some flights in December that we won't fly that we thought we were going to fly," Leskinen said. "If fuel remains high, we'll make some adjustments into the first quarter and beyond into 2027." Southwest Airlines CFO Tom Doxey and American Airlines CFO Devon May similarly said demand is strong and that if high fuel prices persist, they would trim capacity and raise fares in response. However, the airline CFOs said it takes time for those increases to show up: "Jet fuel price gets passed through with a lag," Leskinen said. "Period." Doxey said that "both from the booking curve and just kind of a natural lag, it takes a while for that to come," but Southwest has the "ability to recover a good portion" of those added costs. Sally French, a travel analyst at NerdWallet, said that, beyond high airfares, airlines have also increased checked-bag and seat-selection fees. "The true cost of flying is higher than ever," she said. What flight cuts could mean for travelers It's unclear which specific flights and routes will be axed and how the airlines will rebook those affected. When trimming schedules, airlines have historically looked for markets that are already oversaturated, flights on less-busy travel days like Saturday, and flights that depart at less desirable times and may have lower demand. Considering the record demand for premium travel, it's also possible airlines will focus resources on more business-heavy markets with strong corporate demand, especially long-haul international routes. Several airlines are banking on their affluent customers continuing to book as they have grown desensitized to the volatility. Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said in an April earnings call that "as difficult as it is to see what's going on with the conflict in the Middle East, I'm not sure that our premium customers are feeling affected by that." Another wrinkle for travelers looking for affordable flights is that this year marks the first holiday season without Spirit Airlines, which shut down in May, taking its famously low fares off the table. "Generally speaking, booking now to lock in a good price is best practice, particularly if we're talking winter travel," French said. "That sweet spot window for booking domestic travel is 1-3 months in advance, or 2-8 months for international travel." She added that booking refundable fares that you can cancel and rebook if prices drop is also a smart move.

item.title: Stock compensation gives Big Tech workers a powerful reason to stay. Layoffs and the AI boom are changing the equation.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.53
The day after Rob Waters learned of his layoff from Google last year, he was encouraged to apply for a new role there as an AI sales specialist. Google soon offered him the position, with a six-figure salary. Waters wasn't sure he wanted to return. He'd grown frustrated with the bureaucracy at Google and how the reorganization that eliminated his team had been handled. But walking away meant giving up about a few hundred thousand dollars in unvested equity. "I killed myself working and dedicating myself, and then all I got to show for it was getting let go," said the 42-year-old, who lives in San Francisco. He'd also dreamed of starting his own company. The layoff, he said, "ripped the bandaid off." Waters decided to bet on himself and pursue Kanawai AI, a startup he cofounded. "All the equity that was unvested was gone," he said. "I went from making very high six figures to zero." Stock compensation has long given Big Tech workers a powerful incentive to stay put. Since the end of 2022, shares of Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft have all at least doubled. But years of Big Tech layoffs have reminded some workers that their stock compensation isn't guaranteed. Meanwhile, the AI boom has created another path to potential equity riches. And for some workers, years of gains on vested stock have given them the financial security to leave Big Tech on their own terms. When Big Tech stock makes leaving easier Julie Zhu, 29, had wanted to become a founder since she was 18 and said she'd developed a "love-hate relationship" with Apple, where she worked as a product designer. She was grateful for what she'd learned at the company but said it was a high-pressure, high-stress environment. She wanted more control over her work. Still, Zhu wanted to make sure she could afford the risk of leaving. Her goal was to have three to five years of runway. Her Apple stock came in handy. "I didn't sell anything during my time at Apple, and Apple has been doing really well," she said. Last year, after nearly four years at Apple, Zhu resigned to focus on Odd One In, the artist collectible company she'd been building on the side. She said it felt like the right time, though leaving meant forfeiting the remaining quarter of her Apple stock grant that hadn't yet vested. Yousuf Imran also built up a financial cushion during roughly six years at Google, where his compensation included company stock. He set aside $350,000 for business and personal expenses before leaving in April to start an AI sales tools company. Imran said the potentially "life-changing" equity packages at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic shaped his decision. "If the only way to get real upside in this AI moment is equity, at some point, you ask yourself whether the equity should be in your own company," he said. Dave Lewis also credited stock compensation for giving him the flexibility to consider career options outside Big Tech. Lewis, who spent more than a decade working at Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, said the wealth he'd accumulated from stock compensation gave him enough of a financial cushion to be selective after he was laid off by Microsoft last October. With AI reshaping the tech industry, Lewis said he wanted his next role to position him for where he thought the industry was headed. In May, he joined Emberos, an AI startup, as head of partnerships. With stock compensation, timing can be everything For all its potential upside, stock compensation can leave workers' finances exposed to luck and timing: of when they join the company, vesting schedule, stock performance, and their decisions to sell or hold. One former Meta employee got lucky: Meta's shares had fallen sharply when he joined in 2022 and received a "boatload" of restricted stock units on the cheap. The stock then surged over the next few years. Not everyone is as fortunate. A former Microsoft employee in her 60s said she still held a large amount of company stock when she lost her job last year after more than a decade there. She initially thought her savings and stock holdings might allow her to retire, but after Microsoft shares fell sharply, she began to question whether she could afford to. The golden handcuffs only go so far For all its complications, stock compensation remains one reason Big Tech is so appealing. A former Amazon employee said the company's salary-and-stock compensation was lucrative and also felt more predictable than the bonus-heavy pay structure she had at her previous employer. But even a predictable compensation package depends on keeping the job. After a few years at Amazon, she was laid off last year. Even for workers who do retain their jobs, the financial incentives to stay only go so far. As Bushra Amiwala weighed whether to leave her sales associate role to run for Congress, she said she felt the pull of Big Tech's so-called "golden handcuffs." Staying at Google offered the salary, stock, and stability that could help her continue supporting her immigrant parents financially. For Amiwala, the deciding question wasn't whether she'd win the race — she ultimately left Google but lost the election — or what she'd give up financially by leaving Google. It was whether, five or 10 years later, she'd regret not taking the chance. "For me, it was a no-brainer," she said. "I knew I'd regret not doing it." Do you have a story to share? Reach out to the reporter via email at jzinkula@businessinsider.com, or via Signal at jzinkula.29.

item.title: 12 game-day foods you can make in a slow cooker or Crock-Pot
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.05
Football season is finally here — which means Sundays are once again all about touchdowns, trash talk, and a very serious spread of game-day snacks. Whether you're locked in on the game or mainly showing up for Buffalo Chicken dip, ribs, and hot wings, you don't have to spend the entire day hovering over a hot stove to feed a crowd. Business Insider spoke with cookbook authors Sarah Olson, who wrote "The Magical Slow Cooker," and Kim Laidlaw, author of "Everyday Slow Cooking: Modern Recipes for Delicious Meals," for ideas for easy game-day recipes. These recipes can all be made in a slow cooker, allowing you to throw everything into your Crock-Pot and get back to the game. Meatballs are a filling game-day appetizer you can make in a slow cooker. Olson recommends her slow-cooker meatballs recipe for game day. "I love grape-jelly meatballs, which only have three ingredients," she said. "They're so good, everyone will ask you for the recipe." Another recipe from Spend With Pennies suggests placing your seasoned, raw meatballs in the slow cooker, topping them with sauce, and letting it finish them off. Beer brats can also be made in a slow cooker. Brats with onions, peppers, and garlic, simmered in the slow cooker with beer, are another of Olson's favorite game-day recipes. "When the guests arrive, they get to choose when they want to eat since the slow cooker keeps these brats nice and warm during the game," she wrote on her website, The Magical Slow Cooker. Plus, you can even choose peppers to reflect the colors of your favorite team. Brisket is perfect for feeding a larger family. "Brisket is a natural partner for the slow cooker, as a gentle braise renders it meltingly tender," Kim Laidlaw wrote in "Everyday Slow Cooking: Modern Recipes for Delicious Meals." Laidlaw's recipe for slow-cooked braised brisket features garlic, onion, dry red wine, carrots, and either chicken or beef stock, accompanied by a chimichurri sauce. Pork shoulder is a slow-cooker staple you can use to make game-day sliders. "One dish I think is so versatile is pork shoulder in a slow cooker with broth and a little salt and pepper," Laidlaw said. "I just braise that, and then you can turn it into so many different things." One of the best ways to use slow-cooked pork shoulder is to make pulled-pork sliders with all that tender meat. Then, top with barbecue sauce and slaw. You can even make Buffalo chicken wings using a slow cooker. Olson's recipe for slow-cooked Buffalo chicken wings calls for thawed chicken wings, hot sauce, and unsalted butter. To get the wings super crispy, remove them from the sauce after 2.5 hours of cooking, then broil them in the oven before adding them back to the slow cooker. Pulled chicken with barbecue or Buffalo sauce is another great way to use your Crock-Pot. One of the benefits of using a slow cooker is that you can start with a basic protein and jazz it up. From Mexican-food-inspired spices to Indian simmer sauces, there are many ways to transform shredded chicken into something show-stopping by adding it to tacos, sandwiches, or salads. Mac and cheese can also easily be made in a slow cooker. If you want to add some carbs to your game-day menu, look no further than a piping hot pot of mac and cheese. Olson's recipe uses cream cheese, milk, sharp cheddar, and white sharp cheddar. Martha Stewart's recipe for slow-cooker mac and cheese is also easy to make. "It is important to use pungent cheeses, such as sharp cheddar, mixed with a little Gruyere or pecorino Romano for extra bite, since the white sauce and pasta will absorb a lot of flavor," Stewart writes. Buffalo-chicken dip is another quick and easy favorite. One of the benefits of making a slow-cooker Buffalo chicken dip — or any other slow-cooker side dish — is that the recipe can be prepared well in advance and reheated when you're ready to eat. "There are so many different dips that can be made in the slow cooker, you can make Buffalo-chicken dip, bacon-cheeseburger dip, cheesy bean dip, Rotel and Velveeta Dip, and even artichoke dip," Olson said. "I like to serve all these dips with tortilla chips. Can't choose one dip? Make two or more for a variety for your guests." Spinach-and-artichoke dip is another game-day favorite you can make in a slow cooker. Spinach-artichoke dip is a game-day classic, and making it in a slow cooker keeps it extra warm, creamy, and scoopable from kickoff to the final whistle. This recipe from Delish is made with full-fat cream cheese, shredded cheese, and mayonnaise, Queso is a go-to game-day food that can be easily prepared in a Crock-Pot. Chili is another popular recipe to make on game days. Spicy chili and chipotle turkey chili are ideal game-day recipes because they can simmer in a slow cooker for hours, letting the flavors deepen while you watch the game. Serve with warm cornbread for a cozy, filling meal. Slow cookers work perfectly to create an impressive — and tasty – nacho bar. A DIY nacho bar is an easy way to feed a crowd while letting everyone build their perfect plate. It also puts those smaller slow cookers to work, keeping every topping warm and ready to scoop. "I use three slow cookers for a nacho bar, which is a great way to use those smaller slow cookers," Olson said. "I use one slow cooker for nacho cheese (store-bought), one for seasoned ground beef, and one for refried beans. I also make a toppings bar that has salsa, sour cream, guac, olives, onions, and tomatoes."

item.title: I stayed at a Chicago hotel that was once a Gilded Age men's club. The history drew me in, but playful details won me over.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.18
I've never been good at sports, and I've never been fond of exercise, so you might be wondering why I chose the Chicago Athletic Association when booking hotels for my first-ever trip to the city. I wanted to step back in time. The Gilded Age hotel was a private club where professional athletes and high-profile individuals trained and socialized from 1893 to 2007. Following its closure and a lengthy transformation project, the Chicago Athletic Association reopened as a hotel in 2015. I spent one night there in February for $250. It felt extremely luxurious for the price point, and some surprising details made me certain I'd book it again. Parts of my stay felt like a time warp, but the hotel's history also came out in ways I didn't see coming. Welcome to the Chicago Athletic Association, the 19th-century private club that's now a hotel. The Venetian-Gothic-style building was designed by architect and club member Henry Ives Cobb, who took inspiration from the Doge's Palace in Venice, according to the hotel's website. The hotel stood out to me among modern buildings on Michigan Avenue in Downtown Chicago. It's just across from Millennium Park and the Bean (formally known as Cloud Gate) and within walking distance of many tourist hot spots like the Art Institute of Chicago, the Chicago Theater, and the Chicago Riverwalk. Inside, the past lives on. The Chicago Athletic Association began as a Gilded Age gentlemen's club joined by influential sports icons. Membership opened to women in 1972. It was a stomping ground for industry moguls like William Wrigley and Marshall Field. It was a training base for five-time Olympic gold-medal swimmer Johnny Weissmuller and the first professional football player, William "Pudge" Heffelfinger. The building's history is celebrated inside the hotel, with 19th-century relics and refurbished materials, from wood paneling to marble flooring, Elizabeth Story, the hotel's sales and marketing director, told Business Insider. As I stepped into the lobby, I felt like I'd traveled back in time. The lobby, also known as the drawing room, looked as if it had been designed 100 years ago, with restored 19th-century trim, moldings, and replicated historic details. "Teams of craftsmen restored the 1893 grandeur of the Lobby Lounge by removing, refinishing, and reinstalling every piece of millwork, and recreating original light fixtures from old photographs," Story said. I noticed other contemporary details that pay tribute to the city and club's history. The check-in desk, designed with long strips of wood in different colors, was inspired by vintage athletic equipment. "A mural above the desk depicts the elevated train tracks that encircle Chicago's Loop," Story added. Restored Gilded Age interiors made communal spaces look as lavish as they were historic. I was mesmerized by the preserved luxury finishings as I walked through the hotel. Restored Italian columns, stained-glass windows, and golden doors made me feel as if I were inside a palace. The ballrooms had an old-world, luxury feel. The hotel had many event spaces, including the White City Ballroom. During the restoration process, Story said that the Italian Carrara marble floor was buried under an inch and a half of carpet, glue, and concrete. I was surprised by another event space that used to be a swimming pool. Known as "The Tank," this space still has the swimming lane flooring tiles from its pool days. "Artists hand-made 167 individual stalactites as part of the atmospheric design," Story said. Although the highlight of this room is the historic pool tiles, I thought repurposing the space for events was surprising and innovative. The game room had a mix of historic and fresh details. The game room was the billiards room back in the club days, Story said. It didn't feel frozen in time like some of the other spaces. The walls blended antique woodwork with whimsical murals, such as chalkboard sketches of athletes and an aerial view of a basketball court. I thought it was a playful, creative way to showcase the building's history. Some aspects of the hotel were completely new, like the rooftop bar and restaurant. "The past was honored at every turn, but the transformation also called for thoughtful new additions," Story explained. For example, Cindy's, the rooftop restaurant and bar, was built ahead of the hotel's 2015 opening. I thought the space had a midcentury modern vibe with vintage influence. Cindy's brought the outdoors in with a steel-framed, windowed pavilion inspired by 19th-century train sheds. The fitness center was sleek and modern. Here, I found cardio machines with tablet attachments and fun cartoons of men stretching on the walls. The fitness center is open 24 hours a day. My room had a vintage aesthetic without feeling dated. I booked a standard room with a comfy king-sized bed and a downtown view for about $250 a night. I immediately noticed the custom metal bedframe with brass accents — a vintage design inspired by the 19th-century club. The furniture creatively combined elements of old-fashioned gym equipment in a functional way. The desk was unlike any I'd seen before. Wooden bars, inspired by stretching racks, climbed the wall to a netted shelf that appeared large enough to hold a typical checked suitcase. The bars were cleverly used as vertical storage, with leather pouches of varying sizes hanging from them. I used these pockets to store my wallet, keys, and chargers during my stay. The bathroom blended old-school locker room vibes with opulence. "The bathrooms were conceived as a quiet luxury counterpoint," Story said. A black-and-white palette and a simple striped backsplash were paired with a Carrara marble vanity and a rainfall shower. There was also a boxing-style robe in the bathroom, which almost made me feel like an athlete myself. At the Chicago Athletic Association, I got my trip back in time, with some surprises. While parts of the hotel felt 100 years old, fresh designs inspired by its private-club past gave other spaces a modern twist. "The goal was never a museum-quality freeze in time, but something more alive," Story said. "A touch of disorder in the new space was introduced to draw in a younger generation, balanced bravely with references to the building's past." From the palace-like common spaces to the creative nods to the past, the Chicago Athletic Association was more luxurious and distinctive than I expected for $250 a night. I would definitely stay there again, and maybe next time, I'll bring a jock with me.

item.title: I fell for my surf instructor in Morocco. We got married and turned an abandoned riad into a hotel.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.16
This interview is based on a conversation with Nina Ottevanger, 31, a surf instructor and co-owner of Ilyana Surfhouse, a small business in Rabat, Morocco. It has been edited for length and clarity. Eleven years ago, I was traveling in Morocco with two friends. While in Rabat, we wanted to surf and found a place online. We were greeted by a man named Ilyass. The main group had already left, but he offered us a private lesson. Something clicked between us. He shared his number in case we wanted to go out that evening, but we chose an early night so we could continue traveling the next morning. I texted to say I hoped our paths crossed again, and we kept chatting. He suggested I finish my trip with a return visit to Rabat, which I did, and we hit it off. I'd just finished my second year studying international tourism and leisure management at a university in the Netherlands, where I'm from, so starting a long-distance relationship had to feel right. Thankfully, it did. I saw Ilyass in Rabat every few months during study breaks. In 2016, he took a job managing a surf camp on Morocco's Atlantic coast. I found a six-month internship at another nearby surf camp. Sharing an apartment gave us a taste of normal life together. But I still had one year left in school, part of which I spent in Bali, writing my thesis and doing market research for a retreat. One foot in the surf, one foot in Western Europe Ilyass had worked at his uncle's hostel and surf school in Rabat, where he's from, for years, but always wanted his own business. I'd been looking for a way to swap the Netherlands for somewhere I could be outside year-round. Running a B&B had always appealed to me, so we dreamt up a surf concept. But we had neither the money nor enough experience to build it. The following year, I graduated and got a job at a travel agency in The Hague, and Ilyass moved to the Netherlands. We got married on Kijkduin beach in 2021. Ilyass realized he wasn't built for cold winters, so I quit the agency and joined him at a beach club and surf school in The Hague. We agreed to work there in the summer and spend winters in Morocco developing our business. Ilyass' students in the Netherlands wanted to come to Morocco for lessons, and many booked without knowing where they would sleep. They trusted us. For three years, we ran Ilyana, a mashup of our names, as a surf school, arranging accommodation through local homestays. But splitting the year between two countries tired us out. It was hard to build a life when we were only there half the time. Renovating an abandoned riad In 2024, we started searching for a riad — a traditional Moroccan house built around a courtyard — on the ocean side of the medina, so guests wouldn't have to carry their boards far. We found a very rundown one with no bathrooms. Except for a few birds, it had been abandoned for over 20 years, but it had gorgeous features, including traditional tiling. It was priced higher than other riads in the medina, but we later learned that the original details made it more valuable. We wanted to restore that beauty. We bought it outright, paying 40% with our savings and 60% with loans from family and friends. We started renovations in April 2025. At first, my parents thought we were mad, but they were convinced when they saw it. My dad, who had worked on similar projects, helped me sketch every room and design the architectural plans. We project-managed the renovation ourselves, using local plumbers, electricians, and builders. We estimate we spent €75,000, or about $86,800. After five months of working day in, day out, we welcomed our first guests in October. The five guest rooms at Ilyana Surfhouse sleep 16 people, with rates starting at 500 Moroccan dirhams, or about $53, per night, including breakfast and dinner. Ilyass' mother cooks dinner, his sister makes breakfast and welcomes guests, and his brother helps teach surf lessons. We're happy with how the business is going. Our hope is that the house will be paid off with our profits within eight years. Making the most of Rabat's surf scene It's been a huge and satisfying lifestyle change. We live in wetsuits and do much less than before. We keep more at the end of the month because there's less to spend on. On Sundays off, we go to the beach and find our whole friend group there. We laugh, share food, and chill. Morocco is getting more expensive, though, especially Rabat. A simple life here is affordable, but anything considered elite or luxe, like yoga or Pilates, costs much more than in the Netherlands. We chose Rabat because it's where my husband grew up and because of the surf scene. Here, you're in the water with 10 or 20 people, not hundreds. Our friends are teachers, engineers, shop owners, and barbers, and we want to show people a normal life, not a surfer's paradise. We're a great team. We each have our own specialties and love swapping stories at the end of the day. It's important that we're husband and wife, too, so we make time for fun things just the two of us. Editor's note: Ottevanger did not share the price they paid for the property. Comparable riads in Rabat's medina are listed for roughly $230,000 to $550,000, according to current listings on Moroccan property site Avito.

item.title: Canada and EU: A look at the bloc's special relationships
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.44
Canada and the EU "see the world with the same eyes," according to European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen. And the feeling appears mutual. "Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said. In that spirit, and with both parties grasping for an effective way to deal with Donald Trump and his tariffs, von der Leyen floated the idea that Canada could become the European Union's first associate member on Thursday. Given the concept of associate membership does not yet exist, it's difficult to determine exactly what that would mean. Germany proposed a similar arrangement for Ukraine earlier this year, only for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reject the idea on the grounds that the country wants full membership. Though not officially recognized as associates, there are plenty of countries that have strong ties or agreements with the bloc. DW looks at some of them and how they work. EFTA and single market access — Norway, Liechtenstein, Iceland Under this model, the ‘European Free Trade Association (EFTA)' countries are part of the EU's internal market, so people, goods and services can move freely in the Schengen area. The three countries also follow many EU rules in areas like tourism, environment and education. But there are some key distinctions. The countries have no part in the decision-making process, bar some input into policy preparation, such as participation in expert groups. They are also not in the customs union, do not use the Euro and are not bound by the EU's common trade policy or justice laws. Iceland held a referendum on whether to go for full membership last month, but the government's push to do so failed and they remain an EFTA country. Bilateral agreements — Switzerland While it borders four EU member states (Germany, Italy, France and Austria), Switzerland has never been a full member. Instead, more than 120 bilateral deals have been agreed upon by the EU and Switzerland over the last 50 years. These relate to areas such as trade, transport, security and education. A new package of deals was finalized last year, 20 years after they were last agreed. More than 1.5 million EU citizens live and work in Switzerland, while 466,200 Swiss have gone the other way. That is possible as Switzerland is also part of theSchengen area, allowing for free movement of people across borders. Switzerland makes financial contributions to a number of EU member states that joined after expansion in 2004, mostly in the east of Europe, but it has no EU voting rights and adopts only some EU laws. Switzerland can also participate in certain EU programs and research projects, through individual negotiations. The post Brexit agreement — UK More than four years after the UK voted to leave the EU in a 2016 referendum, the two parties signed a trade and cooperation agreement. Negotiations were fraught and complex, and the UK now has limited access to the EU market and is aligned with the EU on some areas of policy and regulation, for now at least. There is no longer free movement of people from the UK to the EU or vice versa, and the UK are not in the single market or the customs union. Since the center-left Labour party replaced the Conservatives in government in 2024, talk of a return to the customs union and alignment on other selected EU policy areas has been more frequent. But any return to full member status seems unlikely for now. Stabilization and association process – Western Balkan countries The EU has not admitted a new member state since Croatia in 2013. Several nearby countries in the region are hoping to join the bloc, but must first fulfill a number of criteria under the EU's "stabilization and association process" designed for the "Western Balkans." These are: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia. Under the plan, the EU has promised to "prepare Western Balkan partners for accession through economic reforms and investment and to bring some of the benefits of EU membership to citizens in the region." States must first become official candidates for member state status by applying to the EU, with each of the member nations agreeing to them as a candidate country. Then follows a process of negotiation, such as that currently underway with Ukraine, Serbia and Montenegro. Finally, an accession treaty is prepared, which the European Commission, the European Council and the European Parliament must agree with. Only once that treaty has been signed and ratified by all member states and the candidate country will said country become an EU member. Edited by: Carla Bleiker

item.title: Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.37
It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down? Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job. In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election. The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience. But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat. Option 1: Resignation Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance. Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved the necessary majority, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years. How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up. Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor. An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years. The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no-confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers. Option 3: A confidence vote Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue. As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy. Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament. If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does. It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low. So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Airport malaria in Germany remains infrequent
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.84
Eight people are known to have contracted malaria in the vicinity of Frankfurt Airport in central Germany since July; three of them have died. Those affected are mostly employees of the airport operator Fraport. The Frankfurt Public Health Department believes the outbreak is due to "airport malaria," which occurs when a female Anopheles mosquito carrying the malaria parasite travels by aircraft to a country where the disease is not common from one where it is, bites a person and infects their red blood cells. "We are dealing with a very rare occurrence, not a new frequent disease in Germany," said Achim Hörauf, the director of the Institute for Medical Microbiology, Immunology and Parasitology at Bonn's University Hospital (UKB), in a press release. Airport malaria is very infrequent The last documented case of airport malaria in Germany before the current ones was in 2023, according to the Epidemiologisches Bulletin of the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an online journal that regularly provides information on infectious diseases and public health. Normally, those with the disease in Germany were infected elsewhere and brought it back during a long-haul trip. But a mosquito can make its way to Germany as a "stowaway" if it was trapped in a suitcase or in clothing. Hörauf said that under certain circumstances, it might be able to survive in warmer areas of an airport. Frankfurt cases are of dangerous malaria tropica According to a UKB press release, the cases in Frankfurt involve malaria tropica, which is considered to be the most dangerous and potentially life-threatening form of malaria. To contract the disease, a person needs to be bitten by a female anopheles mosquito infected with the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. This pathogen passes to the human and then attacks the red blood vessels. "Simply put, it can lead to many small blockages in the blood vessels," explained Hörauf. "Depending on which organ is affected, various serious complications can arise." Fluid can accumulate in the lungs, or neurological damage can result if the blood vessels of the brain are affected. Acute kidney failure is also possible. About 20% of those affected die if the disease is left untreated. "If a diagnosis is made in time, there can be targeted treatment," Hörauf said. "If the disease is overlooked, however, it can very quickly take a severe turn." At first, symptoms are not specific, resembling those of the flu: sudden high fever, chills, headaches and muscle pain. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are also possible. Frankfurt authorities tell public to seek advice in case of symptoms The Frankfurt Public Health Department has advised anybody who lives or works near Frankfurt Airport to seek medical attention immediately if they experience any such symptoms. Rapid diagnostic tests can provide evidence of malaria in human blood and then a blood test can help to confirm this. The RKI says treatment should take place at a hospital, which has expertise in tropical medicine. As summer comes to an end and temperatures cool in Germany, particularly at night, the conditions are becoming less favorable for mosquitoes and malaria parasites. However, experts warn that there could still be other cases of malaria in Germany despite the cooler weather. Plasmodium falciparum has an incubation period of seven to 15 days, so more than two weeks can pass between a mosquito transmitting malaria to somebody by biting them and the onset of symptoms. According to Hörauf, the biggest challenge is to ensure that people think malaria could be a possibility even if they have not traveled abroad. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.82
Berlin has a reputation for being unruly. When Joseph Goebbels was appointed the Nazi Party's district leader in 1926, he described Berlin as "the reddest city in Europe besides Moscow." From the Tailors' Revolution of 1830 and the barricades of 1848, to the rise of a vast industrial working class later in the 19th century, revolution, protest and rebellion run deep throughout the city's history. While the future German philosopher and revolutionary socialist Karl Marx was still in high school in the small town of Trier in Prussia's Rhine Province, Berlin was fast becoming a center of the country's labor movement. It was during the March Revolution of 1848, a failed attempt to create a democratic German nation-state, that the General Workers' Brotherhood was founded, one of the first workers' organizations to become active in Germany. By the 1870s and 1880s, major industries from mechanical and railway engineering to ready-made clothing were located in the city. As the working-class population grew, this, in turn, impacted the city's political culture. "It became more populist in a positive sense: moving away from the traditional, elitist politics of the bourgeois liberals who had long dominated Berlin, and toward the inclusion of ordinary people, since at least men were now also important voters," Axel Weipert, a historian and author of the book "Red Berlin" (2019), tells DW. Emergence of a radical labor movement Berlin's labor movement became increasingly radical, partly in response to heavy-handed repression under the Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Although Bismarck created the first modern welfare state to try and undercut the rising popularity of the socialist movement, he also introduced laws banning socialist and communist organizations, newspapers and public gatherings, as well as independent trade unions. After Bismarck resigned in 1890, the anti-socialist laws were repealed, and the ideas of Karl Marx and his fellow revolutionary socialist Friedrich Engels became the ideology of what Weipert describes as a "genuine mass movement" in Berlin. The Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany's oldest political party, was formed out of a merger between the General German Workers' Association and the Social Democratic Workers' Party in 1875. Before World War I, the SPD was able to win far higher vote shares in Berlin than elsewhere in the country. In 1914, the labor movement was seriously discredited when the SPD leadership and the trade unions decided not to oppose the war pushed by Kaiser Wilhelm II. But from 1916 onwards, Berlin became the center of mass labor strikes against the war. One of the earliest strikes was against the trial of anti-war socialist campaigner Karl Liebknecht. Together with Rosa Luxemburg and other left-wing radicals, Liebknecht founded the Spartacus League in Berlin, an underground group that later became the Communist Party of Germany (KPD). Triggered by war-weariness, severe food shortages and economic ruin, around half a million Berlin workers joined the January Strike of 1918. Supported by the Spartacus League, the anti-war strike was led by the Revolutionary Stewards, a clandestine network of factory workers and trade unions from large munitions and metal-working factories. The same group became a core organizing force behind the overthrow of the Kaiser in Berlin on November 9, 1918. From left-wing unity to division In the chaotic, war-torn city gripped by violent revolution, the Spartacist Uprising of 1919 was launched to overthrow Germany's provisional government and establish a republic of workers' councils. Its violent suppression, which resulted in scores of deaths — Liebknecht and Luxemburg were both murdered by soldiers of right-wing paramilitary militias — permanently fractured the political left. As the capital of the newly founded Weimar Republic, Berlin remained a hotbed of radical politics in the interwar period. This was especially true in neighborhoods with large numbers of tenement buildings, such as Wedding, Kreuzberg and Neukölln, where thousands of factory workers lived in squalid conditions. Berlin's many large factories also created shared interests and laid the groundwork for collective action. "Bloody May" in 1929 saw brutal attacks on illegal May Day demonstrations, which left over 30 people dead. The SPD police president of Berlin had issued a ban on all public demonstrations for May Day, which the KPD defied. In response, the police opened fire on protestors in the streets and also shot through windows in residential buildings, primarily in the working-class districts of Wedding and Neukölln. During the Great Depression era, the SPD lost much of its support between 1929 and 1933, as joblessness ravaged the city. "Unemployment is critical — it meant that men were no longer attached to the SPD-led factory floor and trade union and the social bonds of these spaces and organizations," explains Pamela Swett, a historian at the University of Rhode Island. "Unmoored from the rhythm of daily life, men sought new bonds — new ways to feel self-respect and camaraderie with others." Some joined the KPD, which became known as the "Party of the Unemployed." Others joined far-right paramilitary groups such as the Nazi stormtroopers. From student sit-ins to the housing crisis After the Nazis took power in 1933, many of the labor movement leaders were killed or exiled. Then, in the aftermath of World War II, Berlin was divided into two separate political systems. East Berlin became the capital of the communist German Democratic Republic. Isolated from the Federal Republic of Germany, West Berlin deindustrialized, the labor movement weakened, and the SPD moved to the right. During the Cold War, many left-leaning young men moved to West Berlin to evade military service. This intensified the student movement, the center of which was Berlin's Free University (Freie Universität). It was there, in leafy southwest Berlin, that historic sit-ins were held to protest the perceived authoritarianism of the government and the presence of former Nazi officials in positions of power. The fatal shooting of student Benno Ohnesorg by a police officer during a demonstration against the visiting Shah of Iran in 1967 radicalized a generation that led the widespread protests of 1968. In the early 1970s, a housing shortage led parts of the student movement, as well as apprentices and young migrant families, to squat in West Berlin's empty buildings. "You have migrant laborers and young laborers participating, so this was part of working-class rebellion against capitalist housing," says Ralf Hoffrogge, a labor movement historian at Berlin's Free University. Today, as gentrification sweeps the city, Berlin is home to the strongest and most radical tenants' movements in Germany. In a 2021 referendum, 59% of voters in the city approved the expropriation of property from private real-estate companies. Hoffrogge was part of the campaign, and his 2025 book "Loud Berlin" ("Das laute Berlin") explores how the housing crisis has become a catalyst for a "socialist renaissance" in the city. "It's not Berlin tenants against Berlin landlords. It's tenants against global capital. I think people have started to realize these contradictions, and this is why class-based policy concepts are becoming popular again." Edited by: Brenda Haas

item.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.81
"People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW bluntly. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway." According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year. Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered cars in the country. The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%. Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall The boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm in the German government, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes. Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 euro-cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 euro-cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax. With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club. The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite." Energy tax revenue in decline "If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses. According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year. In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050. Pressure to reform road funding "The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report stated. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, the report added. In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023. Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits. In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act. That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued. Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said. How other countries are responding Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation. In the UK, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro-cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids. Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees. In Switzerland, meanwhile, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations. Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls. Are road tolls the answer? In Germany, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account. "The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster. "If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report. Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period. "If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.75
French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced deeper cooperation between their countries in many areas, including defense, energy, and business. The two leaders made the announcement on Sunday from Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a small French territory just off the Atlantic coast of Canada. According to a statement from Carney's office, the leaders discussed aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing. This move is another step in Canada's accelerating turn toward Europe, as both countries are experiencing strained relations with the US. The meeting between Macron and Carney follows up on Carney's visit to Brussels, during which the EU offered Canada "associate member" status. What did the leaders say? "We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so," Macron said at the joint news conference, adding that France and Canada would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy. "We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for free and fair trade, the science on which our decisions are based, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," Macron said. "And this is what very deeply unites Canada and France, Canada and the European Union." Meanwhile, Carney said: "The time has come to tighten our links between Canada and France, between Canada and the European Union — links based on the values we share." "History remembers those who... defend their sovereignty, those who stay true to their values," Carney stressed in his speech. However, he also proposed that France, Canada, the United States and China work together on artificial intelligence. Where is Saint Pierre and Miquelon? Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French overseas territory, is located off the coast of Newfoundland and has a population of fewer than 6,000 people. It is France's only remaining possession in North America and a remnant of its former vast territories in what are now Canada and the United States. One of Canada's provinces, Quebec, has French as its sole official language. Macron's three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon is the first by a French president in over a decade. Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to visit the territory. The leaders' meeting comes at a time of strained relations with the US. Ottawa has strongly rejected President Donald Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state. Last Monday, Trump posted a map of North America on social media. The map depicted Canada, Greenland, Mexico, much of Central America and the Caribbean, and Iceland in the colors of the US flag. Several French overseas territories were also included in the image, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon. However, upon his arrival in the territory late Saturday, Macron reaffirmed its status as French territory and dismissed "strange ideas" on the subject. Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.52
Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday. Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia. What happened at Luxembourg airport? National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt. Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue. The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft. Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible. "We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers. Have other drones been spotted? Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days. "This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said. Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark. "We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said. European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights. There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Beethoven and Andy Warhol: Rebel icons on show in Bonn
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.50
Andy Warhol portrait of Ludwig van Beethoven offers an unprecedented visual take on the great composer. Warhol's 1987 silkscreen dispenses with the stern face usually seen on historical portraits and statues of the musical genius. Instead, Warhol uses pop art's vivid colors and striking visual language to turn Beethoven into a modern icon. Originally conceived as a commercial work for the pop art guru's New York City studio, known as The Factory, the image was produced in a limited edition of 60 and proved to be one of the most innovative artistic engagements with Ludwig van Beethoven in the 20th century. Warhol created the famous Beethoven color silkscreen prints just a few weeks before his sudden death on February 22, 1987. The series is among his final works. How did Warhol approach Beethoven as a subject? And in what context did the work emerge in its numerous colored variations? A special exhibition, "Beethoven by Warhol," on show until April 2027 at the Beethoven House in Bonn — the composer's birthplace — explores these questions and more. Like-minded geniuses? The exhibition presents rare works that visitors would otherwise never get to see. Over the course of three years, the team of curators at the Beethoven House and Archive Bonn, led by Malte Boecker, unearthed these valuable pieces from the depths of archives and private collections. Alongside Warhol's iconic depiction of Beethoven, visitors can see drawings the artist did while searching for his Beethoven motif in Bonn. There are also proofs of prints that document his exploration of the series' color scheme. The curators highlight an elaborately crafted Beethoven print on canvas, which belongs to an anonymous collector from the Rhineland. Curator Silke Bettermann said that, with such works, "Warhol tells us: Look here! This man, Beethoven, is completely modern! He's a superstar!" Warhol's approach to subjects Whenever something looks effortless and easy, there's almost always a great deal of work behind it. The same is true of Warhol's Beethoven series. In his research process, Warhol compared numerous depictions of the composer before developing his own concept. He also did drawings based on likenesses of Beethoven, including the statue of the composer at Münsterplatz in Bonn. Ultimately, Warhol decided to base his work on the iconic portrait by Joseph Karl Stieler, painted in 1820 on commission from the Frankfurt couple Franz and Antonie Brentano — a merchant family and patrons of the arts who were friends with the composer. The portrait sought to capture not only Beethoven's outward appearance but also his rebellious personality. Warhol adopts the graphic design of Stieler's work, transforming its colors and overlaying it with a handwritten Beethoven score. However, rather than using the notes of the "Credo" of the "Missa Solemnis," as Stieler did, he chose music from the "Moonlight Sonata," probably Beethoven's most famous work. "Warhol's Beethoven speaks to us quite literally through and by means of his music," curator Silke Bettermann told DW. Sports star at Beethoven House Bonn-based Warhol gallerist Hermann Wünsche played a key role in the creation of Warhol's Beethoven works. He not only visited the artist in New York, but also brought him to the Rhineland several times. It's thanks to Wünsche that the artist created numerous Germany-related pieces, including the portraits of Chancellor Willy Brandt from 1976 and soccer star Toni Schumacher, whom Warhol portrayed in 1983. The exhibition's organizers brought the work depicting Schumacher to Bonn — on loan from the soccer star's private collection. The former goalkeeper himself also paid a visit. In 1983, Schumacher sat as a model for Warhol. "It really gave me goosebumps!" he said. Schumacher recalls his meeting with the US artist: "Back then, in the mid-1980s, in all modesty, I was already a star, too. But then Andy Warhol came along. And when we were together in the same room, I felt like I was looking at a superstar, so I took a bit of a back seat." Warhol and music Also on display for the first time at the Beethoven House is a unique collection of record covers designed by Warhol, assembled by Belgian collector and Warhol expert Guy Minnebach. Over the course of three decades, Andy Warhol designed strikingly beautiful and individual covers for more than 50 records. The range extends from a relatively classical, yet already whimsically playful, Mendelssohn record featuring Vladimir Horowitz, whom Warhol also knew personally, to the legendary jeans cover with a real zipper for The Rolling Stones' "Sticky Fingers" (1971) and the famous banana album cover for The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967). According to eyewitness accounts, music played continuously at Warhol's studio. His record covers offer a glimpse into the artist's musical tastes. Beethoven, notably, is not among them. Wolfram Weimer: 'We need more Beethoven' The Warhol exhibition is the prelude to an important event at the Beethoven House. In March 2027, people around the world will commemorate the 200th anniversary of Beethoven's death with a special edition of the Beethoven Festival. "This exhibition is a wonderful opening to the Beethoven commemorative year," Wolfram Weimer, Germany's state minister for culture and media, told DW. As patron of the exhibition at the Beethoven House, he traveled to Bonn to see it and speak at the opening ceremony. "Today, we need more Beethoven," he said during his speech. "Beethoven was not only a musical genius who delighted the world with the greatest musical works of art imaginable," Weimer said. The composer also embodied the idea of freedom: "He was a rebel, he broke norms, and he questioned the power structures of his time. He was a messenger of freedom, and that is a good message for us today. We need more freedom today, too!" This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Dual citizenship means Germany now in competition for talent
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.20
When Jürgen Klopp named his oversize squad for Germany for the upcoming international break, a number of other national team coaches will have taken notice. Among them was Mohamed Ouahbi, of Morocco, who lamented that he had already had Eintracht Frankfurt striker Younes on his radar since last season. "He had a profile that interested us. I spoke to him on the phone and explained the Morocco project to him — without making any promises," Ouahbi said. If the 23-year-old Ebnoutalib sees any action in the UEFA Nations League over the next couple of weeks, as expected, he will be cap-tied to Germany — and ineligible to play for Morocco in the future. Several players with multiple options This is by no means a unique situation. A growing number of Germany players in recent years have held another citizenship through their parents and thus have other options for their international careers. This applies to several members of Klopp's 44-man squad. Vitaly Janelt, whose father moved to Germany to play professional ice hockey, is also eligible to represent Czechia. Bambase Conte's father is from Guinea, and Josha Vagnoman has an Ivorian father. Finn Dahmen has an English mother, while fellow goalkeeper Noah Atubolu has Nigerian roots. Said El Mala's father hails from Lebanon, and Brajan Gruda's father was an Albania international. All of them were all born and raised in Germany and have represented the country at youth levels. Vagnoman has even made two senior international appearances for Germany, though he has yet to play a competitive match. High number of dual nationals There are also numerous established Germany players who could have chosen another nation.
