These include Felix Nmecha (England), Kevin Schade (Nigeria), Jamal Musiala (Nigeria, England), Karim Adeyemi (Nigeria, Romania), Jonathan Tah and Serge Gnabry (Ivory Coast), Malick Thiaw (Senegal, Finland), Nathaniel Brown (USA), Nadiem Amiri (Afghanistan), Aleksandar Pavlovic (Serbia), Waldemar Anton (Russia), Yann Aurel Bisseck (Cameroon), and Ridle Baku (DR Congo). The men's national team reflects German society as a whole: According to the Federal Statistical Office, 21.8 million of the country's approximately 83 million inhabitants have an immigrant background. "More than 40% of children in Germany under the age of 5 have a migration background. This means they will later have the option to play for one country or the other," Andreas Rettig, the managing director for sport for Germany's DFB football association, told DW prior to the 2026 World Cup. This forces the DFB to compete with other countries for talent for its national teams — and it hasn't always been successful. A prime example is Ibrahim Maza of Bayer Leverkusen. Born and raised in Berlin to an Algerian father and a Vietnamese mother, he holds not just German but also Algerian and Vietnamese citizenship. The midfielder possesses many qualities that could help Germany, yet two years ago he opted to play for Algeria and represented the "Desert Foxes" at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and the 2026 World Cup. Germany also missed out on Paul Wanner and Can Uzun. Wanner, a top prospect developed at Bayern Munich, chose Austria—his mother's home country. Can Uzun of Eintracht Frankfurt has been playing for Turkey since September 2024. Both took part in last summer's World Cup. International break a cap-tying opportunity Had Maza, Wanner and Uzun chosen Germany instead, each of them would have stood a good chance of being named to Klopp's first squad as national team coach. With this international break featuring four instead of the previous customary two matches — and to see as many players as possible, Klopp named two squads for this break — every player selected has a strong chance of getting playing time. The upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures — away against the Netherlands, home and away against Greece, and at home against Serbia — are all competitive matches. This means that, even if it wasn't the primary factor in his selection process, over the next couple of weeks, Klopp could wind up cap-tying a few more players for Germany. This article was adapted from German.

item.title: Oktoberfest opens as Munich mayor taps first beer keg
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.19
The 191st Munich Oktoberfest officially opened at noon on Saturday, with the city's new mayor tapping the festival's first barrel of beer. The annual ceremony, which takes place at midday, is always an eagerly awaited event, with no beer served until it has taken place. Relief for Munich's new mayor Green Party politician Dominik Krause needed just two strikes of the mallet for his first ceremonial tapping before handing the first liter mug of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). Krause had practiced for the occasion with a personal tapping coach. The 36-year-old had said he hoped to open the barrel with two or three strikes. His predecessor, Dieter Reiter of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), had set a high standard by regularly opening the first barrel with two strikes. After the tapping, Krause then presented the first liter of beer to Bavarian Premier Markus Söder of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). It's the first time Söder has received the ceremonial drink from a Green mayor. Cannon fire then signalled that beer may be served throughout the festival grounds. Revelers race to grab drinking spots Crowds had earlier rushed onto the Oktoberfest grounds in the southern German city of Munich shortly after the gates opened at 9 a.m on Saturday. Some visitors ran toward the beer tents to claim the best seats after waiting for several hours. Members of the first group in line said they had arrived at 7 p.m. on Friday with camping chairs, sleeping bags and emergency blankets. Organizers briefly held back sections of the crowd at the entrance, allowing people onto the grounds in stages and preventing a more concentrated rush. How big is Oktoberfest? More than 6 million people are expected to attend the 191st Oktoberfest, which runs for 16 days until October 4. The festival, known locally as the Wiesn, features beer tents, fairground rides, traditional Bavarian food and live music. Opening day was expected to bring blue skies and temperatures of up to 24 degrees Celsius (75 degrees Fahrenheit). How much is an Oktoberfest beer? A 1-liter (1.8-pint) beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90 ($17–$18.27) this year. The average price has risen by 2.38% compared with last year to €15.61. An analysis found that the average price has almost quintupled since 1985, when a liter of beer cost about 6.25 deutschmarks — equivalent to €3.20 at the fixed conversion rate. Consumer prices have risen by about 120% over the same period. Edited by: Karl Sexton If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: German-Russian relations at freezing point
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.60
For many years, Germany and Russia had a perfect partnership. Russia supplied cheap energy, which helped German industry succeed in exporting its goods worldwide. This partnership began in the early 2000s. On the German side was Chancellor Gerhard Schröder from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), followed later by Chancellor Angela Merkel of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Their counterpart was Vladimir Putin. Even when Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014, business continued as usual. It was then that the agreement to build Nord Stream 2, a direct gas pipeline between Russia and Germany designed to bypass Ukraine was signed. At the time, other European countries and the US warned that the pipeline would provide Russia with powerful leverage. The warnings proved to be correct. On February 24, 2022, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. German hopes for a stable European order, the democratization of Russia, and the continuation of its lucrative business model were shattered. How could so many German politicians be so wrong? "Shortly before the invasion, the widespread view was that there were no rational grounds for an attack on Ukraine, because the economic, military, and political costs to Russia of starting a war would be far too high," Russia expert Mario Baumann of the German Council on Foreign Relations told DW. "People [in Germany] had projected their own rationality onto Russia. They underestimated the regime's imperialist and revisionist ambitions." After that, nothing in the bilateral relationship was ever the same again. Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) spoke of a Zeitenwende (epochal shift) in foreign and security policy, in the days after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine began. Since then, the German armed forces have expanded. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the following year, "We must become capable of waging war," a statement that critics still say was an escalation of tensions. Germany ended its decades-long energy dependence on Russia and shut down Nord Stream 2. In September 2022, the pipeline was blown up. The Federal Prosecutor's Office suspects a Ukrainian group was responsible. A series of EU sanctions have long since reduced Russian-German trade relations to a minimum. Government cooperation in culture, science, and education has also practically ceased to exist. A new low point While the German government under Scholz initially hesitated to take dramatic steps on military aid to Ukraine, Friedrich Merz, then the leader of the opposition, stepped up his rhetoric. "Ukraine must win the war. Russia must lose the war," he said in 2024 as leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in parliament. In 2025, as chancellor, he then spoke of Russia's "economic exhaustion," which the West must "help bring about." But that has yet to materialize. To this day, Russia has shown no serious willingness to compromise. Meanwhile, Germany is feeling the consequences of its military support for Ukraine. The German government has long suspected Russia of being behind cyberattacks on government agencies and critical infrastructure. So when an armed drone was discovered and defused in August 2026 at Leipzig Airport close to Ukrainian transport aircraft — which transport a large portion of the military aid to Ukraine — the government was certain: For the first time, it publicly blamed the Kremlin. A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg. Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe." AfD wants to resume relations with Russia The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive. "German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves." In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig. Carry on or change course? So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts. Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution." Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners. The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Decolonizing perceptions about Africa
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.52
The Correct the Map resolution to promote map projections that more realistically reflect the true size of continents endorsed by the United Nations in New York at the beginning of September was a huge success for the African countries that led the campaign. In the General Assembly, 164 member states voted to encourage the use of Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps instead of the 16th-century Mercator projection. Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, which sponsored the Correct the Map campaign at the UN, spoke of a "feeling of pride." Correct the Map is also supported by the African Union. "Finally, Africa is fighting to regain its place in the community of nations," he told DW. "The place it has been reserved to this day is unfair. It does not correspond to Africa's reality, not in historical, geographical or economic terms." Dussey made clear that the debate about global maps was also clearly about symbolically redrawing the maps of facts and knowledge, culture and identity and redressing misperceptions about political and economic realities and power. Trump's US only state to reject UN resolution The only UN member state that rejected the resolution was the United States, whose president Donald Trump has engaged in various acts of political symbolism, having issued orders for places to be renamed on maps which he would presumaby also like to redraw Trump has signed executive orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, and Lake Ontario as Lake America. The UN resolution, meanwhile, is part of a broader, global trend, as French historian Romain Tiquet from the African Worlds Institute (IMAF) told DW. "Since the late 2000s and early 2010s, there has been a great deal of debate about the decolonization of knowledge — in universities, museums and cultural institutions, as well as within social movements and civil society." He said many questions were being explored: "Who established the categories through which we conceptualize the world? From which locations? And what power dynamics result from this? And cartography fits right into this context." Mali breaks with former colonial power France Many African states have also been trying to free the school systems from colonial influence, often for political reasons. In October 2025, the Malian government decided to remove French history from the school curriculum. The decision was made to stop teaching about the French Revolution but to focus on Malian history and the other ancient West African kingdoms. In just a few years, the country's military government has made a clean break with the former colonial power. Mali ended its military cooperation with France in 2022, and French soldiers began to withdraw from the country. Burkina Faso and Niger did the same and the three formed the Alliance of Sahel States in 2023. Philemon Mtoi from Tumaini University Makumira in Tanzania said Mali had made an important step: "As a historian, I believe that a country without a strong understanding of its own history is like a country without clear leadership and direction. This decision is important because it seeks to strengthen patriotism and foster a stronger sense of national identity." By investing in the research and preservation of African history, Mali — like Africa as a whole — was making a strong contribution to global scholarship, Mtoi explained. He spoke of "reclaiming and documenting African histories from an African perspective" and said that this was not only "an act of decolonization" but also an "important step toward intellectual independence." Mtoi said that many other African countries, such as Ghana, Namibia, South Africa and Kenya, had adopted a similar approach. He added that his own country, Tanzania, had also made major changes to the school curriculum recently. He said that "Tanzanian history and ethics" was now a compulsory subject that had replaced global history and that it would be taught in Swahili, the country's national language. The historian warned, however, that knowledge of other countries and histories should not be erased. He said it was important to acquire a profound knowledge of significant events in global history, such as the French Revolution, but that this could be done at a later stage. #NotWaiting campaign to abolish stereotypes School education in a formal setting is only one part of the puzzle. The non-profit Africa No Filter was one of the organizations behind the Correct the Map campaign. It works to challenge and change harmful narratives about Africa. In a report titled "The cost of media stereotypes to Africa," it says that "Africa could be losing up to $4.2 billion (€3.6 billion) annually in inflated interest payments due to biased media coverage." Francois Bouda, an officer for arts and culture at Africa No Filter, said that media outlets continued to portray Africa as being poor, corrupt and crisis-ridden. The new campaign #NotWaiting is meant to change this perception. "We are addressing Africans because we, too, need to change the way we view the African continent. We've accepted the image of a continent incapable of taking care of itself, one that is poor and has no opportunities. We've internalized this and come to believe it, even though many positive things are happening. First of all there has to be an internal change," said Bouda. 'Millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day' The #NotWaiting campaign is part of a larger movement, which aims to highlight positive developments and initiatives in Africa, to focus on political programs and actors, to counter crisis-reporting. It comprises figures on the continent and in the diaspora, people who are "not waiting for an external hand to dictate what path to follow," said Bouda. "This is good for Africans," he said, adding that there were many actors but that the only problem was that they "aren't visible." The campaign is about Africans themselves painting a positive picture of Africa as a continent on the move, about people sharing stories, which are not curated by international institutions or media outlets. "We've been building all along," says a video clip to promote the campaign. "From village roads to crowded cities, across the 54 countries that make up the continent, millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day." This article, to which Sandrine Blanchard and Jean-Claude Abalo contributed, was originally written in German.

item.title: Russia: Ukrainian drone strike on Moscow kills 2
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.40
Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit. Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia, despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop. Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine." "Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X. According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed. This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election. Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections." Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported. Three children killed in Kyiv region In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said. Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died. The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings. Russia's Defense Ministry said a warehouse of drone and missile maker Fire Point was struck in the Kyiv region. It also hit a cargo vessel and a postal logistics center in the Odesa region, saying both were used for military shipments. Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks. Edited by: Karl Sexton If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google by clicking here and hitting the "star" or "preferred" button, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.21
Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator. On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border. Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station. A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled. 'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukrainebegan in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system. The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet). "Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country." Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill." Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year. In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons. Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics. The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines. Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector. Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine. The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger." Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously. The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers. Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said. This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

item.title: Fact Check: False video alleges Berlin votes destroyed
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.19
Berliners will vote in state and district elections on September 20. In the days leading up to the vote, a video circulated on social media that allegedly shows a man opening postal voting envelopes and destroying ballots cast for the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD). DW Fact check reviewed more than a dozen posts sharing the footage. The posts use similar captions, presenting the video as evidence of election fraud in Germany. Several have amassed hundreds of thousands of views on X. How widely has the video spread? And is its reach driven by genuine public interest? Or is something else boosting its visibility? DW Fact check investigated the video and the accounts sharing it. Claim: A video shows a man destroying AfD ballots in Berlin with a carpet knife. One post sharing the footage claims: "A video circulating in Berlin shows a man opening mail-in voting envelopes and destroying ballots marked for the AfD, while ballots for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU are left intact. The footage appeared days after the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Berlin holds its state election on September 20." The post had received about 327,000 views when DW Fact Check reviewed it on September 18. DW Fact check: False At first glance, the ballot paper appears authentic. Its names and layout match those of the official ballot paper for the Spandau 2 constituency in western Berlin, which is publicly available online. However, there are several inconsistencies in the documents shown in the video. Berlin's state returning officer, Stephan Bröchler, told DW that the documents shown in the video are not authentic election papers from Berlin. Bröchler said the envelopes shown in the video did not match the official ones used for this election. Bröchler also noted that the way the envelopes are sealed appears suspicious. According to official guidelines issued by Berlin's election authorities, postal voters receive a voting package containing a "Wahlschein," or a voter declaration that needs to be signed, plus two envelopes and the ballot papers for the elections. For the September 20 vote, Berliners receive two ballot papers: a grey-and-blue ballot for the election to the city-state House of Representatives and an orange ballot for their District Assembly. In the video, however, the documents do not correspond to the official postal voting package. The person in the video opens a red envelope and removes a white envelope. The signed voter declaration is missing. Without it, a mail-in ballot would be invalid. The person then takes out only the grey-and-blue ballot paper for the Berlin House of Representatives from the white envelope. Although voters may choose to vote in only one of the two elections, it would be unusual for three envelopes in succession to contain only one ballot paper. However, the footage does not clearly show whether the second envelope is really empty. Another detail raises doubts about the video's authenticity: In the background, large grey bins allegedly containing postal ballots are marked with a version of Berlin's coat of arms featuring the Berlin bear. Bröchler said such features were not used by Berlin's election authorities. "Marking the ballot boxes with a Berlin bear is also unknown and uncommon here," he said. Bröchler's conclusion is clear: "It can be ruled out that any actual Berlin election documents are involved. The video is clearly intended to discredit postal voting." Has the video really gone viral? One of the accounts that shared the video has previously come under scrutiny. An investigation by the Lithuania-based research organization Debunk linked the account to the so-called "Sprinter" network, a group of X accounts. The researchers identified what they described as signs of coordinated and inauthentic activity, including unusually high posting volumes, frequent account renaming and evidence of purchased followers. Debunk said the network was used to amplify pro-Kremlin narratives. DW Fact check reviewed more than 15 other posts sharing the footage, many of them using nearly identical captions. Together, the posts had accumulated more than 3.2 million views by the time DW Fact check examined them. The accounts sharing the video also showed several suspicious characteristics. Almost all of the 15 accounts examined exhibited at least one sign of potentially inauthentic behavior, including rapid follower growth, frequent username changes or limited evidence of normal user engagement. One account, which presented itself as an independent media company based in West Asia, had more than 43,000 followers despite having been created only in April 2026. During that period, the account changed its username nine times. On their own, these characteristics do not prove that the accounts are coordinated or that the video's engagement was entirely artificially generated. They do, however, show that the video's apparent reach should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread, organic discussion on X. A pattern seen before The video resembles other false election-related claims that have circulated about Germany in recent months. Ahead of the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, DW Fact check examined a video that similarly purported to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed. The claim was false. Among other inconsistencies, all three crossed-out ballots shown in the footage carried the same name on the signed voter declaration. The envelopes had already been opened, and the ballots lacked a hole punch required for use with voting templates designed for blind and visually impaired voters. DW Fact check has also investigated and debunked numerous other false claims targeting Germany's postal voting system. Julia Smirnova, who investigates influence operations as a researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), told DW that these similarities, together with the way the new video is being disseminated, indicate that it is "highly likely" to be part of the Storm-1516 influence operation. German security authorities and researchers have attributed Storm-1516 to Russia. The operation has previously used fabricated videos, forged documents and purported eyewitness accounts to spread false narratives about elections and other political issues. In February 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry said it had indications that two fake videos alleging manipulation of AfD ballots were connected to the Storm 1516 campaign, citing similarities in their content and distribution. Edited by: Thomas Sparrow

item.title: As global crises grow, Germany cuts development aid
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.91
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan opened her speech in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, with a litany of catastrophes and suffering: floods in Nepal, heat waves, forests engulfed in flames, rivers running dry, and crop failures caused by drought. "Millions of people are facing hunger," said Radovan, of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD). "And one thing is clear: The climate crisis is threatening the entire world. No country can tackle it alone." Radovan opened the debate on the federal government's proposed 2027 budget for her ministry with a stark assessment. The budget is set to shrink for the fifth consecutive year, falling from just over €10 billion to just under €9.5 billion ($10.9 billion). In 2022, it stood at nearly €14 billion, meaning that the ministry's budget has been reduced by roughly one-third over the past half decade. How does this sharp decline square with the dramatic picture painted by Germany's development minister? She pointed to a strategy she unveiled in January, when she declared that "development policy will become an even more important pillar of German security, alongside diplomacy and defense." Funding for humanitarian aid stagnates Aid organizations reacted skeptically to this policy shift when it was first announced, and their concerns have deepened in light of the latest funding cuts. "The renewed reductions in funding for international cooperation are further exacerbating an already critical situation," said Michael Herbst of VENRO, the umbrella organization representing around 150 development and humanitarian NGOs. Herbst criticized the stagnant budget for humanitarian aid administered by the German Foreign Office. While it exceeded €3 billion in 2022, it has remained at just €1 billion since 2025. In light of worsening global crises, VENRO is calling for a change of course. "Next year, we will need to invest more in combating hunger because the conflict involving Iran and the dry summer are expected to trigger a sharp decline in agricultural yields," Herbst said, explaining the organization's demand for substantially higher funding. Ten million people left without assistance The impact of the cuts is already clearly visible, according to VENRO. A survey of its member organizations found that the number of funded projects is declining significantly. "Our sample of 34 organizations shows that, among these organizations alone, more than ten million fewer people are being reached with assistance." "And many local partner organizations, which are indispensable to effective development cooperation and humanitarian assistance, are no longer able to operate," Herbst said. He added that the full impact of these far-reaching cuts is unlikely to become apparent for another three to four years. A 'debt brake' exemption for development? The federal government's belt-tightening across virtually all ministries is a consequence of the Zeitenwende announced by 2022 Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Since then, Germany has embarked on a major military buildup, increasing its defense budget year after year, while nearly all other ministries have had to make do with significantly less funding. Herbst, a member of VENRO's executive board, is calling on the Bundestag to exempt both development cooperation and humanitarian assistance from Germany's "debt brake." "After all, exceptions have already been made for the modernization of the Bundeswehr and for military aid to Ukraine," he said. Herbst said an exemption would enable Germany to once again assume greater responsibility on the international stage. Less money, less impact? Jamila Schäfer, a member of parliament from the opposition Green Party, made a similar argument during the Bundestag debate on the Development Ministry's budget. Climate action and development cooperation, she argued, are not acts of charity but are firmly in Germany's own interest. "Germany must invest in its defense capabilities, but security is not created through investments in the defense budget alone," Schäfer said. "Those who strengthen military security while cutting support for international stability have a blind spot in their security policy." Nicolas Zippelius, a lawmaker from the governing center-right conservative alliance, the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), sees the ongoing cuts to development spending differently. In his view, every ministry must contribute to consolidating the federal budget. "Less money does not necessarily mean a smaller impact. Instead, it should encourage us to focus more clearly on priorities and critically review existing structures." Zippelius dismisses demands to exempt the Development Ministry from Germany's debt brake. "The key question is whether every euro spent is directed to where it can make the greatest difference." The Christian Democrat argues that success in development cooperation, as in other areas of policy, should be judged not by the size of the budget but by the impact it achieves. The case for more prevention Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, who heads the humanitarian and development aid organizationAction Against Hunger, has a very different view. "The cuts planned for the 2027 budget are short-sighted and dangerous. As a result, up to 22.6 million people worldwide could die by 2030," he said in a written statement to DW. Cuts to development cooperation and humanitarian aid are also fiscally short-sighted, Friedrich-Rust said. "Hunger, crises and instability generate long-term costs that far exceed the cost of prevention. Those who cut spending today are merely postponing the bill and ultimately making it much more expensive," he warned. To underscore its concerns, the Action Against Hunger alliance delivered a petition to the leaders of the governing coalition of SPD and CDU/CSU parliamentary groups on the eve of the Bundestag's budget debate. About 100,000 people added their names to the appeal, titled "Don't Balance the Budget at the Expense of Solidarity: Strengthen International Aid!" This article was originally written in German.

item.title: India news: PM Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.78
What you need to know - Indian Prime Minister Modi tells a climate conference in Delhi that developing nations are unfairly blamed for emissions - IIT Bombay professor booked over alleged caste abuse after a student killed himself - Scottish-Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without being convicted, has been granted bail - India had to replace Asian Games opening ceremony male flagbearer over missing ceremonial kit This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of some of the top headlines from across India on Saturday, September 19 and Sunday, September 20: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. Smriti Mandhana becomes leading run-scorer in women's T20I history India thrashed Bangladesh by 114 runs in the Asian Games women's cricket semi-final on Sunday, with opener Shafali Verma striking a maiden century and Smriti Mandhana becoming the all-time leading run-scorer in women's T20 internationals. Verma finished unbeaten on 100 off 49 balls, reaching triple figures off the final delivery of India's innings. It marked the first century in the history of Asian Games women's cricket, Indian wire service ANI reported, making Verma just the third Indian woman to score a T20I hundred, joining Mandhana and captain Harmanpreet Kaur. Verma called the milestone long overdue: "It took a lot of years but finally it came, so I'm happy." Mandhana reached her own landmark earlier in the innings, surpassing New Zealand's Suzie Bates to become the leading run-scorer in women's T20I history during a knock of 37 off 19 balls. The pair put on a 71-run opening partnership inside the powerplay, setting up India's total of 195-4 in 20 overs at Korogi Athletic Park in Nagoya. Bangladesh could not keep up the pace, with India bowling them out for just 81 in 15.4 overs. The result sends India into Tuesday's gold medal final against Sri Lanka. Pakistan will face Bangladesh in the bronze medal match, also on Tuesday.
WATCH — How foraging could protect Mumbai’s green lung In Mumbai, urban foraging is helping residents get in touch with nature, and this kitchen, associated with a Gujarati community, has unexpected environmental benefits. Watch the full video below: Allahabad High Court orders police to protect interfaith lesbian couple The Allahabad High Court has directed Uttar Pradesh Police to ensure protection for a Hindu-Muslim same-sex couple whose live-in relationship was being threatened by their family members, local media reported. In an order dated September 14, Justice Gautam Chowdhary held that the two women are free to live together peacefully without interference from family or anyone else, after personally interacting with the couple and finding both to be adults who had chosen to live together voluntarily, "without pressure, fear or undue influence," according to Bar & Bench, a legal news outlet. The court directed that if any obstacle arises to their relationship, the police must immediately provide security once they verify both women are of legal age and living together by choice. The petitioners' counsel told the court the couple faced serious threats to their lives from family members and needed immediate police protection. The state government opposed the plea, arguing that "there was no acceptance for same-sex relationships" and that such relationships "affect the natural and traditional framework of society," the Times of India reported. The court rejected that position, holding that living in a relationship is a fundamental right for consenting adult citizens, and that the absence of legal marriage recognition does not entitle anyone to threaten a couple's dignity or physical safety. The ruling is the latest in a line of similar Allahabad High Court orders protecting same-sex and interfaith couples in Uttar Pradesh, building on earlier decisions, which cited the Supreme Court's 2018 ruling decriminalizing homosexuality in India. IIT Bombay under fire over caste abuse allegations after student's death Mumbai police have filed a case against an IIT Bombay professor after a 20-year-old second-year student, Sahil Wakode, was found dead in his hostel room late Thursday, following allegations from his family that he had faced months of caste-based harassment. Police registered charges against Suryanarayan D. and unidentified others under India's abetment-to-suicide law and provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, local media reported. Wakode's father, Ravindra Wakode, alleged in his complaint that his son had been subjected to sustained casteist remarks and mental harassment over roughly three months, and that the professor — who was invigilating an exam Wakode was attending on the day he died — used caste-based slurs against him. The complaint also mentioned the institute's director. Similar complaints were shared by other students, according to The Wire. These allegations have not been independently established. Meanwhile, IIT Bombay claimed Wakode was found using a mobile phone during the exam, but no disciplinary action was taken. Instead, he had been counseled and assured it would not affect his academic record before he returned to his hostel room. Students at the scene allege that the professor was seen yelling at Wakode. IIT Bombay said in a statement shared by local media that "the circumstances surrounding the death are being looked into by the appropriate authorities." The case has drawn campus protests, with students at IIT Bombay demanding the resignation of both the director and the professor involved. It is reportedly the third student death by suicide at the institute this year, following earlier incidents in February and July. Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output. Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal. Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average." "In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India." He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule. The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change." The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office. Welcome back to our coverage Hello, this is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again bringing you the latest from around India this weekend. Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the inauguration of an international climate conference in New Delhi, saying that developing countries are being unfairly blamed for carbon emissions. Meanwhile, the Allahabad High Court has directed the Uttar Pradesh Police to ensure the protection of a same-sex couple living together. Finally, a professor at IIT Bombay is facing allegations of caste abuse after a young student killed himself. For this and more, follow our blog. We are pausing our coverage Over 10 years after my last day as a Delhi University student, I will wrap up this Saturday's coverage of events with the 2026 DUSU elections. But we will be back tomorrow, so follow DW for more! WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the race for recognition One of the world's most valuable rice varieties, basmati carries strong historic ties to the Punjab region, which spans both India and Pakistan. Both claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin. But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the fight over basmati rice is far from over. Watch for more: ABVP sweeps DUSU polls as student safety, identity dominate campaign The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), affiliated with the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and its ideological parent Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), won three of four central posts in this year's Delhi University Students' Union elections, with its candidate Yash Dabas coming in from behind to be elected president. Independent candidate Deepanshu Shokeen made history by winning the vice-presidential seat, defeating candidates fielded by both ABVP and the National Students' Union of India (NSUI), the student wing of the Indian National Congress. In a university facing an acute shortage of hostels, student housing and safety dominated this year's campaign. This came after the September 6 collapse of a paying-guest building in Satya Niketan, near Delhi University's South Campus, which killed seven students. High rents, non-functional hostels, and a lack of affordable lodging near campus were central issues in candidate platforms. Declaring his win, Dabas stressed the issue as he addressed the media: "We all witnessed the accident that occurred in Satya Niketan; we do not want such an incident to happen to anyone in the future, and that will be our first priority — conducting safety audits for every college, hostel, and PG." Shokeen, an NSUI rebel who ran independently, built his campaign partly around the tragedy, vowing not to wear footwear until affected students got justice. The election also unfolded in the shadow of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led satirical protest movement that organized weeks of demonstrations at Delhi's Jantar Mantar earlier this year, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged irregularities in national entrance exams. While the CJP was not involved in the DUSU race directly, the movement shaped how many voters approached the election. "Students were talking about what or ganisations stand for, whether they agree with their politics and whether voting can give them a greater say in issues concerning students," one student told news agency PTI, adding that many felt they "should not simply vote because a particular organisation has always been influential on campus." More uncertainty for Indian workers as Trump extends $100,000 H-1B visa fee US President Donald Trump has extended the $100,000 fee on H-1B visa petitions through September 2027, the White House has said — a move that will be strongly felt in India, the largest source of H-1B recipients. The extension, announced on Friday, keeps a policy first introduced in September 2025 in place. It excludes visa renewals and student visa holders transitioning to H-1B status. Trump also signed a proclamation directing tighter scrutiny of applications, instructing agencies to weigh employers' recent layoffs of American workers when reviewing petitions. The policy remains under legal challenge, with an appeals court reviewing a June ruling that found the fee unlawful. The stakes are high for India: USCIS data for fiscal year 2025 showed Indian nationals accounted for 69.9% of approved H-1B petitions, far ahead of China's 12.1%. When the fee first launched last year, it caused panic among Indian travelers, including passengers who deboarded a Delhi-bound flight fearing they'd be barred from returning. Opposition Congress party leader Pawan Khera criticized the extension on social media, warning it would make it "harder for Indian students to enter the US workforce" and could drive a "talent drain" toward the UK, Canada and Australia. He also targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his perceived camaraderie with Trump, adding: "Modi bent over backwards to appease Trump. Trump got the appeasement. India took the humiliation and the hit." Surendra Koli, acquitted in Nithari serial killings case, found dead in suspected suicide Surendra Koli, a key figure in India's notorious 2006 Nithari serial killings case who was acquitted of all charges last year, was found dead at a tea stall he operated in Haridwar. Police are treating the case as a suspected suicide. Residents discovered Koli's body inside the rented stall and alerted authorities, Haridwar City Deputy Superintendent of Police Shishupal Singh Negi told local media. No suicide note was found and the body was sent for post-mortem examination as investigators look into the circumstances. Koli first drew national attention in 2006, when he was a domestic worker at businessman Moninder Singh Pandher's home in Noida. The discovery of human remains, including children's, in a drain behind Pandher's house sparked a major investigation and nationwide outrage. Koli was convicted and sentenced to death in multiple cases beginning in 2009. In October 2023, the Allahabad High Court acquitted both Koli and Pandher for lack of evidence. Two key observations were made: Koli's confession was inadmissible, as it was extracted after a long, unauthorized interrogation in police custody without adequate legal safeguards, and the prosecution could not prove that the remains uncovered from the "open, public" drain were based solely on Koli's statements. The decision was upheld by India's Supreme Court in late 2025. Reports suggest he moved to the northern city of Haridwar after the acquittal. Police identified Koli through an Aadhaar card found on his body. India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan. Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer. Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India. "I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony. The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue." The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4. Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team. A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway. Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody. The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail. Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding. He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017. He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued. Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary. "Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture." Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed. What did the court say in its ruling? In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon." The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached. Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported. "I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison." Welcome to our coverage Hello! This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the big news from and about India this weekend. We lead our coverage with the news that British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal, who had been detained in India for almost nine years without conviction, has been granted bail. A UN panel in 2022 recognized it as a case of arbitrary detention, putting the Indian government's human rights record under the microscope. The Asian Games kick off in Japan on Saturday, but it's not all smooth sailing for the Indian delegation's preparations. India has announced a last-minute change of its male flagbearer for the opening ceremony after star shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor's ceremonial kit reportedly went missing. Finally, counting is underway in elections for the Delhi University Student Union, this time under the shadow of the Cockroach Janata Party protests and the collapse of a building in the student hub of Satya Niketan. For the latest on these stories and more, follow our blog.

item.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.73
A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water. Experts have identified these and many other visual signaturesin the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude that there's an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk. One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill. Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills. There are likely several other spills that we don't know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an "ecological catastrophe" and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems. "People should be concerned," Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken "a very, very heavy toll on the environment," she said, with the damage now reaching new scales. Where is the oil spreading? Greenpeace identified five major oil slicks earlier this week with a total visible area of 240 square kilometers (about 90 square miles) in the Strait of Hormuz. That's about four times the size of Manhattan. These patches of oil floating on the ocean's surface are getting smaller — now about 80 square kilometers — according to more up-to-date satellite images, as weather conditions have likely made the slicks disperse. But that does not mean the ecological impact is any less severe, Noelle said. "Oil can also sink into the sediment and impact the ecosystems for years and years." What's concerning is where the slicks were identified. One was found near Musandam National Park, a protected area in Oman that's home to coral reefs, sea life and important breeding grounds for sea birds. Another is close to Iran's Minab River Delta and its protected mudflats and mangrove forests. This kind of damage can take decades for ecosystems to recover from. Tracking an unclear picture It's hard to say exactly how far the oil has reached and how severe the damage is. "What we have put out is the conservative estimate," Noelle said. "It might be worse. It's definitely not better." Greenpeace and other environmental organizations are relying on satellite images provided by the Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. They're part of the European Union's Earth observation program and are publicly available. There are also private satellite providers such as Planet Labs that tend to have higher-resolution images. But they've limited access to satellite imagery during the war to prevent their data from being used for military targeting. And there are limits to on-the-ground reports too. "We don't have a lot of information coming from the country itself, both in Iran as well as the Gulf states," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher who uses open-source methods at the Dutch peace organization Pax, told DW. "There is quite restrictive policies of people posting imagery from what's happening on the shore." The toll on wildlife and people Oil pooling into the Gulf poses a number of threats — both to biodiversity and to humans. Oil can be deadly for seabirds. It coats their feathers, reducing their natural waterproofing and buoyancy, making it harder to stay afloat, fly, and hunt for food. Even small amounts of oil can damage eggs too, causing them not to hatch or to be born with deformities. Mangrove habitats, which provide safe harbor for coastal species, are also hit hard. "Mangroves have aerial roots, and the oil is covering these roots like a film and actually hindering the mangroves in exchanging gases," Noelle said. "They're kind of suffocated by the oil. Most of the time, it leads to the trees dying." The risks extend to people, as well. Coastal communities rely on fish that die off after being exposed to oil. And oil spills contaminate water used for Gulf states' drinking supply. Desalination — or converting seawater into drinkable water — is where 90% of drinking water in Kuwait comes from, along with about 86% in Oman and 70% in Saudi Arabia. Cleanup is no easy fix. "It's unlikely that it will be addressed quickly, because of the war," Zwijnenburg said. "War in general makes it very difficult to respond fast to these kind of emergencies. There are a range of limitations because of the military movement, because of mines — so it's very difficult to get vessels and cleanup operations to start." Environmental groups have pointed to the war in Iran — and the rising scale of oil spills it has caused — as further evidence that the world needs to move away from its dependence on fossil fuels. "The most sustainable long-term damage prevention for things like that would be to reduce and ultimately end our dependency on oil and gas," Noelle said. "Because, as long as our energy systems and transport routes are centered around fossil fuels, there will be a continued environmental risk." Edited by: Sarah Steffen

item.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.60
Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing. The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26. "This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone." How the disaster unfolded The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years. The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow. Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours. How did this happen? It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events. Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades. Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it. Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable. In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean. An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater. Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure. A disaster beyond adaptation Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one. Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation. The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in. "When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said. "Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come." Edited by: Sarah Steffen

item.title: Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.14
Paris will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities closed a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the French Foreign Ministry said on Sunday. "This new attack against France's cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and unacceptable," the ministry's spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement. What do we know about the center's closure? Earlier on Sunday, Iranian authorities announced the closure of a French language center in Tehran following a judicial order from the prosecutor's office. "The illegal center affiliated with the French embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, was closed," the judiciary's Mizan news website said, referring to the French Language Center (CLF). The Iranian judiciary accused the center of conducting "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions". It also accused the center of having "abused its status as a language training facility" and of having sought to "identify and build networks among the country's elite figures while facilitating their departure." Tensions between Paris and Tehran France has previously dismissed such allegations. The country claims that there has been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as it has sought to increase support for and contact with Iran's civil society following the crackdown on protests at the beginning of this year. Tensions between Tehran and Paris have been escalating in recent years. Last month, France expelled two Iranian diplomats in response to the brief detention and prohibition of two French envoys to the Islamic Republic. Tehran accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs. Diplomats said Iran was also upset by a recent social media post from French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot commemorating the fourth anniversary of Mahsa Amini's death, which sparked protests nationwide. In response, on Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi called the post "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of slaughtering 1.5 million Algerians during Algeria's war of independence. The two ministers are scheduled to meet on Tuesday at the United Nations' annual gathering of world leaders. Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah Don't let the algorithm hide the news.
