item.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.05
Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media. A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK. She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain. What did Greer's husband say about her death? Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life." Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness. He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together. "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated. Who was Bonnie Greer? Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers. Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings. She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career. Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer. Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities. She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play. Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time". Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time. She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

item.title: The Right Way to Sanction Russia
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.71
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Western countries responded with aggressive economic restrictions, freezing Russia’s official foreign exchange reserves, placing export controls on critical technology, and sanctioning scores of its political, military and business leaders. Yet more than four years later, the war is still going on, and Western sanctions have inflicted only limited pain on the Russian economy. Russia continues to trade oil and other commodities, recently receiving a massive windfall as the closing of the Strait of Hormuz caused global oil prices to soar. These profits are raising the government’s tax revenue at a critical time, helping it fund the war in Ukraine and stabilize the country’s financial markets. If sanctions were looking ineffective before, Russia’s economic rebound since the start of the United States’ and Israel’s war with Iran have only strengthened that perception. But it is wrong to write off sanctions as a policy tool. When Western policymakers portray them as a wasted effort or counterproductive, their governments are playing right into Moscow’s hands. And they are discounting the enormous strain that sanctions could still place on the Russian system if properly enforced. By reducing the flow of hard currency into Russia, sanctions have the potential to send the ruble into a spiral of depreciation, which in turn would send inflation soaring and destabilize the country’s broader economy. It is not too late to make sanctions effective. One-fifth of Russia’s GDP is directly linked to oil and gas extraction, and exports account for nearly one-third of government revenues. Russia evades Western oil sanctions primarily by using a shadow fleet of oil tankers, and that fleet is vulnerable to European pressure. It passes through European-controlled waterways, replenishes its numbers with European-owned ships, and can be forced to engage with a Western-dominated insurance industry. All of this gives Europe the power to restrict the fleet’s operations, and thereby drastically reduce Moscow’s ability to finance its ruinous war. THE RISE OF THE SHADOW FLEET The sanctions that the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada placed on Russia in early 2022 ran the gamut. They included export controls on sensitive goods such as semiconductors, computers, and lasers as well as the freezing of Russian foreign exchange reserves held by Western central banks. Yet efforts to curtail Russia’s oil exports back then were limited. The world economy was still rebounding from the COVID-19 pandemic, oil demand was strong and rising, and Russian oil accounted for roughly one-tenth of global supply. Western countries did not want to drive up prices by embargoing Russian oil, but the mere fear that they might do so caused oil prices to surge anyway, delivering enormous profits to Moscow. Russia’s current account surplus, or the amount by which its export receipts exceeded its import payments, soared to an all-time high of $235 billion in 2022. Within one year, Russia had nearly recouped the foreign exchange reserves that were frozen by Western countries. Western countries needed to figure out a way to prevent Moscow from generating large amounts of cash from oil exports without causing global prices to spike. Many oil and commodity analysts worried that any attempt to take Russian oil off global markets could lift crude prices from their prewar baseline of around $75 per barrel to $200 or higher, allowing Russia to make enormous profits from its remaining exports even if the volume of exports were lower. Such a substantial price increase would almost certainly drive the world into recession. The solution the G-7 came up with in December 2022 was an oil price cap. Around 70 percent of the vessels shipping Russian oil were Western-owned and close to 90 percent used Western insurance, financing, and brokering services. G-7 members, Australia, and the EU agreed to allow Russian exporters to use those services—but only if the crude oil they were selling was priced below $60 per barrel. There were also separate price ceilings for high-value refined products, such as diesel, and low-value refined products, such as naphtha, which is used in refining and in the production of plastics. The idea was to set the caps high enough that Russia would continue to export oil but low enough to constrain its revenue. Together with a European ban on purchasing any seaborne Russian oil regardless of price, the cap immediately reoriented the global oil trade. Suddenly, Russia was selling most of its crude oil to Asian markets, especially China and India, where buyers were able to negotiate prices well below those of Western grades. By January 2023, Russian crude was selling for almost 40 percent less than the global benchmark, depriving Russia of billions in profits each month. The country’s current account surplus began to decline, falling to $50 billion in 2023 and bouncing back only slightly to $63 billion in 2024. One-fifth of Russia’s GDP is directly linked to oil and gas extraction. Yet Russia found ways around the cap as time wore on. Because enforcement depended on Western ownership of the vessels shipping Russian oil, Russia could evade the restrictions by loading crude exports onto ships flying third-country flags but controlled, through a labyrinth of shell and holding companies, by Moscow. By 2023, the shadow fleet was expanding by about seven oil tankers per month. Around half the ships were purchased from Western owners, most of them based in Greece. The EU attempted to block such transfers in a December 2023 sanctions package, but the sales continued, although they are now routed through shell companies before reaching Russia. Western countries eventually cracked down on the shadow fleet, sanctioning large numbers of vessels known to carry Russian oil subject to the price cap. The United States led the way, placing almost 200 ships on its sanctions list in the final days of the Biden administration, and the EU and the United Kingdom followed suit soon after. When a tanker is on Washington’s sanctions list, in particular, any entity that does business with it risks exclusion from the U.S. dollar payment system. Losing access to that system would be so debilitating that the mere threat of these secondary sanctions is enough to deter most companies from doing business with sanctioned entities. Yet this success proved short-lived. The United States stopped sanctioning additional ships under President Donald Trump, even as the EU’s and the United Kingdom’s sanctions lists grew to more than 600 vessels. Without the threat of U.S. secondary sanctions, the 524 vessels that currently are subject to EU and British but not American sanctions have continued to ship Russian oil unimpeded. As of today, the shadow fleet constitutes around two-thirds of the tanker traffic out of Russia’s Baltic ports, which makes up about half the country’s seaborne oil exports. The Trump administration did sanction Russia’s two largest oil producers, Lukoil and Rosneft, in October 2025, which drove down the price of Russian oil. But it undid that progress a few months later by granting multiple waivers to buyers of Russian oil as global prices were rising amid the war with Iran. With these waivers in place and much of the shadow fleet operational, Russia was soon able to export oil on its own terms and profit from the price spikes. By April, the discount on Russian oil relative to global prices had all but vanished. Moscow’s oil tax revenues from April through July were $14 billion higher than they were a year earlier. TIGHTENING THE SCREWS To put real pressure on Russia’s oil revenues, Western countries must defang the shadow fleet. Washington has been dragging its heels on sanctioning additional vessels in the fleet, however, and a new piece of legislation, the so-called Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act—approved by a wide margin by the Senate in August and currently under consideration in the House of Representatives—will probably not make a significant difference. The bill would give the executive branch new authority to impose tariffs on importers of Russian oil, but there is little reason to think this would have much effect; the Trump administration’s 25 percent tariff on India has not stopped the country from importing Russian oil. Although the bill would pave the way for the United States to sanction shadow fleet vessels directly, the Trump administration has so far refused to enact such measures and may continue to do so. That leaves the task of taking on the shadow fleet to Europe. Earlier EU and British sanctions on their own have not meaningfully restricted Russian exports, but that is only because Europe has left critical gaps in its enforcement regime. Until now, Europe has been reluctant to expand its sanctions on Russia. It is now time to close those gaps, starting with the continued supply of Greek and other oil tankers to Russia. The ships in the shadow fleet are around five years older than the average operational oil tanker because their owners want to minimize their losses in the event the ships are sanctioned. As these vessels approach the end of their service lives, keeping the fleet’s numbers steady requires frequent replacements. Until now, the single largest source of those replacements has been Greek ship owners. The EU forbade sales of such tankers to Russian nationals and entities in a sanctions package introduced in December 2023, but European vessels are still making their way to Russian buyers. Brussels now needs to extend the prohibition to any transaction conducted through holding companies that ends in the transfer of a vessel to the shadow fleet. New regulations should oblige European vessel owners to sell only to reputable buyers approved jointly by the EU and the United Kingdom and to provide tracking information for vessels after they are sold. Of course, there are many other sellers from whom Russia can buy tankers, but finding alternatives for such a large number of its purchases would be more costly and take more time. Europe has substantial economic power and a strong legal system, and it can use both to impose consequences on third countries that enable the shadow fleet’s operations. To hide their connection to Russia, ships in the shadow fleet are usually flagged in other countries—ones that do not require tankers to hold insurance. International maritime treaties, however, allow states to demand that vessels navigating their territorial waters adhere to certain requirements, including coverage by a reputable insurer. The EU and the United Kingdom should pressure flag states to enforce those rules. They could threaten to cut aid to countries that fail to verify the insurance coverage of the ships they register, for instance, or make clear that these countries could face legal action in the event of an oil spill or other accident. If flag states start enforcing insurance requirements, many of Russia’s aging tankers would be rendered obsolete because they are insufficiently seaworthy to be covered by reputable insurers. And because Western companies dominate the shipping insurance market, most of the ships that qualify for insurance plans would purchase them from Western firms, making it easier to enforce the G-7 oil price cap. European countries would also have legal grounds to interdict old, poorly maintained ships that pose immediate environmental dangers. Such action is not as escalatory as it may sound. Countries including Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom have all stopped, inspected, and occasionally seized shadow fleet vessels over the past two years, but these interdictions have yet to invite any overt retaliation by Russia. NO TIME LIKE THE PRESENT Cutting off Russia’s supply of ships and forcing vessels to meet the regulatory requirements of Western insurers would go a long way toward reducing the shadow fleet’s evasion of price caps. Once those means of enforcement are in place, Europe can then go further in restricting Russia’s oil profits by lowering the price caps on refined products. Right now, the caps on high- and low-value refined products are set at fixed dollar amounts that are well below market prices, but the EU and the United Kingdom should have a plan in place for adjusting the caps after the Strait of Hormuz reopens and oil prices normalize. The preferred model should be the cap on crude prices established in 2025, set at 15 percent below the market prices over the previous six months. An automatic adjustment of this kind would allow Europe to offer consistent guidance to well-intentioned companies engaged in the oil trade and to accommodate frequent swings in energy prices without needing every EU member state to approve every change to fixed-rate price caps. EU policymakers have little to lose from implementing these measures. They are designed not to confront Russia directly, but instead to focus Europe’s coercive power on flag states and on ship owners inside the EU. If applied correctly, they should not result in increased global energy prices, either, because they would preserve Russia’s volume of exports. But Moscow’s revenues from those exports would be limited, because more of the Russian oil trade would be pushed from the shadow fleet to legitimate tankers that are subject to European price caps. Until now, Europe has been reluctant to expand its sanctions on Russia, for fear that such steps could be escalatory. But policymakers’ appetite for bolder measures is growing amid the United States’ inaction, Russia’s increasingly effective evasion of sanctions, and rising concern that the war could spread beyond Ukraine. The absence of action, meanwhile, hands Moscow an easy win. Russia will continue to replace aging tankers with newer ones and collect enormous oil profits from maritime trade that will feed directly into its war machine in Ukraine. Europe has policy levers it can pull to stop the shadow fleet, and that is an opportunity it cannot afford to pass up. item.title: The Emerging U.S.-China Détente
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.22
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump met in Beijing, in May, they agreed that their two countries should build a constructive relationship of strategic stability. Although many observers in Washington responded skeptically to this new framework, dismissing it as empty words, it marks the first time in more than a decade that China and the United States established a consensus about how to define the relationship that leaders on both sides broadly recognize. Strategic stability does not refer to nuclear détente; rather, it suggests a new equilibrium in which both sides can avoid further deterioration of the relationship and even expand cooperation where interests align. Leaders in Beijing do not expect that this new framework can resolve most of the differences between China and the United States or that it can stop new frictions from emerging. In June, for example, the U.S. Department of Defense placed more Chinese companies—including private-sector giants Alibaba, Baidu, and BYD—on its list of firms involved in civil-military fusion activities, barring the Pentagon from contracting with them. In retaliation, China placed ten U.S. entities on its dual-use export control list, which prevents any company from supplying them with items that have the potential for both military and civilian use. But Beijing hopes that a consensus built around strategic stability can help China and the United States manage their differences more effectively and that it will prevent the worst outcomes: military conflict or a new cold war. So far, ongoing friction has not derailed the overarching consensus established in May. By keeping sanctions and countermeasures relatively limited, Beijing and Washington have avoided dangerous escalation and kept the relationship moving forward. The goal of the new diplomatic framework between Beijing and Washington is a pragmatic one. It aims to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations rather than try to achieve an unlikely grand bargain that would resolve all conflict. It also represents a changing approach in Beijing to dealing with the United States. Unlike in the past, when China rejected U.S. frameworks focused on competition, it is now willing to recognize that the fundamental nature of U.S.-Chinese relations is competitive. Allies or partners, after all, would not set strategic stability as the overarching goal of their relationship; only competitors, or even adversaries, need to do so. Beijing’s willingness to accept a formulation to manage, rather than exclude, competition shows that it is gaining confidence and seeing itself more as an equal to Washington. Adopting this confident mindset could lead China to act with more restraint in its dealings with the United States—which could in turn bring a further degree of calm to the relationship. It now appears plausible that bilateral relations have turned a corner and entered a more stable phase. Although fundamental challenges remain that could cause new turbulence, the peak tensions of the past eight years may well be receding. The upcoming leaders’ summit in late September, when Xi and Trump are scheduled to meet in Washington, is a chance to further move the relationship forward. The two leaders can now add more concrete measures to support this new framework of strategic stability, including taking steps to reduce economic friction, increase military-to-military communications, improve crisis management mechanisms, expand citizen exchanges, and offer reassurances about Taiwan, thereby defusing tensions that could escalate into potentially catastrophic military conflict. With Xi and Trump likely to meet again multiple times in the next few months, the new framework is the first chance in years to lay the groundwork for enduring stability in bilateral ties. BEYOND STRATEGIC COMPETITION For a long time, leaders in both Beijing and Washington sought to define the bilateral relationship in terms of some kind of partnership. In 1997, when Chinese leader Jiang Zemin visited the United States, Beijing and Washington announced aims of “a constructive strategic partnership oriented toward the twenty-first century.” In 2005, the George W. Bush administration urged China “to become a responsible stakeholder” in the international system; Chinese leader Hu Jintao responded in 2006 that the two countries were not only stakeholders but “should also be constructive partners.” But between 2009, when President Barack Obama and Hu agreed to “steadily grow a partnership” to address common challenges, and the Trump-Xi summit earlier this year, the countries’ leaders were unable to reach a new consensus on how to position the relationship. The United States moved away from seeing the relationship as a partnership earlier than China did. During Trump’s first term, the United States began to define U.S.-Chinese relations in terms of “strategic competition.” At first, China tried to accept the competitive element in bilateral relations. Beijing acknowledged that some competition was inevitable while hoping that the relationship could remain positive overall. But as U.S.-Chinese relations deteriorated sharply in the final year of Trump’s first term and continued to worsen into the Biden administration, Beijing began to see “strategic competition” as a narrative designed to foreclose China’s rise. It felt that the U.S. approach threatened its development prospects, leading Beijing to push back more forcefully against the concept. In July 2022, during a phone call with President Joe Biden, Xi told his counterpart that it was a mistake to make competition the defining feature of the relationship. To policymakers and analysts in China, the framework of strategic competition turned all U.S.-Chinese interactions into something akin to the Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. They saw the United States’ actions such as export controls on semiconductors as concrete manifestations that the United States was trying to suppress China, to undercut its political system, and to constrain its development. Although official statements from Washington discussed bilateral ties in terms of cooperation, competition, and confrontation, in practice competition and confrontation snuffed out any potential for cooperation. After almost a decade in which China rejected and criticized strategic competition, transitioning to a relationship of constructive strategic stability reflects Beijing’s recalibrated assessment of both countries’ positions and roles in the international system, as well as the new realities of U.S.-Chinese relations. China is looking at bilateral relations from a position of greater equality and with more confidence, and it is less anxious that competition will undermine its national development prospects. Instead, Beijing believes that competition can be effectively managed without presenting an existential threat. MORE THAN ONE MAN Whether strategic stability succeeds as the basis of a new phase in U.S.-Chinese relations depends on whether it is rooted in the personal wills and agendas of Trump and Xi or it arises from structural forces that are more powerful than any individual leader. Many observers in both Beijing and Washington view the emerging consensus as a contingent result of the interests of the two men currently in charge. Trump, for instance, has taken it upon himself to change the direction of U.S. policy. His unexpected turn toward embracing a more stable relationship with China coincides with other unexpected turns in his second-term agenda, including adopting a cold and even hostile attitude toward European allies and launching a war against Iran despite frequently decrying U.S. military involvement overseas. But these shifts also obscure more durable structural factors in the U.S.-Chinese relationship that have pushed the two countries toward more stability, and which make it more likely that the new diplomatic framework can survive. The current rapprochement is the fourth time in the past eight years that a period of tension between China and the United States has given way to an announcement of some kind of stable state. Ongoing friction has not derailed the consensus established in May. After China and the United States first aggressively confronted each other on trade and technology, culminating in the trade war in 2018, the two countries reached the Phase One trade agreement, in January 2020, which stabilized ties. The COVID-19 pandemic, which broke out soon afterward, severely inflamed tensions, sending the relationship to its lowest point since before U.S. President Richard Nixon first visited China, in 1972. In November 2022, Biden and Xi met in Bali and announced that they wanted to restabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, but just months later, in February 2023, recriminations over a Chinese object floating over the United States—described by Beijing as a civilian meteorological airship and by Washington as a spy balloon—interrupted such efforts. That November, Biden and Xi smoothed over ties for a third time at their San Francisco summit. This set the tenor of relations until April 2025, when Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs spawned a new trade war. Across this period, the United States went through three different presidential terms under both Democratic and Republican administrations, yet U.S.-Chinese relations repeatedly swung back to a stable state. Structural factors independent of any individual leader’s views encourage stability in the relationship. This includes the prohibitive cost of total economic decoupling and the catastrophic consequences of potential military conflict. Put differently, since the beginning of Trump’s second term, it has become clear to both sides that the bilateral relationship is simply too big to fail. The two sides occupy such important positions in global and international affairs, each with enough power to cause enormous damage, that neither wants to see the other become an enemy. The intense clashes between China and the United States over tariffs and rare earths in 2025 revealed that each side could exploit the other’s vulnerabilities, reminding them both that the two countries are highly interdependent and need to act prudently in an economic confrontation. Moreover, as nuclear powers, Beijing and Washington are aware that they cannot afford the prospect of a steadily deteriorating relationship that increases the risk of military conflict. If U.S.-Chinese relations again become more volatile after the next U.S. president takes office, it will test the resilience of the relationship. Yet the structural forces at play are unlikely to have changed. Even if future American leaders announce a new approach to the U.S.-Chinese relationship, therefore, in the end it is likely that they will come to the same realizations as their predecessors and seek stability. TANGLED UP IN RED Other critics argue that the consensus on strategic stability is, at most, a temporary truce. In their view, both sides will use this time to shore up their weaknesses, seek new sources of leverage, and prepare for a future confrontation. The United States could find alternate suppliers for the rare-earth elements it needs, for instance, and China could find new sources of semiconductors or develop its own advanced chips. But despite intense trade and geopolitical frictions, global supply chains have proved more resilient—and more deeply intertwined—than most observers anticipated. U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology have fragmented global supply chains, but they have not severed them. Attempts to route production away from China have merely dispersed Chinese enterprises across a wider array of countries and partners while retaining their irreplaceable role in most supply chains. In 2023, for instance, as the Biden administration sought to limit U.S. battery supply chains’ reliance on China, Chinese firms such as CATL actually expanded their market share by increasing production and supply networks in Asia and Europe, and CATL licensed its technology to Ford to produce batteries on U.S. soil. Even if China and the United States patch up their vulnerabilities in chips and rare earths, respectively, the two countries’ broader connections ensure that other areas of interdependence will remain. The rapid development of technologies such as artificial intelligence will make it particularly difficult for either the United States or China to eliminate the other’s sources of leverage. New technologies create new vulnerabilities. With the possibility of artificial general intelligence on the horizon, the frictions in the U.S.-Chinese relationship are unlikely to be concentrated in the same fields and to manifest themselves in the same ways as today. The likelihood of either China or the United States creating what Chinese martial arts novels call an “iron shirt”—a training regimen that makes someone impervious to blades and bullets—is very low. As both countries acquire more powerful, faster, and less predictable technological capabilities, what is needed to preserve stability is likely to change. Attempts by either side to achieve an overwhelming advantage or to ensure absolute security could instead heighten the other’s insecurity and intensify bilateral competition, ultimately forcing both countries to accept some mutual vulnerability and a different strategic equilibrium. The two countries are already realizing that they will have to manage the enormous challenges that AI presents, especially safety risks, whether through joint action or parallel efforts. U.S.-Chinese relations have stabilized four times over the past eight years; this also means that, viewed from the opposite perspective, the relationship has repeatedly devolved into confrontation. With each successive clash producing renewed grievances and hostility, a palpable fatigue has set in on both sides. Lowering their ambitions to the limited goal of stability makes it possible to dampen volatility, achieve tangible progress, and work with the reality of interdependence in more productive ways. THE EAST IS RISING One of the most significant changes underlying the acceptance of strategic stability is China’s growing confidence. When the first Trump administration began pushing for more decoupling, in 2018, many Chinese policymakers and citizens alike worried that escalating tensions with the United States would harm China’s progress and end the prospect of China developing into a stronger and wealthier country. In contemporary China, development is linked to openness: the more international cooperation there is, the faster technological development proceeds. The United States’ embrace of strategic competition challenged this basic premise. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which further drove countries apart and into blocs, made decision-makers and ordinary citizens worry even more. But after eight years of on-and-off trade and technology wars with the United States, China’s economic fundamentals have remained stable. Real estate markets are struggling and traditional industries are mired in distress, but high-tech industries have advanced by leaps and bounds and the manufacturing sector, particularly advanced manufacturing, has become stronger. China’s inability to obtain semiconductors from the United States has forced it to strengthen its own chip industry. The mainstream view in China now is that U.S. government restrictions on high-tech sectors have forced China onto a better path toward more self-reliance and innovation, rendering Washington’s containment policies ineffective and ultimately counterproductive. Structural factors have pushed the two countries toward more stability. China’s successes are mounting. In early 2025, the Chinese firm DeepSeek released a large language model that achieved near-parity with U.S. frontier AI models at a fraction of the cost. In April of that year, China successfully retaliated against Trump’s tariffs, forcing Washington back to the negotiating table. In those negotiations and later talks, China’s rare-earth dominance gave the country a chokepoint over U.S. supply chains. These episodes have increased China’s confidence and made its policymakers and strategists less worried about discussing competition as part of China’s relationship with the United States. Western commentators often believe that a confident China will become more assertive. The opposite is true. When China’s leaders believe that they can manage their external environment and that the country’s core interests and development prospects are not threatened, they are more willing to show restraint, engage in consultation, and focus on solving problems at home. In the 1990s and the first decade of the twenty-first century, for example, as China’s economy grew rapidly, it shelved disputes in the South China Sea with its neighbors. It was only after the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia,” when Beijing felt that the United States was uniting countries in the region against China, that it adopted a tougher approach to resolving disputes in the South China Sea. In 2026, a more confident China did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran, but instead quietly promoted peace talks behind the scenes. Likewise, now that China is less worried that the United States has either the intention or the ability to block China’s development prospects, it is more willing to accept a bounded competition with the United States. From a position of confidence, Beijing can engage the United States pragmatically on an issue-by-issue basis, looking to find specific policies to manage an inevitable amount of competition. A NEW BALLAST The fundamental requirement of the new framework of strategic stability is maintaining peace. That requires that the Chinese and U.S. militaries establish more mature measures for crisis avoidance, crisis management, and confidence building. The two sides can reduce the likelihood of conflict at low cost by setting up regularized military-to-military exchanges and fleshing out and expanding existing maritime and air encounter protocols. They can also coordinate on issues related to outer space, such as preventing near-earth-orbit collisions, regulating space traffic, and building trust around their respective strategic intentions. Addressing concerns in more politically sensitive domains, such as nuclear weapons and the military application of artificial intelligence, will require a more gradual approach. Although the Trump administration has shown heightened interest in discussing nuclear arms control with China, Beijing believes that formal negotiations are premature because of the vast disparity between U.S. and Chinese nuclear capabilities. Progress does not need to be confined to top leaders. More exchanges at all levels between China and the United States are another low-cost way of solidifying a framework of strategic stability. The United States and China could increase opportunities for engagement by easing visa restrictions and reviewing and reducing sanctions, removing entry or exit bans, and limiting other travel restrictions on institutions and citizens, as well as allowing more of the other side’s news media to operate there. Trump could take the opportunity to explicitly remind Chinese students that they are welcome to study in the United States, and Beijing could formulate clearer policies to guide scholars and students about the boundaries of acceptable research in China and guarantee openness, safety, and academic freedom for any scholarship falling outside those boundaries. Taiwan remains a dangerous flash point that could set back progress toward a relationship of strategic stability. Taiwan is the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict between China and the United States, and pressure is increasing. Continued rule of the island by the more pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, combined with Beijing’s strong desire to advance national unification and uncertainty about what kind of Taiwan policy the United States is going to pursue, has inflamed tensions on all sides. A new equilibrium can emerge only through an arrangement in which no party is completely satisfied yet each can live with the result. The goal is to build a floor under U.S.-Chinese relations. As long as Beijing believes that cross-strait integration remains achievable, it has no reason to resort to military force. The United States could shift its declared policy to align more closely with Beijing by recognizing Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan or by explicitly opposing Taiwan’s independence, which would reassure Beijing that the prospect of “peaceful reunification” remains viable. This would allow China and the United States to reach a consensus that realizes the U.S. objective of a peaceful resolution to the dispute yet also maintains the ability of the people in Taiwan to preserve their political and social systems. By keeping the prospect of peaceful reunification alive, the core concerns of all three parties can be accommodated as much as possible. Washington’s decision to pause $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, reached during Trump’s May summit with Xi, defused a rapidly escalating flash point in U.S.-Chinese relations. But it presents a new challenge to the nascent framework of strategic stability. Although Beijing certainly welcomed the delay, the pause has also raised expectations for future U.S. policy regarding Taiwan. Should the Trump administration eventually resume arms transfers—an outcome deemed likely by most Washington observers—Beijing will fiercely oppose the move, potentially jeopardizing the strategic stability framework. This scenario represents a concrete and salient threat that both countries must manage in the period ahead. A relationship of strategic stability is not a concept that one side imposed on the other or that will benefit Beijing but hurt Washington. It is the result of joint efforts by both countries, which makes it a rare opportunity. The next step is to build out this basic framework, breathe life into it, and make it sustainable. The September summit and additional scheduled leaders’ meetings this year offer a timely window of opportunity to make further small steps toward solidifying this baseline of stability. Some believe that this goal is too modest. But if two major powers such as China and the United States can keep fluctuations in the relationship within a manageable range and avoid any kind of war, it would be far more than a modest achievement. item.title: Iran’s Second Front
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.92
Seizing opportunity amid the war in Iran, the Houthis have launched a major new bid for military dominance in and around Yemen. On Tuesday, the Iranian-aligned group unleashed a wave of drones and ballistic missiles strikes on Saudi Arabia, setting fire to oil facilities in the country’s south and injuring more than 70 people. Then on Thursday, after days of heavy fighting along key frontlines inside Yemen, the Houthis routed Saudi-backed government forces along the Red Sea coast and captured the strategic port of Mokha. And on Friday, the Yemeni government reported that the Houthis had seized Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab el Mandeb Strait, the narrow waterway that connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. The takeover marks a profound shift in the balance of power in Yemen, with potential consequences for the entire region. Until this week, Mokha had been home to a vital part of the anti-Houthi coalition and served as a bulwark against the rebels’ advance. With this offensive, the Houthis have shattered a status quo along the coast, upended a truce that had largely held since 2022, and set the stage for further consolidation of their control of the north. But the victory is also Iran’s, since Houthi control of both Perim Island and Mokha, which lies less than 50 miles from the Bab el Mandeb, will allow the rebels to establish themselves as the power brokers of the strait and more easily harass shipping. The timing of the Houthis’ escalation, which began with attacks on Saudi interests in July, is especially significant, given that the Red Sea has become a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for Saudi oil during the Iran war. Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened. By attacking Saudi shipping and Saudi Arabia itself, they have effectively opened a second front in the Iran war, broadening that conflict and placing further pressure on global energy and financial markets. Iranian officials have said that reaching a deal with the United States will require ending the blockade of Yemen—a shorthand for Saudi Arabia’s lifting all transit restrictions on Houthi-held territories, including the capital, Sanaa, and ending support for the Yemeni government. In this evolving regional order, Iran and its partners are trying to establish a new status quo by controlling the Middle East’s most critical maritime checkpoints. Options for addressing the Houthi challenge are moving from bad to worse. While the frontlines will likely continue to evolve, a few hard realities have been laid bare. A decisive military solution to Houthi threats is not credible. For all their public bluster, Yemeni government forces remain internally fragmented. During this week’s offensive, their backer Saudi Arabia also failed to provide close air support and other necessary assistance, suggesting continued poor coordination between the anti-Houthi coalition and Riyadh. Moreover, the Houthis’ gains also undermine the prospects for a negotiated settlement. The militant group is now likely to be even more maximalist in its demands and in its ambitions to assert control across the Red Sea. There are no easy solutions. For now, the priority for Saudi Arabia, the United States, and their Yemeni allies must be protecting other key frontlines from Houthi advances and hindering Houthi efforts to consolidate control over northern Yemen and the Bab el Mandeb. But beyond that, the anti-Houthi coalition must finally address the fissures that continue to tear it apart and agree on a credible political vision for resolving the Yemeni conflict. If it does not, there is a real risk of greater upheaval on the government side and expansion of the Houthi threat across the region. FROM THE STRAIT TO THE SEA For nearly five months after the Iran war began in late February, the Houthis mostly stayed on the sidelines. That relative calm gave way in mid-July, when the Iranians flew a Houthi delegation from Tehran to Sanaa, challenging the Yemeni government and Saudi-led coalition’s control of Yemen’s airspace. To prevent the aircraft from landing, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government bombed the Sanaa airport’s sole runway. Although the plane landed at the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah instead, the Saudi action gave the Houthis a pretext for abandoning the 2022 truce. It was at that point that the group began their bold escalation against Saudi interests and launched their new offensive against coalition forces in Yemen. The Houthi campaign is clearly designed to exploit new Saudi vulnerabilities. As Iran has throttled the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea has become a lifeline for the Saudi oil industry. But since the Houthis resumed their attacks in July, Saudi oil exports through the Bab el Mandeb have plummeted 95 percent. Now, by targeting infrastructure and ships near the Red Sea port complex of Yanbu, the Houthis are threatening the transit of oil exports northward through Egypt as well. Meanwhile, the U.S. war with Iran has given new fuel to the Houthis’ maximalist goals in Yemen itself. The group became frustrated by the “no war, no peace” situation that prevailed after the truce, and they blame Riyadh for slow walking a formal political settlement to the 12-year-old civil war. In reality, such a deal was obstructed by the Houthis themselves. In 2023, the UN helped negotiate a road-map agreement that would have allowed the Houthis to pay all public-sector salaries and obtain a share of oil and gas resources in return for a permanent cease-fire and the launch of a political process. It would have been a good outcome for the Houthis, who control none of the country’s hydrocarbon resources and have been shut out of the international economy. But instead of taking the offer, they began attacking Red Sea shipping to show their support for Hamas in the Gaza war—all the while assuming they could return to the table when they were ready. During the final phase of the war in Gaza, Israel and the United States caused significant military and economic damage to Houthi strongholds in Yemen. In the spring of 2025, the Trump administration undertook more than 1,000 airstrikes during Operation Rough Rider; a few months later, the Israelis targeted Houthi infrastructure and assassinated the group’s de facto prime minister and its military chief of staff. Yet these campaigns appear to have emboldened the group. By attacking global shipping, the Houthis bolstered their importance within Iran’s axis of resistance. And by engaging with these powerful militaries, the group reinforced its self-image as a major regional player that was uniquely capable of liberating the Muslim world from corrupting American and Israeli influence. Since then, the organization has intensified its effort to acquire new and more powerful military capabilities. During the Gaza war, Russia had provided the Houthis with intelligence to assist its targeting of ships. It considered providing the Houthis with advanced weapons as well, although it was ultimately dissuaded by Riyadh. Today, as described in a recent analysis in Foreign Affairs, the Houthis are harnessing diversified supply chains and shadowy financial networks while building up domestic production capacity. As a result, they have been able to strengthen their arsenal—even without direct arms transfers from Iran. Now the Houthis think they can get the Saudis to offer them even better terms than the 2023 UN-backed road map, including war reparations. As their military offensive progresses, those demands will likely continue to rise. The Houthis also face significant pressure at home to pay long-promised public-sector salaries and address increasingly desperate living conditions. More than half the population of Yemen is experiencing acute food insecurity, with six million people facing “emergency” levels of deprivation bordering on famine. RIYADH’S REDLINE Given Saudi Arabia’s heightened dependence on the Red Sea, the Houthis may have calculated that the kingdom would quickly concede to their demands. Instead, Houthi actions seem to have steeled Riyadh’s resolve to confront the group. While Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman may have preferred de-escalation, or at least postponing a confrontation until a U.S.-Iranian deal reduced his kingdom’s dependence on the Red Sea, the Houthis have not given the Saudis leeway to wait. With an unpredictable administration in Washington, Saudi Arabia has been preparing for confrontation by diversifying its security partnerships. On July 30, Riyadh announced a 14-country naval defense coalition for the Red Sea that included Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Sudan and Djibouti. A week later, the crown prince signed a mutual defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan at a ceremony in Mecca with the leaders of both countries at his side. The military value of these accords is unknown, and indeed, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are a first test for the latter agreement. Thus far, the results have been lackluster. According to Reuters, Pakistan warned the Iranians to rein in their Houthi allies shortly before the Houthis’ dramatic takeover of Mokha. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan has directly entered the fight in Yemen, and Islamabad has confirmed that the Mecca accord has not been invoked in response to the Yemen war. Still, for Saudi Arabia, diplomatic support is important, given the criticism Riyadh faced over a military intervention in Yemen in 2015. The Saudis have also continued to solicit support from the United States. Axios has reported that Washington gave Saudi Arabia the green light to strike the Sanaa airport, and the kingdom has asked for further U.S. support. On July 28, Riyadh teamed up with Washington to strike Iranian-backed Iraqi militias that have aligned themselves with the Houthis, a hint that Washington might join Riyadh in its military effort against the Houthis if the conflict continues to grow. Yet U.S. involvement is far from assured. Amid the demands of the Iran war, the administration has been keen to maintain a bilateral truce with the Houthis that has been in place since May 2025; many of its military assets in the Middle East are bogged down in the Strait of Hormuz, and expanding the war would be unpopular at home. While the Houthis’ seizure of Mokha and Perim Island puts greater pressure on Washington to respond, the Trump administration may be more concerned about avoiding new military entanglements ahead of the midterm elections: Axios reported that Trump declined Saudi requests to launch airstrikes against the Houthis after their advances on Thursday. Riyadh’s efforts to bolster the Yemeni government, meanwhile, have had decidedly mixed results. In January, Saudi Arabia pushed aside its longtime ally in Yemen, the United Arab Emirates, when UAE-aligned separatist forces led by the Southern Transition Council (STC) tried to assert control over all of south Yemen. Since then, the Emiratis have withdrawn from Yemen entirely, allowing Riyadh to unify government military forces under its direct command. But the Houthis’ rapid capture of Mokha raises large questions about the strength and cohesion of these forces. In battle, the unified command did not produce effective cooperation between different government-affiliated groups. As government troops from Mokha withdrew, there were even reports that they had clashed with southern forces who refused to let their northern allies enter the south with their weapons. In particular, the absence of the UAE and the dissolution of the STC have alienated an important southern constituency in the anti-Houthi coalition and deprived the coalition of a militarily capable external backer. If the Houthis are able to consolidate their gains in and around Mokha, the losses of territory could deal a powerful blow to morale among government-affiliated troops and stoke further division. DOUBLE CHOKEPOINT Iran’s greatest leverage against the United States has been its ability to shut the Strait of Hormuz. For much of the war, Saudi Arabia has been exporting three to five million barrels of oil per day via its Red Sea ports in what has become a crucial backstop for Riyadh and global oil markets. Through the Houthis, Iran can now restrict those exports as well. Tehran’s longer-term aim is to establish a daunting status quo: Houthi control over the Bab el Mandeb alongside Iranian control of Hormuz. If it could be sustained, such a strategy would make Iran and its regional partner de facto gatekeepers for trillions of dollars’ worth of trade each year. Although Tehran does not exercise command and control over the Houthis, it exerts enormous influence on the group. Iran’s decision to send the flight to Sanaa in July, setting off the current Houthi escalation, suggests the many ways that Tehran can stoke the Yemen conflict for its own ends. In turn, the Houthis’ decision to enlist Iraqi militias in their attacks on Saudi Arabia has further entangled the Yemen conflict with the Iran war. The Houthis’ growing alliances with armed groups in Somalia, Sudan, and elsewhere across the Horn of Africa also suggest the extent to which their current escalation could quickly spill over into the broader region. In the decade after Yemen’s civil war broke out in 2014, its effects reverberated into Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and finally the Red Sea. With the Iran war, the Houthis’ expanding regional ambitions and partnerships, and their combined ability with Iran to affect the global energy trade, the stage is now set for a more dangerous conflagration. This time, it could be much harder for the Houthis to preserve their earlier autonomy from Tehran. The war in Yemen has long been a battlefield for regional powers. But the latest stage could see expanding involvement from Israel, Russia, Turkey, and the United States. Rather than a battleground for regional influence, Yemen could become a platform for major-power competition centered on a critical maritime chokepoint. KNOCKING HEADS OR THROWING BOMBS Now that a dangerous cycle of escalation has started, much will hinge on what happens next. Saudi Arabia may use the recent Houthi advances to rally international support for a major campaign against the Houthis, potentially involving the United States and its new partners in the Mecca agreement. But such a response could expand the conflict without addressing the fundamental weaknesses of the anti-Houthi coalition fighting on the ground. Such an open-ended escalation is likely to favor the Houthis and further Iran’s strategy of controlling the Middle East’s chokepoints. A sustained Yemen war could also complicate U.S. efforts to reach a settlement with Iran. Alternatively, if the Saudis capitulate to the Houthis after their battlefield gains, it could deal a damning blow to the anti-Houthi coalition and further inflame Houthi regional ambitions. Yet there is still a narrow window of opportunity to prevent uncontrolled escalation and return to the negotiating table. To do so, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government—together with other regional and international partners—will need to agree on a credible plan for securing a political resolution to the Yemen conflict. The plan must address the divisions in the anti-Houthi coalition and settle the political questions that continue to tear that coalition apart while avoiding maximalist military objectives. Getting to such a settlement now will require both Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces, with support of regional and international partners, to apply effective military pressure to stem the Houthis’ advances and persuade them to accept a deal. Indeed, the Houthis themselves are under considerable economic pressure at home and stand to benefit from such talks, if they can be convinced that they cannot impose their will militarily. For a political settlement to deliver stability in Yemen, the Houthis will also have to agree to terms that address core regional and Yemeni government concerns and set out a viable governance structure. An earlier approach taken by the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen is instructive in this regard. In 2021, the Houthis walked away from negotiations and launched a major new ground offensive. The Saudis and Emiratis responded by mounting a coordinated operation that focused on getting the Houthis back to the table rather than aiming at total victory. Ultimately, the campaign helped bring about the truce months later. Any new campaign by the Saudi-led coalition today should be similarly focused on getting the Houthis to take part in negotiations. But success will first require preventing further losses on the ground and making an immediate effort to bridge divisions within the anti-Houthi coalition. It is well past time to end the failed strategy of addressing Yemen’s problems through short-term military escalation and pressure campaigns. Reviving a political settlement will not be easy or happen immediately. But the alternative is far worse: stumbling into a renewed, protracted, and increasingly regional war that, as with the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran, could prove much easier to start than to end. item.title: Avoiding the Next Famine
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.83
In a world of great-power standoffs, climatic tipping points, and technological arms races, global hunger may not seem like a particularly significant problem. Yet last year, a total of 2.1 billion people, or more than a quarter of the planet’s population, experienced food insecurity—meaning they either ran out of food over the course of a year or were forced to reduce the quality or quantity of their diet. Over 260 million faced acute food insecurity, meaning their lives or livelihoods were in immediate danger because they could not get enough to eat. Almost a quarter of all children under the age of five were permanently stunted because of malnourishment and will likely reach lower levels of education, earn less over the course of their lives, and live with more chronic health challenges than properly fed kids. And these startling figures do not reflect the food crises that could be unleashed this year by rising energy and fertilizer prices, decreases in grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, and an intensifying El Niño weather pattern. Food insecurity is terrible in and of itself. But it also has disastrous political consequences. It inhibits economic growth, heightens the risk of violent conflict, and destabilizes governments. These problems, in turn, create trouble for the whole world. That means countries that are not overwhelmed by food insecurity still have strong, self-interested reasons to tackle it—the United States included. In fact, a U.S.-led effort to address hunger would do more than create a healthier and more stable planet. Given the waning goodwill toward the United States, Washington needs an agenda through which it can rebuild global confidence in its leadership and demonstrate the value of international cooperation. Addressing global food security could be at the center of such a plan. Different parts of the world, after all, may have different geopolitical ambitions. But almost no government—northern or southern, democratic or autocratic—wants to see so many people go hungry. There may be no better way to rebuild confidence in the liberal world order and in the United States as a committed member of it than for Washington to address this challenge. FOOD, GLORIOUS FOOD It is difficult to overstate just how intertwined food security is with global development, state security, and even international competition. Malnutrition leads to reduced educational attainment, compromised human capital, and lost productivity, costing the world economy $3.5 trillion a year in forgone economic growth and in added health-care costs. Food price spikes can also exacerbate grievances and lead to riots that destabilize governments; anger over hunger, for example, set the conditions for the Arab Spring protests. In rural areas, food insecurity helps armed groups recruit soldiers and causes disputes over scarce land and water resources. And it causes people to migrate to wealthier states. These reasons are, by themselves, enough for Washington to helm a global campaign to reduce hunger. But so should the fact that leading on global food security means helping shape the future of the world’s entire agricultural system—something China is on a path to do. In 2019, Beijing invested significant capital in securing leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, a role with substantial influence over how governments work together on food-related issues. It is also quickly developing other ways to lead the world on matters of food security. China spends double what the United States spends on public agricultural research and development, and its output of agricultural patents and scientific publications has skyrocketed while U.S. output has stagnated. Thankfully for American officials, the United States is still well positioned to lead the world when it comes to food security. The United States is among the world’s largest agricultural exporters. It was instrumental in founding the UN architecture dedicated to food security, including the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program. And for much of these institutions’ history, Washington has been their largest donor. In fact, for decades, the United States’ international development agenda was the most ambitious in the world, and it was backed by a willing public. Washington retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. The country still has such a public: in early 2026 polling, a strong majority said that the United States should be a moral leader in the world. But a strong majority didn’t believe it was. Perhaps this is because the United States has been walking away from this legacy and this opportunity to lead. In mid-2025, for example, Congress clawed back nearly $8 billion in foreign assistance funds. The United States is now a reluctant international donor and a surly member of key international organizations. Washington, however, still retains many of the tools needed to combat global hunger. In addition to increasing foreign assistance, it can leverage trade policies, public investment in innovation, and even its impressive data collection systems. Washington, however, will also need to work multilaterally. And to build credibility, it should advance a practical and achievable agenda with clear benefits for all. One overarching goal for collective action should be increasing predictability wherever possible. The global food system is afflicted by uncertainty across many domains—weather, supply chains, labor, trade, and beyond. This wreaks havoc on policymaking, markets, and livelihoods. Being able to better understand these trends and know what tools will be available to manage them could thus do much to shore up food networks and prepare for disasters. Washington should, for example, work with partners to strengthen the world’s fractured early warning systems and the data that enables them. Early warning of shocks to the food system—such as extreme weather, supply disruptions, economic turbulence—buys critical time for preparation and response. The United States should also spearhead the transition of international emergency food assistance funding away from voluntary, ad hoc contributions to preplanned, multiyear commitments. It should simultaneously encourage more donors to contribute in amounts commensurate with their abilities, starting with itself. Food security is one of the few issues that can bring the whole world together. Solving food emergencies requires more than just additional funding. The United States also needs to work to strengthen international norms that protect access to food during conflict. That means making sure humanitarian groups can get into conflict zones, protecting agricultural infrastructure from attacks, and prohibiting the use of starvation as a weapon of war. These concepts have a long-standing basis in international law, but the conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine have demonstrated they need reinforcement. Washington should advance these norms through resolutions and interventions in the UN Security Council and General Assembly and use diplomacy to try to get violators to change their behavior. Food security diplomacy, however, must extend beyond conflict zones. The United States should forge a broad global commitment to avoid unilateral, reactionary policies to agricultural shocks—such as when a grain exporter suddenly bans external shipments in response to price spikes, leaving international buyers in the lurch. Such policies may be politically attractive for governments that want to show citizens they will keep costs down. But they leave other states worse off and often don’t even work at home. Instead, the United States should promote more international financing options that maintain the flow of traded agricultural commodities during periods of price volatility and that fast-track funding to countries facing shocks. Finally, the United States should lead a collective action campaign aimed at protecting agricultural systems from a particularly pernicious challenge: agricultural pests and diseases. Pests and diseases destroy up to 40 percent of global crop production each year, pushing down rural incomes, driving up consumer prices, and wasting natural resources. The existing international surveillance and response systems for these ailments are limited in scope. But Washington can build global support for more comprehensive ones. MORE WITH LESS The world certainly needs better ways of managing food crisis and risk. But it also needs to foster sustainable agricultural productivity growth—or the ability to produce more food with fewer inputs. Such growth is particularly important where populations are rising, as most food consumed is produced domestically. Only certain food commodities can be easily traded across long distances, so international commerce cannot fully solve food and nutritional supply challenges. The most important step countries can collectively take is to promote innovation. To encourage that process, U.S. officials should start by focusing on international agricultural research centers, such as the World Vegetable Center in Taiwan and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center in Mexico (both of which the United States helped found). These facilities have long been an engine for progress in productivity, food security, and natural resource management, particularly in the developing world. For example, over the last few decades, international centers have developed flood-tolerant rice and drought-tolerant corn that have prevented crop failure for millions of poorer smallholder farmers. In fact, according to studies by a variety of economists, research undertaken by these centers offers an impressive return on investment—for every dollar spent, ten dollars are gained in the form of yield increases, lower production costs, lower consumer prices, and other benefits. But like many institutions, these research centers have suffered from mission creep and bureaucratic accretion. To maximize their effectiveness, the United States should build global support for refocusing their strategy, streamlining their operations, and making new investments in them. The world needs research to keep just ahead of the latest challenges—such as rising temperatures and new strains of old agricultural diseases. But it should also aim higher. Washington thus ought to work with other actors to tackle tough, high-reward problems that have never had the benefit of a truly concerted international effort. This could include, for example, trying to develop high-yielding perennial or nitrogen-fixing grains that would promote healthier landscapes, reduce labor requirements, and need less fertilizer. It might also feature an endeavor to increase photosynthesis efficiency so that plants can produce more from the sunlight they receive. Such inventions would not only change the world, they would also showcase the power of American innovation and deepen Washington’s ties with its partners. But to enable ambitious research, the United States should take steps to reform the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. The agreement was designed to make plant genetic resources, or seeds and tissue, fully and freely available to researchers everywhere. These resources can be used to breed new varieties of crops that are higher yielding, more resilient to climate change, and more nutritious. But the treaty is falling short. Researchers see benefit-sharing provisions as too costly; developing countries see them as offering too little. As a result, fewer researchers seek material that could accelerate innovation, and fewer countries are willing to share it. The United States should thus push everyone to reinterpret the benefit-sharing provisions in a more generous manner. It should also properly fund the Global Crop Diversity Trust’s endowment, which funds the international seed banks that conserve the biological foundation of food crops (particularly since governments, including Washington, are doing an inadequate job of conserving their collections). And if U.S. officials determine that the treaty cannot be saved, they should lead an effort to draft a new one. Lastly, Washington must do whatever it can to make sure that new agricultural and food technologies are quickly adopted. This will require reforms of the international Codex Alimentarius Commission, which is responsible for developing food safety guidelines that protect consumers and facilitate trade. The commission’s guidelines have significant ramifications for technologies that could strengthen global food security, but the body is slow, underfunded, and controversial. The United States should therefore try to enhance its capacity and legitimacy, including by pushing for increased support to the scientific committees that help set Codex standards. REAPING AND SOWING At a time of rising global competition, there are few issues that can bring the whole world together. Food security is one of them. Almost every government knows that hunger is a problem, and almost all of them at least say they want to address it. If the United States can spearhead a strong effort do so, it could bring the planet together under its leadership. That does not mean Washington should instrumentalize food aid or other agricultural endeavors. The United States should not echo its 1970s policies around food power, during which officials boasted of altruism while attempting to exert political strength by alternatively deploying and withholding its grain supply. Instead, the United States must emphasize mutual benefit. It must persuade other actors that it is a constructive and reliable partner. Doing so will strengthen its diplomatic relationships and increase stability around the world—inherently advancing U.S. interests. Rarely do Washington’s strategic imperatives and humanitarian principles align so neatly. It is rarer still for a U.S. foreign policy agenda to clearly reflect what the American people want their country to be: not just strong, but moral. Food security, in other words, is a unique opportunity for the United States. The country cannot afford to waste it.
