item.title: The Other War on Terror
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.12
For years, the United States’ political dysfunction has been attributed to large-scale social and economic changes. Experts point to the failures of globalization, rising inequality, reduced social mobility, or the long aftermath of the “China shock” more than two decades ago to explain today’s extreme polarization, collapsing trust in institutions, democratic erosion, immigration backlash, and struggling middle class. Yet there is another widely overlooked factor that is equally central to understanding the United States’ current predicament: the war on terror. Typically, when policymakers and analysts speak of the global war on terror—the defining fact of international affairs for two decades—they discuss the damage done to terrorist groups, the plots that have been thwarted, the rise and fall of jihadi ideology, the many intelligence failures, and, perhaps above all, the two forever wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. These are the scorecards of contemporary counterterrorism. But left out of this framing are the profound effects of this vast war on terror on domestic politics and society. The human statistics alone tell an appalling story: more than 7,000 U.S. troops were killed in action, 53,000 were wounded, and well over 30,000 took their own lives—a staggering number. According to Brown University’s Costs of War Project, these conflicts added $8 trillion to the U.S. national debt, with trillions more projected in the future for veterans’ health care, including for the half million GIs with traumatic brain injuries and posttraumatic stress disorder. Yet even these numbers fail to show the myriad ways in which two decades of war transformed the United States. For years, the fixation on Islamist terror shaped a culture drenched in fear, as voices from politics, the media, civil society, and a swelling counterterrorism-industrial complex insisted that the country faced an existential threat. Amid this climate, the government was given broad new powers to root out and prosecute potential jihadi activity wherever it might be, and the widespread assumption that there might be another terrorist attack began to reshape American society itself. Rather than bringing the country together behind a shared—and narrowly defined—enemy, however, the result has been a dramatic decline in social cohesion. It has contributed to the demise of political bipartisanship, already weakened in previous decades. At the same time, the war on terror fueled an alarming rise in xenophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment and discredited the country’s political and foreign policy elites. Above all has been the uncontrolled expansion of executive power. This impetus did not begin with the war on terror; generations of American leaders and scholars have sought to increase presidential power, drawing up mechanisms that could sideline civil liberties and intertwine military and police activities. But after 9/11, these contingencies were used to give the executive branch sweeping new authority in the name of domestic security. And today, an authoritarian president is using these powers to target his political enemies. The United States, then, is overdue for a reckoning with the political legacy of the war on terror. THE POWER OF NIGHTMARES Anxiety about extended war has preoccupied American officials throughout U.S. history. In the first years after the country’s independence, James Madison, who would become the country’s fourth president, observed that “no nation can preserve its freedom in the midst of continual war.” More than a century and a half later, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower sounded the alarm about “the acquisition of unwarranted influence” by what he famously called “the military-industrial complex.” As Eisenhower forewarned, “The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist.” For many of the decades since, much of that apprehension has been focused on the concentration of power in government and in the broader machinery of war. Yet during the war on terror, parts of society mobilized in parallel with the state and sought to cast a much wider net against a class of perceived enemies. Terrorist acts are typically carried out by secret actors operating within a country’s borders, and 9/11 was the ultimate case in point. The attacks on the Twin Towers and the Pentagon—the first on U.S. soil since World War II—were carried out by foreign nationals inside the country. They were motivated by the al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s particular brand of jihadi ideology, which held that major attacks on the U.S. homeland would lead Washington to withdraw support for the apostate rulers of the Muslim world. These themes—which also carried notions of proportional revenge for the number of Muslims previously killed by the United States—and the attacks themselves gave license to Islamophobes throughout American society, including in the political world and policy establishment. The most influential came from the evangelical churches: to their huge audiences, leading televangelists such as Franklin Graham, John Hagee, and Robert Jeffress described Islam as “satanic” and a “heresy from the pit of hell” and its followers as a cult of pedophiles. President George W. Bush sought to tamp down the hatred by insisting that the war on terror was not a war against Islam. But for all his protestations, many saw the war on terror as a crusade—a word that Bush himself used early on until he was told how poorly that played in the Islamic world. His message was further belied by such government actions as the detention of at least 1,200 Muslim men—many of whom were held on immigration charges but treated as high-security risks—and the severe curtailment of Muslim civil liberties by the FBI and other law enforcement in the name of addressing the terrorist threat. The fact that the 9/11 hijackers had been sustained by an efficient Muslim support network within the United States no doubt contributed to these measures, as did reasonable concerns about the potential for online radicalization. Trump blurs the lines between Islamophobia and anti-immigrant sentiment. In the decades since, the persistence of fear-mongering and the growth of anti-Muslim sentiment and hate crimes has been hard to miss. When the Obama administration sought to transfer foreign detainees captured in the war on terror from Guantánamo to facilities in the United States, Republicans depicted them as superhuman terrorists that no U.S. prison could safely secure. The plan was nixed. In 2014, when it was revealed that a jihadi’s laptop found in an Islamic State (ISIS) hideout in Idlib, Syria, contained some basic information on bioweapons, members of the flourishing counterterrorism commentariat claimed that terrorists planned to cull the African Ebola virus from victims’ corpses and spray it widely in American urban centers. Candidates for high office found the terrorist threat to be the gift that never ceased giving. Political scientists at Dartmouth, where both of us have taught, recall hearing former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, a candidate for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016, tell elderly women in a remote New Hampshire village that jihadis might take them hostage in their homes if they didn’t vote for the tough-on-terror candidate. Claims such as these were contradicted by the actual state of the threat. By 2016, it had been several years since U.S. Navy SEALS had killed bin Laden, and al-Qaeda had not managed a second attack against the United States in 15 years. The few, ostensibly Islamist-related attacks that had happened on U.S. soil were mostly lone-wolf actions, in the sense that they were not deployed and directed by al-Qaeda operatives based outside the United States. Instead, they were radicalized in place through exposure to news reporting, online propaganda, preaching, and the fellowship of like-minded individuals. (A partial exception was the 2009 Fort Hood massacre, carried out by a U.S. army major, who had corresponded with Anwar al-Awlaki, the American cleric with links to al-Qaeda who was later killed by the United States in Yemen.) In 2014, ISIS captured global attention with its claim to a caliphate and insurgency in Iraq and Syria, and it was better than al-Qaeda at recruiting followers in Europe and North America. This group carried out or claimed responsibility for bloody attacks in Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, and Spain. Several of these were devastating mass casualty attacks, but none were in the league of 9/11. Notably, ISIS’s rise in the vacuum created by the U.S. toppling of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein was a result, not a cause, of the war on terror. The lack of attacks was not simply luck. Throughout these decades, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement professionals—operating far from the overheated rhetoric of the era—dealt methodically and capably with the terrorist threat. During this period, government agencies achieved a level of integration that had improved dramatically since pre-9/11 days. Foreign intelligence services and civil authorities were tightly coordinated in the effort, making it possible to know who was attempting to cross the United States’ borders. Indeed, by the time al-Qaeda struck the United States again—a 2019 shooting at a Florida naval base that killed three and injured eight—the group was a shadow of its former self. As ISIS made clear, the fading of al-Qaeda did not usher in an age of Aquarius. Yet according to solid longitudinal polling, the degree to which Americans prioritized terrorism no longer reflected quotidian reality. The unanswered and perhaps unanswerable question emerging from this period is whether the relative security Americans enjoyed in the decades after 9/11 owed more to intelligence and law enforcement and domestic security measures than to the progress of the expeditionary wars and targeted killings that were meant to root out the problem at its presumed source. Nonetheless, the question remains a vital one for those who are responsible for anticipating terrorism threats and constructing both defensive and offensive approaches to them. FOREVER WAR TO CIVIL WAR In hindsight, 2016 marked a decisive hinge point in the war on terror, when the primary question shifted from faraway military conflicts to allegedly dangerous new threats at home—and not only those from Islamists. The United States had plenty of experience with nativism before 9/11. But a decade and a half of fear-mongering produced something entirely new. Perhaps nowhere was the legacy more pernicious than in the fusing of terrorist fears with broader anti-immigration sentiment. As numerous postmortems for the 2016 presidential election made clear, stoking anti-Muslim sentiment helped mobilize the Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump’s base, even though economic concerns won him that close election. On the campaign trail and then in office, Trump continually blurred the lines between Islamophobia and broader anti-immigrant sentiment. One day he decried murderers, criminals, and rapists coming across the southern border; the next, he asserted that the migrant flows were cover for jihadis. Perhaps the perfect symbol of Trump’s fusion of the threat of terrorism with the challenge of illegal immigration was his repeated warnings in 2018 about a migrant caravan making its way from Central America to the U.S.-Mexican border—a caravan he claimed had “unknown Middle Easterners in it.” To be fair, the U.S. intelligence community was concerned that jihadis were exploiting chaotic conditions at the border to infiltrate the United States, but the fractured nature of interagency databases made this hard to know. In his effort to appear tougher than any competitor, Trump called for bringing back waterboarding and some unspecified technique that was “a helluva lot worse than waterboarding.” Speaking of ISIS operatives, he also said he would “take out their families.” Still more striking, candidate Trump managed to radiate Islamophobia even as he decried the post-9/11 forever wars, stymieing his Republican rivals and his eventual Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. In a way, this marked a decisive shift in the war on terror toward the American homeland. One of the two candidates for president, one of the country’s foremost politicians, was expressly lumping together a sizable American ethnic minority with external enemies. Even when the subtext of previous policy suggested suspicion of American Muslims, federal leaders never expressed explicit hostility. Trump did. Once elected, he implemented a Muslim travel ban, which he introduced just a week into his term and reformulated repeatedly until the Supreme Court finally approved it 18 months later. He also created a permissive structure for xenophobes and racists, spurring a dramatic increase in hate crimes with victims from minority groups of all kinds and accelerating the disuniting of the United States. In his second term, Trump has gone much further. In 2025, the administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 against alleged members of the Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang, described them as an invading force, and sent detainees to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center. The Supreme Court required adequate notice to permit habeas challenges, but removals had already begun. In Florida, the government opened a remote Everglades detention compound called “Alligator Alcatraz” that might usefully be thought of as Guantánamo transplanted to U.S. soil, with its geographic isolation and removal from the domain of law. The facility shuttered after a year, but only for reasons of expense; it cost over a billion dollars per year to run. And by then, the administration was making an even more direct connection with the war on terror, as some immigrant detainees were now sent to Guantánamo itself. The Pentagon also became involved, with active-duty personnel providing logistical and operational support for a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) detention mission. In other words, institutions created for external war, border enforcement, and domestic policing have now become components of a punitive system against immigrants who may not even have a criminal record. As a practical matter, it became a test bed for the detention of political prisoners, or, as Trump described them, “enemies of the people.” The Trump administration is not alone in using Islamophobia to drive an anti-immigrant agenda. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, for instance, has long been famous for railing against illegal immigration. But as The New York Times put it in August, citing Republican consultants, “Islam has replaced the border as a major concern” for voters. To date, Texas officials have blocked a real estate development that includes a mosque and threatened to withhold state funding from airports that provide washing stations for Muslim prayer, among other steps. Meanwhile, Republican politicians across the country have denounced the electoral successes of Muslim politicians, including Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Some have even suggested that these officials either are not American citizens or should lose their citizenship. Trump has remarked that “jihadists are being elected all over the place.” COUNTERTERRORISM-INDUSTRIAL COMPLEX The sociologist Charles Tilly’s maxim that “war makes the state; the state makes war” applies not just to early modern state formation but also to how the United States’ counterterrorism efforts led to a dramatic augmentation of state powers. The war on terror propelled the United States to collect and combine information, including on its own citizens; classify individuals it considered dangerous; combine both active and reserve component military units for the purposes of population control and law enforcement; and use coercive power under a variety of emergency authorities. It also reinforced an “us against them” conception of public life in which political disagreement could be recast as disloyalty and whole minority groups treated as presumptively suspect. The perception of an enduring terrorist threat increased support for coercive policies, even among Americans otherwise resistant to authoritarian appeals. Of course, the United States faced security threats before 9/11. Yet whereas the Cold War security state depended on accurate intelligence on adversaries’ military forces and key assets, counterterrorism is focused not on large formations or fixed installations but on locating individuals hidden within large populations, both at home and in foreign societies. Defending against al-Qaeda required officials to identify suspicious people, trace money and travel, map personal networks, and act before an attack occurred. After the shock of the 9/11 attacks, Washington developed an information-sharing network that crossed the foreign and domestic divide and could search customs, immigration, intelligence, and regular law enforcement records. Joint Terrorism Task Forces set up by the FBI and state and city fusion centers created by DHS implemented this model in parallel at the local level. Their missions soon exceeded terrorism to encompass other facets of public safety. In time, national security institutions were routinely vacuuming up ordinary police information, and local law enforcement officers were combing through federal intelligence. The structure was built for finding needles in haystacks. Once built, it could search for needles of all sorts. Such capabilities made it easy to expand political control and executive power, should an elected leader choose to use them for these purposes. Top government officials could identify not only suspects but also their associations, movements, communications, and supporters, making these tools convenient for targeting individuals and groups, both real and invented, and stigmatized communities. Commercial platforms increased their reach. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)—which was founded in response to September 11—has contracted with the American software company Palantir for ImmigrationOS, a system intended to assist in the selection and apprehension of deportation targets. Artificial intelligence, and its inherent scalability, has accelerated the process by eliminating the main bottleneck to comprehensive surveillance: scarce manpower. The logic was visible during the 2020 protests in Portland, Oregon, when DHS officers monitored social media, accessed travel and immigration records, and assembled dossiers on protesters and journalists. Unidentified armed federal officers used unmarked rental vehicles to detain people and took some to holding cells in the federal courthouse without explaining what agency held them or why. The federal government’s evolution since 9/11 is reflected not just in its activities and capabilities. Its sheer mass has grown, as well. Since ICE was created in 2003, its annual budget has risen from $3.3 billion to almost $29 billion; in the same period, its corps of armed officers has grown from 3,000 to 22,000. Meanwhile, police forces across the country have transformed from lightly armed constabularies to small-scale armies. Before 9/11, the Defense Department had transferred only $27 million in hardware to local police forces. Since the attacks, the number has climbed to more than $1.6 billion. In numerous jurisdictions, police can now respond to demonstrations with mine-proof armored vehicles, camouflage, body armor, and large-caliber weaponry. The government’s target set has also expanded. In 2025, the White House issued National Security Memorandum 7, which, among other things, designated antifa—a mostly made up, decentralized, left-wing political movement opposed to white supremacy and (per its name) fascism—as a domestic terrorist organization, a status not formally recognized in the law. The memorandum directed Joint Terrorism Task Forces to investigate organized political violence carried out by those who belong to this supposed network. The offenses were “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity . . . extremism on migration, race, and gender . . . hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality.” The crimes to be investigated by the task forces largely related to protected speech. A subsequent counterterrorism strategy document in May 2026 referred specifically to the “politically motivated killings of Christians and conservatives.” The document treats hostility to Christianity as one of the diagnostic markers for identifying organized political violence, alongside anticapitalism and anti-Americanism. The Trump administration has also used counterterrorism precedents to justify the widespread use of lethal force. Beginning in 2025, the administration labeled suspected drug traffickers as narcoterrorists, giving it legal cover to use military strikes against boats and land sites in Latin America. By August 2026, its operations had killed hundreds of people, often without public evidence to establish a crime or even the basic identities of those targeted. Attacks against Iran in May 2026, meanwhile, killed much of the upper echelon of the Islamic Republic of Iran. Different legal authorities were invoked, but as with the purported drug dealers, the White House used classifications and military practices from the war-on-terror era to justify and conduct its operations. Although Israel’s preemptive and retaliatory reliance on targeted killings has drawn much attention, this mode of warfare characterized the American war on terror very nearly from its outset, including the arming of drones for this purpose; the first armed Predator flew in October 2001. During the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign within the United States, four Americans were killed and three wounded with the same impunity as the 526 targeted attacks conducted outside war zones from 2009 to 2016 during the latter phase of the war on terror. The war on terror’s focus on dangerous individuals, in other words, supplied a template that is now being applied to suspected criminals, foreign officials, heads of government, migrants, and protesters. Domestic military deployment has followed a parallel track. In 2002, Washington established U.S. Northern Command to direct homeland defense and support civil authorities. In 2025, the army created Western Hemisphere Command by combining Forces Command, Army North, and Army South under one four-star headquarters responsible for readiness, homeland defense, and operations across the Americas. Neither change erased statutory barriers to domestic military law enforcement. But both reduced the organizational distance between military forces prepared for overseas combat and missions close to home. Since June 2025, the administration has deployed National Guard personnel or active-duty Marines to six American cities. It has also assigned active-duty personnel to support ICE processing and detention facilities. These steps did not formally merge the military and DHS, but they created recurring joint operations through which domestic coercive missions could expand. Meanwhile, Trump is politicizing the armed forces, basing appointments and promotions on partisan loyalty and degrading or simply ignoring long-standing professional norms. These changes will presumably weaken the institutional barriers to the military’s political use, which concerns the missions the president assigned to military personnel, as in Los Angeles, where National Guard troops and Marines accompanied federal immigration operations. A federal district court found that troops had been systematically directed to perform law enforcement functions, including patrols and traffic control, in violation of the Posse Comitatus Act, and the administration ultimately halted these operations. But Trump has declared that they will resume on a larger scale. The homeland, he thinks, is an excellent place for U.S. armed forces to conduct battles. “We should use some of these dangerous cities as training grounds for our military,” Trump said in September 2025. “We’re under invasion from within. No different than a foreign enemy but more difficult in many ways because they don’t wear uniforms.” Urban opposition has been placed within a vocabulary of war. WHERE DOES IT END? War has not only changed the tenor of American life and enabled a vast expansion of executive power. It has also had a radicalizing effect on parts of the population, including war veterans—a phenomenon that bears echoes of the Freikorps, the groups of disbanded soldiers in Weimar Germany who, once given policing powers against the “Bolshevik” threat, quickly became a lethal paramilitary force. In her history of the white power movement, the scholar Kathleen Belew has shown how a segment of Vietnam veterans joined civilians in building a narrative of betrayal, transferring military skills and organizational forms into paramilitary politics to be redirected against enemies at home. The 1992 Ruby Ridge confrontation and the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing came from that milieu. Today, a recurrence of that pattern can be seen among veterans of Afghanistan and Iraq. Groups such as the Oath Keepers and the Three Percenters recruit current and former military personnel and police officers. Its members used military formations during the January 6 attack, and the founder of the Oath Keepers was convicted of seditious conspiracy. Of these, all had their cases dismissed, were pardoned, or had their sentences commuted by Trump. How dangerous these groups still might be is poorly understood: the Trump administration has banned contact between scholars and military personnel except in the framework of professional military education, so there is no up-to-date survey data or qualitative information on attitudes within the military about political matters. Publicly available government reporting on militias has also dried up. Given that such groups have had practical and rhetorical support from the administration in power, the threat of more violence cannot be discounted. Of course, the war on terror also had an immense role in shaping the international environment that the United States contends with today. Iran is a more capable opponent because the war in Iraq converted Hussein’s Sunni regime into one subject to Iranian influence and helped facilitate an Iranian-backed network (the “Axis of Resistance”) across the region. Islamophobia helped spur the rise of populist right-wing parties in Europe, alongside the migration crisis caused by Syria’s civil war and ISIS’s territorial gains in Syria and Iraq. In Egypt and other Arab countries, authoritarian regimes have consolidated control and gained U.S. support by arguing that they are holding the line against terrorists. And as many as 500,000 foreign civilians were killed or died as a result of the war on terror—a history that has left its own grim legacy abroad. The war on terror created a far more powerful government. In the 25 years since the 9/11 attacks, the commemorations have tended to follow a predictable pattern: recollections of the awful events of that day, the reading of names, the lighting of candles. Beyond the now ritual agreement that Iraq was a huge mistake and that Afghanistan was the neglected theater, the consequences of the United States’ reaction to those attacks—and how it has remade the country—remain surprisingly unexamined. It is well past time to give those consequences much closer attention. The 9/11 attacks accelerated the transformation of U.S. political discord from a disagreement between competing ideological coalitions into a conflict between mutually threatening social identities. Islamophobia was both an early expression of that transformation and an important mechanism through which Americans learned to define internal enemies. Over the following quarter century, this mechanism migrated from Muslims to immigrants, racial protesters, cultural minorities, and, ultimately, partisan opponents themselves. Indeed, the most important domestic political legacy of the war on terror may be that the category “terrorist” gradually shifted from the realm of political violence to a model for thinking about political opponents. Meanwhile, the war on terror created a far more powerful government. After 9/11, the United States built a state optimized for identifying threats before they materialized, relying on ubiquitous surveillance, integrated databases, watch lists, preventive policing, militarized border enforcement, expansive secrecy, remote coercive power, broad emergency authority, and a sorcerer’s apprentice national security bureaucracy. President George W. Bush constructed much of this architecture. But even as he constrained parts of it, President Barack Obama embraced much of what he inherited. Congress repeatedly ratified or declined to dismantle it. Presidential self-restraint became the independent variable in the calculation of democracy’s fate. This posed an obvious latent danger. Institutions created on the assumption that presidents would distinguish genuine national security threats from political enemies were safe only as long as presidents continued to make that distinction. When Trump entered the presidency in January 2017 with an unprecedented vision of executive power that he justified through inflammatory threat rhetoric, he could draw on a highly developed set of tools. The war on terror did not create American authoritarianism, but it certainly reduced the startup costs of an authoritarian presidency. item.title: The Case for Letting China In
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.03
Industrial policy is back in fashion in the United States. As fragile global supply chains and a weakened industrial base present growing economic and national security risks, policymakers in both parties have embraced energetic efforts to rebuild the country’s industrial capacity. With interventions such as the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, Washington has made historic commitments to strengthening the United States’ technology and manufacturing base, which is becoming increasingly important to the country’s economic success and ability to defend itself. As director of U.S. President Joe Biden’s National Economic Council, I helped to design and drive this shift. Initiatives to revive domestic capacity are a necessary response to real dangers. But more and more, American leaders are seeking to support industry at home in ways that are counterproductive. In particular, they are growing hostile to foreign investment. Many policymakers fear that foreign investors could steal sensitive data or gain dangerous leverage over U.S. companies or critical infrastructure. Their aversion is most pronounced with respect to China but has been trained on allies and partners as well. It applies not only to cases of foreign ownership of U.S. companies but also to joint ventures, the licensing of foreign intellectual property, and other arrangements in which a foreign company shares its knowledge or resources. Stephen Miran, the chair of the president’s Council of Economic Advisers, has suggested imposing fees on foreign holdings of U.S. assets, including those owned by allies. Senators Tammy Baldwin and Josh Hawley have introduced bipartisan legislation in the U.S. Congress that would tax foreign capital inflows outright. At the federal, state, and local level, those in power are taking steps to shut global capital out of the United States and prevent American enterprises from harnessing the latest advances in data storage, critical mineral processing, and chip-making. This is a troubling and ultimately self-defeating strategy. Of course, the U.S. government should mitigate the risks of foreign investment. But today, its screening regime is overzealous. The United States is undermining its own industrial policy by denying itself the tools to become competitive globally in crucial sectors. What the country needs is a new framework for selectively encouraging investment from abroad to match its industrial ambitions. The U.S. government’s existing policy toolkit isn’t designed to take on this task. Washington has an elaborate apparatus for saying no to inbound investment but few ways of getting to yes. An improved system would welcome foreign capital and know-how while maintaining transparency, protecting U.S. data, and ensuring that Americans have control of companies when it matters. The fact is, the frontier of knowledge for many industries lies outside the United States. The federal government must get better at weighing the risks and rewards of foreign investment to take advantage of that expertise. THE HIGHEST FORM OF FLATTERY Throughout its history, the United States has used foreign knowledge and tools for its own gain. At the turn of the nineteenth century, for example, the country’s military readiness depended on a fledgling domestic gunpowder industry. Washington could no longer rely on its single foreign supplier, Britain, against which it had just fought a revolution. Supported by a significant French investment, the chemist Éleuthère Irénée du Pont brought French expertise in advanced manufacturing techniques to the United States, establishing a company in 1802 that would quickly become the biggest purveyor of explosives to the U.S. government. The firm, DuPont, remained at the center of innovation in U.S. chemical and materials production for centuries. Foreign knowledge has proved invaluable in more recent cases, too. In the early 1980s, when U.S. car companies were lagging behind their Japanese competitors, General Motors and Toyota jointly reopened a shuttered GM plant in Fremont, California. By bringing in state-of-the-art Japanese manufacturing systems, the companies transformed a failed factory into the most productive auto assembly plant in the United States within two years—while largely retaining the same American workforce. The methods GM picked up from Toyota are now standard across U.S. auto manufacturing. The CHIPS and Science Act was designed to replicate these and other successes, but with semiconductors. American lawmakers understood that creating a domestic chips industry would require investment and expertise from companies such as South Korea’s Samsung and the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Under the 2022 law, Washington issued grants and loan guarantees to firms, domestic and foreign, to build semiconductor fabrication plants in the United States and to train American workers in chip making, which is notoriously difficult to master. The act also funded the National Semiconductor Technology Center, which facilitates technology transfers and shared research and development between domestic chipmakers and foreign ones operating in the United States. Companies that accepted money from the U.S. government were barred from expanding advanced chip capacity in China. The United States is undermining its own industrial policy. If efforts to encourage foreign investment from U.S. allies and partners have proved contentious at times, deciding how to treat investment from the United States’ biggest rival, China, has been downright incendiary. More than any other government in history, Beijing has aggressively wielded the tools of economic statecraft. Its theft of intellectual property and enormous subsidization of domestic industry, combined with Washington’s longtime complacency, have hollowed out manufacturing capacity in much of the world and created dependencies on China for many critical technologies. It is easy in this context to conclude that the United States must keep out Chinese investment. The analyst Oren Cass, for instance, recently argued that allowing Chinese companies to invest in the United States would be “an unforced error of world-historic proportions” because it would cede dangerous economic influence to Beijing. But if the United States wants to produce more advanced goods, it needs to remain open to foreign investment, including from China. Indeed, China itself followed the same playbook beginning in the 1980s, luring U.S. companies to its shores with cheap labor, low taxes, and access to its vast domestic market. Much of China’s expertise can be linked back to foreign companies that set up factories in the country—expertise that Chinese firms later used to outcompete their foreign counterparts. In 2018, for example, China convinced Tesla to establish manufacturing facilities in Shanghai by offering cheap land, low-interest state loans, tax breaks, and permission to fully own its plant. Chinese automakers absorbed what they needed from Tesla and applied those lessons to propel the domestic electric vehicle sector forward. China is now at the forefront of many critical technologies, including electric vehicles and energy storage. Gaining access to that knowledge via foreign investment is, in many cases, the only way for the United States to catch up. BRAIN GAIN Chinese companies are already doing business in the United States in limited cases. In 2023, Ford announced a multibillion dollar plant in Marshall, Michigan, that will manufacture batteries for electric cars with technology and know-how licensed from China’s largest battery maker, CATL. Ford fully owns the facility but has a long-term agreement that enables it to train its workers on CATL’s core technological processes. Eventually, Ford could use the expertise learned from CATL to design and produce its own batteries without Chinese licenses. What Ford is doing in Michigan provides a model for an ambitious industrial strategy: encourage investment, work with foreign firms when necessary, and learn by doing. The partnership was possible because of a novel intellectual property-sharing arrangement with CATL that entailed licensing but not foreign ownership of the facility. In many other cases, however, presidential directives and onerous regulations get in the way of deals that have similar potential to strengthen the U.S. industrial base. U.S. presidents from both parties have used their authority under the Defense Production Act to block major foreign direct investments out of fear that sensitive American technology and data will fall into the wrong hands. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), the government body that reviews deals that could threaten national security, has become backlogged, difficult to navigate, and overly cautious. When the committee identifies a concern with a foreign company’s proposed investment, the firms involved frequently cannot negotiate a resolution within the statutory deadline and end up starting the process from the beginning. In 2024, applicants withdrew and refiled nearly a quarter of all notices. Filings have declined because the lengthy process discourages companies from even trying. In other cases, the problem is a lack of regulation altogether. CFIUS, for example, generally screens only those transactions in which foreign entities seek to acquire an interest in an American business. If a foreign company, say, wants to license out the use of its equipment, there is no formal review process through which it can receive approval. Such an arrangement falls into a gray zone, vulnerable to a political attack. Congress spent years threatening to disqualify Ford’s electric vehicle plant in Michigan from receiving a tax credit and investigated it for national security risks, in part, because the plant was not subject to any review process. DUE DILIGENCE To encourage American companies to pursue strategic foreign partnerships, the U.S. government must cut red tape and stop reflexively rejecting investment. It should treat capital from close allies as different from capital from countries of concern such as China, Iran, and Russia. It should also develop new systems to review and greenlight new models of foreign investment and partnership. When it comes to allies and partners, CFIUS should simplify its process. To reduce the number of U.S. companies and foreign investors that need to apply for approval, it ought to expand its list of countries whose firms are exempt from this requirement—currently just Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom—to include Japan, South Korea, and countries in Europe. Low-risk deals, such as investments in software companies whose only critical technology is routine encryption, should be exempt from filing, and there should be more rapid approval for pre-vetted investors. Most important, CFIUS should change how it judges the deals it does review. It should, for instance, analyze transactions on the basis of whether a foreign adversary could plausibly exploit the investment to harm the United States, instead of fixating on the investor’s nationality and business affiliations. The committee must also change its risk calculus. Today, the body can approve foreign investments in U.S. companies only by certifying that there are no unresolved security concerns. That means even a deal that would benefit national security overall cannot be approved if doubts linger about any single component of the arrangement. If resolving those doubts is impractical, the deal dies altogether. In other words, CFIUS only takes risk into account, not opportunity. Congress should replace this standard with one that lets the committee approve investment deals that are, on balance, in the national security interest. U.S. companies need more options for entering partnerships with foreign firms. For more risky investments, such as those by Chinese companies, the U.S. government should adopt a model similar to the Defense Department’s Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence program, which polices foreign control over defense contractors. The framework allows critical U.S. industries to benefit from foreign investment while guarding against foreign access to American secrets and foreign influence over key industries. Consider BAE Systems. The defense firm is wholly owned by a British parent company, yet it employs roughly 35,000 Americans, generates close to $13.6 billion in annual sales, is among the Pentagon’s largest suppliers, and is deeply involved in classified projects. This arrangement is possible because, under FOCI, a special agreement restricts the parent entity’s control over BAE Systems. The company has a separate U.S. board dominated by American directors with security clearances, and firewalls shielding technology, products, and programs from the foreign parent company. The arrangement gives the United States another major contractor competing for Pentagon work, tens of thousands of domestic manufacturing jobs, and access to British technology and capital. The British parent company, for its part, gets to profit from the world’s largest defense market. Meanwhile, the risk of leaks remains relatively low. Today, the FOCI regime applies only to companies that do business with the U.S. government on classified contracts. A system based on this program, however, should also be used to assess the risk and opportunity of foreign investments in companies that don’t need security clearances but could pose national security risks, such as those that make advanced chips, batteries, drones, or critical software. The Department of Commerce, which has already started negotiating arrangements with semiconductor companies that resemble those the Pentagon reaches with defense contractors under FOCI, could oversee an expanded system immediately under existing authorities (some of which were granted by the CHIPS Act). But Congress should codify the department’s authority to review and request adjustments to deals involving foreign adversaries. In practice, a firm contemplating an acquisition, joint venture, or licensing arrangement would submit a proposal to the Department of Commerce, which could add safeguards to the deal before issuing its approval. The goal is to give American companies more options for entering partnerships with foreign firms, with safety measures tuned to the specific risk presented by the investment. When the risk is that sensitive information may be leaked, a new FOCI-based system might allow foreign ownership as long as the parent company’s access to sensitive technology, data, and day-to-day decisions is severed through proxy boards, security agreements, and cleared American directors. When the foreign firm holds expertise the United States needs but is based in China or another country of concern, the right template may look like the Ford plant in Michigan, where an American company retains operating control but benefits from foreign ingenuity. Under such a system, the government would no longer default to rejecting deals but act as a creative problem solver. NAYSAYER NO MORE Establishing new pathways to approve foreign investment will not be easy. The politics of blocking these transactions are well entrenched in both parties. Regulators are so afraid of approving a deal that leaks sensitive technology or hands adversaries control over a key company that they err on the side of restricting access to knowledge, money, and production capability from abroad. The way to calm those fears and bring in productive foreign investment is to execute foreign deals competently. The Trump administration has treated announcements of major foreign investments as ends unto themselves but has shown little appetite for building a process to encourage safe deals with foreign companies. Democrats should embrace openness to foreign investment but improve on the practical application of that philosophy by championing legislation that institutionalizes a better and more transparent method for vetting agreements. With a system that approves the right kind of partnerships, the United States can gain the experience it desperately needs to revitalize its industrial capacity. From du Pont’s gunpowder to Arizona’s semiconductor factories, the United States has always become stronger not by walling itself off from the world’s know-how, but by making that knowledge its own. item.title: The Rise and Fall of Global Jihadism
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 3.02
Twenty-five years ago, members of the jihadi group al-Qaeda hijacked four American airplanes, flying two of them into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and one into the Pentagon, in Washington, D.C. Passengers attempted to seize control of the fourth plane, and it crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing everyone aboard. The hijackers killed 2,977 people in total—by far the deadliest single terrorist attack in history. To many Americans, the events of September 11, 2001, seemed to come out of nowhere. Few had even heard of al-Qaeda before the attacks. Yet by September 12, the United States had plunged into what President George W. Bush called “a war against terrorism,” a fight that would persist for decades, ensnare multiple jihadi groups, and extend to all corners of the earth. The United States had many setbacks in this war. The ways in which it attempted to prevent another 9/11, or an even larger-scale attack, entailed massive, often inefficient investments as well as troop losses. Some of its efforts, such as the full-scale wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, were brutally destructive. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular, drove a surge in jihadi recruitment. In the years since 2001, various new jihadi groups—some of them connected to al-Qaeda, some opposed to it—have set up shop in the Middle East and across East and West Africa, where they have fueled bloody civil wars, shattered local communities, and launched terrorist attacks both in the region and outside it. But the war on terrorism has not been a complete failure, either. Al-Qaeda itself is devastated. There have been few jihadi attacks on U.S. territory—perhaps the most important measure of success for most American leaders—in the past two and a half decades. According to New America Foundation data, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people in the United States since 2001, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared in the aftermath of 9/11. And although jihadi groups survive, jihadism has lost much of its ideological salience. Consider what has happened since 2023. On October 7, Hamas, a group that al-Qaeda regularly criticized for compromising on theological principles in the pursuit of its political agenda, launched a bloody terrorist attack on Israel, killing more than 1,100 people. Israel went on to kill tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza, many of them civilians, and conduct other attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and the West Bank. In 2025, the United States joined Israel in bombing Iran, and in 2026 the United States and Israel launched a full-scale war with the initial objective of regime change in Tehran. The Israeli war in Gaza led to mass protests around the world, and all of these events offered fodder for conspiracy theories about the enemies of Islam plotting against Muslims. Yet in contrast to the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq or the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, they have triggered no jihadi surge. Indeed, the former jihadis who overthrew the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad, in 2024, quickly sought to make nice with states that have long fought terror organizations, including the United States and Saudi Arabia, upon taking power. A quarter century after Osama bin Laden gave the order for the 9/11 attacks, his successors have not built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States and forcing governments to bend to their demands. The sense of historic possibility that once made the jihadi movement so threatening to Western countries has faded. The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost. THE BIRTH OF A MOVEMENT In late 2001, al-Qaeda appeared ascendant. The movement grew out of the armed struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and it attracted Muslim fighters from around the world. Under bin Laden’s leadership, al-Qaeda had many goals, including helping the Taliban secure power in Afghanistan and training its members for terrorist and insurgent campaigns throughout the Muslim world, but ousting the United States from the Middle East was at the top of the list. Other jihadis prioritized fighting governments that they saw as foreign invaders in Chechnya and Kashmir, toppling supposedly apostate Arab regimes, battling Shiite Muslims, or creating a caliphate. The scale of its attack on the United States gave al-Qaeda an aura of momentum and outsize influence within the jihadi movement and beyond. After 9/11, the movement grew in stature, and fighting the United States and its Western allies, which most jihadis had previously considered a relatively low priority, became a more mainstream objective. The fact that the U.S. government would make few distinctions between al-Qaeda-linked groups and jihadis with a more local focus in its subsequent counterterrorism campaign only reinforced that trend. Several factors had made the 2001 attacks possible. Among them were the many shortcomings in Washington’s approach to counterterrorism, including the mistakes identified by the 9/11 Commission, an independent body set up by the U.S. government in 2002, on which I served as a staff member. Those included poor information sharing among U.S. government agencies, a failure to place on watchlists future hijackers who were suspected of links to al-Qaeda and were believed to be traveling to the United States, a lackadaisical effort to find suspected terrorists believed to be in the United States already, and no response to alarming field officer reports that jihadis appeared to be interested in learning how to fly planes. The Islamic State’s overreach was ultimately its undoing. Just as important was al-Qaeda’s own organizing. Most of its leaders were creative, dedicated, and willing to work with other groups, giving the movement a large network from which to recruit the best operatives. Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, from which it could strategize, plot attacks, and coordinate with its international partners without interference. The CIA estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers attended training camps in Afghanistan in the late 1990s, enabling al-Qaeda to build a small army. Recruits from all over the world, but especially the Middle East, learned the basics of insurgent war. The more promising candidates learned advanced counterintelligence and bomb-making techniques. Some of those who received training went to fight alongside the Taliban against the group’s remaining enemies inside Afghanistan, and the Taliban permitted others to leave the country and rejoin local insurgent groups or terrorist cells around the world. Standout recruits among the mass of volunteers were selected for additional training and assigned to high-priority operations. Many of the 9/11 hijackers, for instance, initially went to Afghanistan with the intention to acquire skills and connections before traveling onward to Chechnya to fight alongside Chechen insurgents against Russian security forces. After they were indoctrinated in the camps, al-Qaeda sent them to attack the United States instead. Most governments around the world paid limited attention to this growing danger and did little to prevent members of terrorist organizations from recruiting, generating propaganda, fundraising, and networking on their soil as long as they did not carry out attacks there. Various jihadi leaders and operatives planned operations in Algeria, Bosnia, and elsewhere from London in the 1990s, for example. Even the United States was relatively lax; Ayman al-Zawahiri, who took over al-Qaeda after U.S. forces killed bin Laden in 2011, had come to the country in the 1990s to fundraise. THE TIDE TURNS, EVENTUALLY After 9/11, the United States’ counterterrorism efforts quickly succeeded in dismantling al-Qaeda’s base of operations. As the wreckage of the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers smoldered, the United States commenced military operations in Afghanistan. CIA officers and special operations forces, working with anti-Taliban groups and bolstered by U.S. airpower, quickly overthrew the Taliban. Many al-Qaeda members died in the fight. Those who survived lost their safe haven and, critically, their training camps, and were forced to flee. Most went to Pakistan and Iran and carried on the group’s operations from there; most of al-Qaeda’s most successful post–9/11 attacks, such as the 2005 bombings of London’s transportation system, were orchestrated from Pakistan. But both Islamabad and Tehran were less accommodating hosts than the Taliban were. Neither allowed al-Qaeda to establish new training camps, and Pakistani authorities, in particular, regularly helped the United States arrest and kill the group’s operatives. Without the large-scale training infrastructure that al-Qaeda had set up in Afghanistan, jihadi groups lost much of their ability to mount as sophisticated or distant an attack as 9/11, but they continued to terrorize local populations across the broader Middle East. The United States gave the jihadi cause new energy with its 2003 invasion of Iraq, a war justified in part by the need to confront terrorism. The subsequent U.S. occupation incited anger across the region and fueled the growth of anti-U.S. militant groups in Iraq. The chaos unleashed by the 2011 Arab uprisings gave these and other groups even more room to grow. The eventual outcome was the rise of the so-called Islamic State (or ISIS), which at its height in 2014–15 controlled territory in Iraq and Syria roughly the size of Virginia and home to millions of people. It attracted tens of thousands more recruits from countries in the Middle East, Europe, and Central Asia. Other groups, such as al-Shabab, in Somalia, also came to hold territory where they taxed and menaced the population and planned their operations. Yet persistent American pressure on the remaining jihadi havens bore fruit over time. In Iraq and Syria, the United States steadily eroded the Islamic State’s control until the group lost the last of its territory. Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which involved tens of thousands of U.S. forces, Washington deployed small special operations teams while local partners, trained by U.S. forces and backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence, did most of the fighting (and the dying). In other places such as Libya and Somalia, Washington supported the national armies and local militias battling jihadi forces and engaged in whack-a-mole with jihadi leaders. The advent of the armed drone aided this effort, enabling the U.S. military to gather more intelligence and strike more quickly, and with less collateral damage, compared with traditional airpower. Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services helped, as well. Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there—but it allowed Washington and its partners to uncover and unravel much of the global jihadi web, arresting members of al-Qaeda and other groups and disrupting their operations around the world. No less consequential were massive U.S. investments in homeland security. The Department of Homeland Security, created in 2002, was meant to bring together airport security, border protection, and other parts of the national security apparatus that would be involved in preventing terrorist attacks on U.S. territory. Increased spending at airports, on disaster response, and on improved communication between federal, state, and local officials was meant to ensure that information about new threats would be shared quickly, that terrorists would be prevented from entering the country, and that the response to any future attack would be better coordinated. The FBI made counterterrorism a top priority, and it aggressively investigated individuals suspected of terrorist activity. At times it was too aggressive; civil liberties organizations contend that the bureau detained and questioned large numbers of Muslim men and monitored mosques without evidence of wrongdoing. But overall, the effort was effective at preventing attacks. Each measure bolstered the others. Without training camps, would-be terrorists had no place to gain skills and network. Insufficient training could make them more prone to small mistakes that made their fundraising and recruiting efforts more easily detected. More active U.S. and allied security services would be ready to catch them, and then make the intelligence they gathered from those they arrested available to help target overseas networks and havens. The erosion of jihadis’ havens in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere steadily damaged the groups’ credibility and appeal. At the height of the Islamic State’s power, holding territory demonstrated its prowess and attracted followers who wanted to live in a place governed by the group’s version of Islamic law. But when the Islamic State lost territory, its calls for new fighters to come to defend its self-declared caliphate began to ring hollow. Recruitment became much harder. Fewer and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that increasingly looked like it was losing. OWN GOALS It was not only U.S. pressure that brought about the decline of jihadism. The jihadis themselves repeatedly made choices that reduced their appeal. For one, they made too many enemies. Al-Qaeda’s foes included not just the United States but also other supposed foreign occupiers, such as India, Israel, and Russia. Some strands within the broader movement also opposed regimes in Muslim countries that they considered impious, including the governments of Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Yemen. The Islamic State’s list of foes was even longer; it fought most fiercely against Shiites and other non-Sunni Muslims. Declaring so many enemies enabled these groups to attract a wide variety of followers, but it also meant that they diffused their energy. Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal. Even more damning, it ensured that everyone would attack them. Fighting jihadi terrorism was one of the few causes that united countries around the world, and the United States was able to solicit support for its intelligence and military campaigns from foreign governments that disagreed with Washington on many issues but shared an interest in quashing these groups. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience. Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups turned Muslim publics against them by mistreating Muslim civilians. People who might have been sympathetic to their fights against the United States and other foreign powers did not approve of jihadis’ killing of Saudi police and security officials in 2003 and 2004, for instance, or of an al-Qaeda affiliate’s slaughter of both Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006 and 2007. Such killings diminished the jihadis’ influence. In Saudi Arabia, the government, with the broad support of the public, killed or arrested al-Qaeda members, devastating the group’s operations in the country. In Iraq, the faction earned rebukes from clerics who had previously supported global jihad as well as from more mainstream religious leaders. The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing. Its declaration of a caliphate in 2014 was electrifying to many Muslims, coming at a time when the group seemed to be successfully expanding its borders and fighting off enemies. Yet the project created the conditions for the group’s eventual defeat. As bin Laden himself had privately warned another jihadi leader in Yemen years earlier, building a state would give the United States and other countries a place to concentrate their firepower. When the Islamic State declared its caliphate, not only did its territorial control make the group easier to target but its governing also exposed the group’s brutality. Its maximalist claims also made it impossible to work with other jihadis, let alone other countries. By the mid-2020s, the jihadi movement was in no position to capitalize on upheaval in the Middle East. The war in Gaza, the fall of Assad to former jihadis, and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran all supplied the kinds of grievances, images, and narratives that once fueled the movement’s global spread. But with the important exception of Somalia and large parts of West Africa, jihadi groups have not managed a mobilization comparable with the ones after the 2003 Iraq War or during the rise of the Islamic State. At those times, their ideology still had international momentum. Yet after the definitive collapse of the Islamic State’s territorial project, in most places the idea of global jihad lost its former appeal. The past few years might have provided an ideal opportunity to recruit disaffected Muslim youth in Europe and the Middle East, but the jihadis could not seize the moment. THE UNFINISHED FIGHT Despite the decline of jihadism and the relative safety of U.S. territory from attack after 9/11, it is difficult to claim that the United States won its war on terrorism. Neither major war fought under that banner, those in Afghanistan and Iraq, ended well. U.S. forces swiftly removed the Taliban from power in Afghanistan, eliminating the safe haven jihadis had enjoyed, but the campaign turned into a grinding stalemate and then, in 2021, a humiliating defeat when a reconstituted Taliban retook control of the country. The war in Iraq eventually allowed a better government than Saddam Hussein’s dictatorship to emerge, but it also set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State. These and other wars in the region came at a huge human cost, too. The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated that almost a million people, nearly half of them civilians, died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria, and Yemen between 2001 and 2023. The United States lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq, and more than 50,000 were wounded between the two conflicts. Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021. Counterterrorism efforts did not stop jihadism entirely, either. For years, U.S. military campaigns and effective al-Qaeda and Islamic State propaganda amplifying American and allied abuses kept alive the political conditions that enabled the ideology’s spread. And although no jihadi group was able to carry out another operation on the scale of 9/11, the United States and its allies were the target of numerous plots and attacks by individuals who were inspired by jihadi ideology even if they had never met an al-Qaeda or Islamic State member. Many attempted attacks have been foiled thanks to better countermeasures, but the desire to kill Americans and citizens of other countries on jihadi groups’ lists of enemies has not gone away. Efforts by successive U.S. administrations to take on jihadi propaganda directly—including numerous programs aimed at “countering violent extremism”—were not particularly effective at winning the hearts and minds of people who opposed U.S. policy and were disinclined to trust the United States while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars. It will take constant effort to ensure that jihadis cannot rebuild. The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however. At their height, jihadi groups proved capable of spectacular violence, forming alliances amid civil wars and even seizing territory. But they failed to translate those achievements into a durable political project or sustained global appeal. Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers anything like the same persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or plausible path to political transformation that it did in the first two decades of this century. Jihadis are not flocking to battle Israel or the United States, and the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers. This leaves Washington with tough decisions about how far it should go to fight the jihadi groups that remain active today. Most of them have survived by getting involved in civil wars that have been highly destructive but have erupted in places that are peripheral to U.S. interests, such as Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. There is a risk that jihadi groups could turn their involvement in these wars into opportunities to create new safe havens from which to organize international attacks. But if the United States attacks them directly, it also risks inviting retaliation and getting bogged down in new conflicts. In places such as Somalia and Yemen, Washington’s solution has been to launch drone attacks on jihadi leaders and operatives and provide limited support to regional governments, warlords, and tribal leaders to keep jihadi groups off balance. Yet as long as the governments in these countries remain weak and security assistance fails to move the needle significantly—or if, as the Trump administration has done in many African countries, Washington cuts its aid entirely—jihadi groups will remain active. The United States must accept that jihadism may never truly vanish. For now, U.S. and allied counterterrorism campaigns and jihadis’ poor track record are keeping these groups relatively contained. But it will take continued, constant effort—intelligence cooperation with allies, drone strikes on jihadi operatives, and military training for local partners—to ensure that they cannot start rebuilding in weak states. All of this is best done behind the scenes, denying jihadis easy propaganda victories and limiting the cost to the United States. If Washington can maintain vigilance without overextending itself, it can keep jihadism a manageable danger rather than letting it once again become a defining threat.
