item.title: China’s Purges Are Working as Designed
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.94
For two decades, scholars believed that the main reason Chinese communist rule endured into the twenty-first century—whereas every communist regime in Europe collapsed—was that it had built sturdy, long-lasting institutions. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had moved away from the unpredictable personalist dictatorship of the Mao Zedong era and established the foundations of a modern state. It set term limits on its leaders, embraced collective leadership, and increasingly promoted officials based on merit, which made it resilient enough to bounce back from the external and internal shocks that had felled other socialist systems. Chinese leader Xi Jinping, however, has spent the past decade demolishing nearly every institution that supposedly kept the party strong. He abolished presidential term limits in 2018, hollowed out collective leadership, and has declined to designate a successor. Xi has also purged high-level officials at will, especially in the most sensitive domain: the military. In January, only months after party leaders expelled nine senior military officers, the country’s Ministry of National Defense announced that General Zhang Youxia and General Liu Zhenli—until that point the People’s Liberation Army’s most senior uniformed officer and top operational commander, respectively—had been placed under investigation. Since 2022, according to data compiled by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the party has formally purged three dozen generals and lieutenant generals, and many more are conspicuously missing. In Washington, many observers see these purges as evidence of China’s weakness. They see a powerful leader consumed by suspicion and obsessed with maintaining his own grip on power. If the party’s strength were indeed based on the freestanding institutions that China had built in the post-Mao era, then Xi’s purges would be a warning sign of fragility and even a potential crackup. But the party has not shown any signs of falling apart. If anything, as these purges have continued, Xi and the party appear to have only gotten stronger. Far from weakening its rule, the way the CCP cleans its ranks can explain part of what makes it durable. A purge is not an event but a process—one that the party has run in nearly identical form for a century. It regularly targets, evaluates, and forces cadres to seek clemency to retain their standing within the system. The goal is to reform them rather than get rid of them entirely, which strengthens the party by encouraging obedience and dedication to the party’s cause. CCP leaders believe it’s working, too: Xi has embraced “self-revolution,” or continuous and permanent rectification, as the means by which China will escape the unhappy fate of the Soviet Union and other socialist regimes now residing in the dustbin of history. What could threaten the party’s longevity, then, is not the count of how many officials have been purged but the one problem that such a strategy cannot solve and can even make worse: how to handle succession. A regime of self-revolution will rise and fall on that question, no matter how hard it tries to avoid internal decay. CURE THE SICKNESS, SAVE THE PATIENT China’s history of purges predates the founding of the People’s Republic, in 1949. In some cases, as has been true in similar regimes, the CCP launches violent purges to remove cadres from its ranks. The type of purge now synonymous with the actions of Joseph Stalin in the Soviet Union aims at eliminating someone from the party, whether through incarceration, exile, or death. The victim of such a purge does not come back. Mao employed this tactic as early as 1930, when he executed more than 700 army officers in a show of total control. But what the CCP has also done, and what is unique to its continued rule, is not a purge in the traditional sense. CCP leaders often turn to a different method of discipline: rectification. Rectification aims to keep a person inside the party, even if sometimes at a greatly diminished status. Whereas the traditional idea of a purge seeks to eliminate enemies in the ranks (the Chinese term qingdang means to “cleanse the party”), rectification aims to retain and remold cadres while keeping them in the party’s orbit. Throughout its history, the CCP has sought to rectify cadres far more frequently than it has sought to eliminate them. In December 1929, in the village of Gutian, in Fujian province, Mao put forward a resolution called “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party” that asserted the party’s control of the military. The resolution also included clues as to how the party understood internal discipline: it described its targets not as enemies but as people who had deviations in their thinking. Cadres might suffer from ailments such as having a “purely military viewpoint” (a perspective untethered from politics), promoting ultrademocracy (a political system lacking party authority), and supporting individualism. Mao’s resolution treated each of these as a sickness that could sometimes be cured through a regimen of criticism and self-criticism in front of peers. And it attached a promise to the cure: if party members submitted to the process, the CCP would retain them rather than destroy them. In the northern Chinese area of Yan’an, where Mao and his followers set up a wartime base camp starting in the mid-1930s, leaders turned rectification into doctrine. Party membership exploded from roughly 40,000 in 1937 to 800,000 by 1940, which meant that almost everyone in the organization was new and not yet trustworthy in the eyes of party leaders. The Rectification Movement of 1942–45 was the solution. Every cadre wrote an autobiography, measured his or her life against printed self-examination outlines, confessed before his or her party branch or work unit, and was examined, graded, and sorted by the party’s personnel department. In February 1942, Mao summarized the approach in a famous line: “Cure the sickness, save the patient.” Rectification aims to retain and remold cadres. None of this was gentle. The Yan’an campaign was brutal: many were tortured, and thousands died. Subsequent campaigns were often even harsher. But Mao’s approach separated Chinese communism from its nearest relatives. Stalin quickly executed unreliable cadres, and Pol Pot sent them to mass graves. In China, in many cases, the strategy was to keep cadres and try to remold them while also building permanent files detailing their every mistake. The basic procedure remains nearly identical today. A person is singled out for deviating in some way and made to write an account of his or her shortcomings. The account is checked against what his colleagues say about him and against what the organization’s records (in that individual’s personal file) already hold. The cadre is placed on a graded scale of possible sanctions, ranging from no action at one end to expulsion from the party at the other. (Most sanctions fall in the middle, including issuing a serious warning or putting someone on probation.) When a verdict on how to deal with a cadre, official, or campaign target is issued, that person, if deemed to have confessed sufficiently, is kept in the party but on terms that are revocable and conditional on the political winds. And every piece of paper the process generates goes into the cadre’s official file, permanently. It is the process used in 1952 against a village storekeeper who skimmed off the top of procured grain. It is also the process used today for China’s Politburo, whose members—the country’s most powerful men—read self-criticisms aloud to one another once a year and have their confessions written down and permanently attached to their files following the same template that was used in Yan’an. Even as Xi has expanded the scope of who can be targeted, the machinery has not changed. The ongoing case of the purged military officers under Xi likely fits this model, too. Zhang and Liu have been placed under investigation, not shot, and there is a chance that they remain on the party’s books, even if they are saddled with a thicker personal dossier and given a meaningless post or sidelined from public life altogether. In 2023, the diplomat Qin Gang, for instance, was removed from his position as foreign minister; news investigations reported that he had kept his party membership but had been reassigned to a low-level desk job at the foreign ministry’s publishing house. And even if Zhang and Liu are expelled from the party, purging remains the exception rather than the norm, as has been the party’s long-standing practice. Of the 101 generals and lieutenant generals that the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified as purged or potentially purged, only 14 had been officially kicked out of the party as of February. SINGLE FILE Rectification rarely, if ever, changes cadres’ beliefs. Eighty years of evidence, much of it the party’s own, shows cadres parroting the scripts given to them, performing the required contrition, and then reverting to their earlier behaviors the moment the campaign ends. It is a process so ritualized that participants learn to say exactly what examiners want to hear. Yet the main goal of the process is not to reform belief but to create a document to put into a dossier on file. Such a file contains objective personnel data as well as observable assessments of a cadre’s political shortcomings. It is this paper trail that enables the regime to maintain discipline even if no cadres change how they act or think. For cadres and others subject to rectification, the process sorts who is in and who has fallen out of the good graces of party leaders. As cadres constantly jockey for status, a purge is exceptional and devastating. For most party members, surviving a rectification process with minimal punishment is grounds for relief (and often accompanied by a desire to recommit to a forgiving regime) combined with a sliver of fear that the next campaign is always just around the corner. Expanded to 100 million party members, this process produces an internalized discipline in each person that strengthens the organization’s grip on power. Each cadre wakes up every day knowing the dossier exists and that it can be used against them at any time. The permanent, standardized, reopenable record of every party member’s history, associations, and vulnerabilities is also an information system that gives party leaders immense power. Autocratic rulers need information to head off threats to their power; the CCP’s personnel file system, filled with information about the party’s cadres, is an irreplaceable channel of information for China’s rulers. Most cadres are willing to go along with the party’s wishes, but for the small minority that does not express the proper attitude in the face of a discipline campaign, the party can expel them or put them in jail, heading off any threat of revolt from within. High-level defection and dissent sometimes occur, but when they do they are rarely organized and quickly fizzle out. Such record-keeping might be expected to generate resentment among party cadres, but the process is designed to spread the blame and thus insulate Beijing from any backlash. There is no single person or entity that issues a rectification verdict. Instead, party task forces (known as work teams) are mobilized to draft the verdict, colleagues from their workplace endorse it, and then a committee at a higher level of administration ratifies it. It passes through enough hands in the process that authorship is aggregated and spread so that no individual leader or party entity can be said to be responsible. Even the cadre, through his or her own self-criticism, is a co-author in the verdict. Disciplining cadres with rectification is also a coordination device. The Chinese party-state is a sprawling network of bureaucratic agencies, regional power bases, and administrative offices that have their own interests and frequently have to bargain with one another. A rectification campaign is one of the few instruments that transcends these fissures. As with the party’s other massive campaigns, such as the one-child policy, cadres understand that compliance with rectification is mandatory and a high priority for leaders. Discipline campaigns offer unambiguous carrots and sticks, including leniency for cadres who show the right attitude and professional purgatory, even exile, for those who do not. Many cadres who normally benefit from taking advantage of the fragmentation in China’s political system know to drop everything else and go along with discipline campaigns, providing Beijing with a highly visible way to impose unified priorities and strengthen party control. WHAT DISCIPLINE CANNOT SOLVE Chinese history is rife with examples of once powerful dynasties weakening and eventually falling apart. To avoid this outcome, Mao’s solution was mass mobilization: only by letting the people supervise the government, he believed, would it not slacken. Xi’s answer, offered in 2021 and elaborated since, is the party’s self-revolution. In this framework, the cure for the party’s ills can only come from inside the party, not from any external force. Ongoing party rectification campaigns require all officials to discipline themselves, and the occasional outright purge of some cadres provides undeniable proof that failure to comply has consequences. It is the first time the party has explicitly located the mechanism of its own survival inside itself. The choreography has been equally explicit. In the fall of 2014, with investigations that felled two senior military leaders underway, Xi summoned some 400 senior officers to the same hall in the village of Gutian where Mao had issued “On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party.” State media called it the “new Gutian conference.” In 2024, Xi convened the military to discuss political work (that is, ideological loyalty) at Yan’an—a clear reminder that the party sees a direct line from past rectification campaigns to its present strength. Beneath the symbolism is Xi’s fear that China could end up like the Soviet Union, whose own Communist Party, Xi believes, let its internal disciplinary mechanisms atrophy and thus was the architect of its own demise. Beijing believes that the purges and rectification must continue permanently if the party is to remain in power. Whether or not the analysis of Soviet collapse is accurate, the CCP’s continued strength suggests that the party’s method of disciplining cadres may indeed explain its durability. Xi’s purges should not be measured by how many cadres they ensnared but whether they continue to produce files, verdicts, and party retention that keep the party firmly in control. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. But what strengthens the party also weakens some of China’s instruments of power. Senior military commands sit vacant or are staffed by less experienced officers, and future officers learn that the safest career record is a thin one. When forced to choose, political control is always more important to the party than operational effectiveness. This is a tradeoff that the party has been willing to make for a century and will continue to make. And China’s method of purges cannot solve the danger of succession. Rectification produces no mechanism for choosing the next ruler—if anything, by ensuring that no subordinate accumulates independent standing, it makes the emergence of a credible successor even harder. Succession, not discipline, is where the system is weak. The older generation of CCP leaders, including Mao and Deng Xiaoping, overcame the challenge of succession by drawing on their unassailable authority as revolutionaries who had fought for the party’s survival, and subsequent leaders relied on the institutions—term limits, collective leadership, and regularized succession rules—that Xi has summarily destroyed. Xi has neither, which makes the succession problem especially acute. The moment to worry about Chinese stability is not when generals disappear amid an investigation, but when the man who reads their files begins to age out of the role without an answer as to who will follow. The CCP is not going to collapse: the file system exists precisely to prevent elite fracture, and it has worked. What is likely to emerge instead is a state that is militarily weaker and politically stronger than most assessments suggest. The greatest source of uncertainty now is Xi’s eventual succession. Beijing’s own theorists are watching this, too, because they know that even a well-engineered system of rectification that has kept the party strong for a century has no answer for an elite power struggle over who comes next. item.title: Shrink the UN
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.91
The United Nations, international officials sometimes joke, is always in crisis. Since its inception in 1945, the organization has had to navigate deep geopolitical tensions, devastating humanitarian disasters, and periodic budget shortfalls. But as world leaders gather in New York for the annual General Assembly high-level week, the UN appears to be in particularly bad shape. China, Russia, and the United States, three of the five veto-wielding powers that dominate the Security Council, have prevented it from acting on wars in Iran and Ukraine and civil conflicts in Myanmar and Sudan. Poor countries complain that donor states have not met their UN pledges on development spending. And the Trump administration halted most U.S. funding to UN activities last year, forcing the organization to cut back on its peacekeeping and relief efforts. With challenges mounting, an upcoming leadership transition may decide whether the UN can stabilize itself and perhaps even regain some credibility—or slide further into decrepitude. Current Secretary-General António Guterres plans to step down at the end of the year, having struggled to reverse the organization’s political fortunes in his decadelong tenure. He has spent much of his last two years in office grappling with staff reductions and other cost-cutting measures to ensure the UN secretariat does not go bankrupt on his watch. His has been a thankless task, but diplomats and UN officials hope a new leader will be able to take a longer-term approach to refreshing the institution and keeping governments committed to multilateralism. The small crop of candidates to succeed Guterres include senior UN trade official Rebeca Grynspan, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency Rafael Grossi, and Guyana’s Ambassador to the UN Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett. Regardless of who wins, Guterres' successor will need to develop a new playbook for revitalizing the organization. Any serious effort must acknowledge an unpleasant reality: as long as the world remains competitive and chaotic, the UN’s ability to forge wide-ranging international agreements will remain constrained. The next secretary-general’s best hope may thus be to relinquish some of the organization’s previous lofty ambitions and slim down, prioritizing international crisis prevention and conflict resolution, the efficient provision of humanitarian aid, and achievable international development goals. A UN that jettisons time-consuming diplomatic processes and inefficient bureaucracies for a few core functions may disappoint ardent advocates of global governance. But it also may be the only version of the organization still viable in an era of great-power competition and austerity. LESS MONEY, MORE PROBLEMS Since the end of the Cold War, UN chiefs have responded to moments of crisis by arguing that the institution should do more, not less. Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the first secretary-general of the post–Cold War era, envisioned the UN as a supercharged global peacemaking body, but during his final years in office, after blue helmet peacekeepers failed to prevent the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia in 1995, the organization briefly retrenched. Beginning in the late 1990s, Boutros-Ghali’s successor, Kofi Annan, set out a new approach, establishing fresh poverty-reduction goals, battling AIDS, and launching UN peace operations in Kosovo, Timor-Leste, and several African countries. The U.S. war in Iraq, in 2003, split the Security Council and temporarily derailed Annan’s agenda, but he organized a global summit in 2005 to persuade governments to recommit to multilateralism and led the establishment of a new Peacebuilding Commission and the Geneva-based Human Rights Council the following year. In the two decades since Annan left office, his successors, Ban Ki-moon and Guterres, have had to contend with a mounting catalog of crises, above all the Syrian civil war, which divided the Security Council for over a decade. As the number of conflicts, humanitarian crises, and natural disasters increased, so, too, did the UN’s budget. The combined revenue of all UN entities rose from $40 billion in 2010 to a high of $74 billion in 2022, driven in considerable part by greater humanitarian spending. Ban and Guterres also repeatedly appealed to UN members to show greater solidarity. Ban championed the Paris climate change pact in 2015. Guterres convened a “Summit of the Future” in 2024, at which member states promised to cooperate on issues as varied as artificial intelligence and intergenerational justice. These agreements demonstrated vision and extraordinary diplomatic effort; the Paris accord won particularly widespread public support. But UN member states have often failed to honor the commitments outlined in past agreements, breeding a skepticism over the effectiveness of multilateralism that has in turn made it harder to get mistrustful members to sign onto new deals with binding legal force and solid enforcement mechanisms. UN negotiations have increasingly generated paperwork and processes rather than concrete results. Over time, the gap between the UN’s ambitious self-conception and its actual track record has grown too wide for even the organization’s advocates to ignore. Presidents and prime ministers continue to turn up at the UN. Diplomats churn out resolutions and statements. But the organization now has to compete with alternative clubs of states, such as the G-7, BRICS, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s nascent Board of Peace, which offer spaces to debate and collaborate without going through the cumbersome procedures of UN diplomacy. A wave of populist and nationalist governments sweeping into power around the world have also taken issue with the organization’s commitments to universal values, especially with respect to the treatment of refugees and migrants, a line of attack that both Trump administrations have encouraged. UN negotiations have generated paperwork and processes rather than concrete results. Trump’s greatest immediate impact on the UN, however, has been on its finances. In the early months of 2025, his administration froze almost all U.S. funding for UN humanitarian work and refused to pay into the organization’s core budget. Last year, it paid less than half of its expected contributions for UN peacekeeping. These cuts initially looked like a coup de grâce for the wobbling organization, but now many diplomats see them as a necessary wake-up call to UN officials to start tightening their belts. Other funders such as China and the EU have refused to fill the financial gaps left by Washington, suggesting that skepticism extends beyond the White House. Many European countries have continued to cut humanitarian aid as they divert money to defense. Beijing is now on the hook for about a fifth of the organization’s core costs, second only to Washington, and U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz has noted that the two powers have found a “kind of common ground” on cuts. The worst of the Trump cuts may have already passed—Washington has released roughly $4 billion for humanitarian work this year and just processed a $725 million contribution to the UN main budget—but the organization’s next leader will still need to get by with reduced means. The incoming secretary-general will therefore face the knotty challenge of fulfilling the UN’s mission and regaining the trust of its members while continuing to economize. Contrary to the institutional instinct to renew itself by expanding its range of activities, the task ahead should be to find a more focused agenda for cooperation that skeptical states can buy into. The candidates all acknowledge the need for financial discipline and a practical approach to global problem solving. None have outlined detailed proposals, but all agree that, in Grossi’s words, “the world does not need more declarations.” Striking a similar note, Grynspan has promised to “make the UN more useful, more agile, and more accountable” to its members. Whoever gets the job will need to be more specific once in office. The secretary-general’s authority over the UN system is complicated by a tangle of different governance structures, budgeting processes, and institutional interests, and the long expansion of UN activities has left behind significant institutional redundancies. Three agencies in Rome deal with different aspects of agriculture and food security. The UN Refugee Agency and International Organization for Migration oversee efforts to help displaced people in the same regions, often competing for “market share” crisis by crisis. A small host of envoys, offices, and trust funds deal with different aspects of climate change. No two UN insiders have the same recipe for boiling down this profusion of entities, although all agree that consolidation is needed—just not in their own agency. The next secretary-general will therefore need to knock heads together and streamline how the UN raises funds, organizes crisis response, and deconflicts between the mandates of its constituent parts. THE PRICE OF PEACE Just as candidates see a case for consolidation, they also share the view that reform should center on reviving the UN’s role in peacemaking. In this they reflect the prevailing view among diplomats in New York that Guterres has too frequently neglected peace and security. In some of the major wars during his tenure, including those in Ethiopia and Sudan, he has concentrated on providing humanitarian access and stayed away from efforts to find political solutions, citing the office’s relative powerlessness. The secretary-general’s reticence in the face of war is understandable. Splits among the Security Council members with veto powers have constrained the UN’s capacity to influence first-order political crises. Russia has used its veto in the Security Council to ensure that the UN has no political role in Ukraine. The Biden administration bristled at UN efforts to promote a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas in Gaza in late 2023, and Trump’s own cease-fire plan marginalized the UN in favor of his Board of Peace. Washington has paid scant attention to UN efforts to ease the humanitarian crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, having already blatantly disregarded the UN Charter’s prohibition on acts of aggression when it launched its war in Iran. China has quietly but effectively made it clear to member states that the UN should limit its role in Myanmar’s civil war. Yet Guterres’s instinct to shrink away from peacemaking duties has also alienated many UN members who still believe that the UN should do more to help resolve conflicts where the veto power’s fundamental interests are not at stake. His tendency to emphasize global issues unrelated to conflict is also increasingly out of step with how many UN members assess the challenges that they face. In an era of expanding conflict, ambassadors in New York say their capitals want to know what the UN can offer in the way of security. They may value cooperation in other areas, but matters of peace and war take precedence. The next secretary-general should focus on quieter, cheaper forms of crisis diplomacy. The candidates vying to succeed Guterres acknowledge this reality. Despite having mainly worked on trade and development at the UN, for instance, Grynspan has said her “priority will be to restore confidence in the UN as a trusted convenor in theaters of conflict.” But it is easier to promise to be a peacemaker than to resolve actual wars, not least when countries with veto powers are involved. And even in conflicts in which permanent members of the Security Council are not directly implicated, influential middle powers can make peacemaking a major challenge: the Gulf powers have largely sidelined the organization in Sudan. To restore faith in the UN’s core mission, the next secretary-general must show both the veto-holding powers and the organization’s wider membership that it can play a useful role in averting and ending conflicts. It can do so with strategies and tools already on hand. During the Cold War, Secretary-General U Thant mediated between the United States and the Soviet Union, making possible the backchannel diplomacy that resolved the Cuban missile crisis. Over the decades since, the UN has built up unrivaled expertise on managing mediation processes, along with logistics and administrative structures necessary to mount large-scale peace and stabilization missions. The Trump administration acknowledged as much last year, when it lobbied the Security Council to mandate that the UN backstop a Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. Although the UN can still get large numbers of boots on the ground where necessary, the demand for large-scale multinational peace operations—the hallmark of UN crisis management in the 1990s and early 2000s—is likely to remain low. Instead, the next secretary-general should focus on quieter, cheaper forms of crisis diplomacy, devoting time and energy to shuttling between the veto-holding powers and middle powers as an impartial source of advice and ideas. This work will involve more behind-the-scenes trust building than dramatic public breakthroughs. But if the UN’s next leader can convince the world that the organization is a reliable peacemaker, it may lay the groundwork for more ambitious work in the future. PARTY’S OVER A renewed focus on peacemaking does not mean the UN must abandon all other goals entirely. The organization’s leaders will, however, need to choose their priorities wisely. In 2015, UN members agreed an ambitious set of sustainable development goals, including a promise to end extreme poverty globally by 2030. After the economic shocks associated with the COVID-19 pandemic, Ukraine, and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, they have little chance of reaching them. Diplomats are preparing to negotiate a new package of goals for the period after 2030. The 2015 goals involved 169 specific targets spread across 17 policy baskets ranging from “life on land” to peace, justice, and security, the sheer complexity of which has made it harder to rally political and public support for the main points of the agenda. Many UN members will want to keep (or even add to) this diversity of initiatives. But the next UN chief may have to call for a tighter agenda centered on poverty reduction, climate change adaptation, and buffering countries against global economic shocks. Many diplomats from developing countries fret that richer states want to dump the development agenda altogether; the Trump administration has partially confirmed their suspicions by disowning the existing development goals. Agreeing on a shorter, better-defined list of post-2030 targets could help donors and developing countries find common ground. A similar tempering of ambition may be necessary on global challenges such as climate change and the regulation of new technologies. The UN’s current preferred method of advancing agreements on these issues tends to involve a surfeit of conferences and statements. For example, 55,000 people representing states, private companies, and civil society groups registered to attend the UN summit on climate change in Brazil last year. Although these generous invitation lists may look inclusive, they are not a recipe for clear decision-making. The next secretary-general will need to reflect on how to initiate policy on complex global problems without all the hoopla. Diplomats recalling the practices of successful secretaries-general emphasize that they developed major policy carefully with small numbers of diplomatic allies. Just as secretary-generals’ conflict-resolution work may involve more behind-the-scenes contacts and fewer large blue helmet deployments, their diplomacy around global issues may involve more quiet gatherings and fewer megaconferences. This has downsides: the UN can use global sentiment as political fuel, especially when powerful states are wary of acting. To be sure, there will be times when the secretary-general wants to rile up global public opinion. But low-key coalition building will just as often work better. GENERAL REASSEMBLY Experts pondering the future of multilateralism often wonder what it would take to get the UN back on track. Some believe that the institution’s internal contradictions will eventually force members to agree to a full-scale review of its charter, a drastic step that could just as easily exacerbate diplomatic tensions as it could ameliorate them. Others speculate that a major shock—a catastrophic AI-enabled attack on multiple countries’ infrastructures or a cascade of climate-related disasters—could jolt governments into recognizing the need for multilateral cooperation. The next secretary-general should quietly plan for such scenarios. If and when one occurs, the better prepared the UN is the more relevant it will be. In the meantime, the incoming UN leadership needs to regain the trust of the government and peoples it serves by showing that it can make a dent in the global rise in conflicts, focus its diplomatic and operational efforts better, and offer a platform for pragmatic global problem solving. This slimmer UN may be the UN the world needs. item.title: Why America Can’t Strangle Iran
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.74
For Iran and the United States, August 24 was Groundhog Day. “We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe,” declared U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime.” It was the same promise he made in April, when he said that the United States was “imposing a financial stranglehold on the Iranian regime” under what the White House called Operation Economic Fury. It was also akin to the May 2018 rollout of the first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” campaign, in which Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced that Iran would be targeted by the “strongest sanctions in history.” And it sounded like U.S. President Barack Obama’s promise, made in 2012, that the Iranian government was to face “even more crippling sanctions.” The Iranian economy has certainly felt the effects of all the successive restrictions. Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term in office, the country has experienced little growth and high inflation. As a result, Iranian firms have built less infrastructure and adopted fewer new technologies compared with peers in other developing economies. Iranian households, once increasingly affluent, are now at risk of falling below the state’s poverty line. Yet for the better part of a decade, Iran has been able to resist U.S. economic coercion. Until the recent blockade, it used sanctions-evasion techniques to continue oil exports to its key customer, China. Its non-oil industries also adapted to the sanctions, as currency devaluation reduced competition from imports and made Iranian products more competitive in regional markets, boosting exports. Iran thereby avoided the kind of runaway economic collapse seen in other sanctioned countries, such as Syria and Venezuela. Today, war is testing the resilience of the Iranian economy in ways that sanctions alone could not. Numerous U.S. and Israeli airstrikes have targeted critical industrial facilities, including some of Iran’s most important steel and petrochemical plants. The damage sustained during these attacks has led to major production outages for key industrial goods. The general decline in maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the specific disruptions caused by the U.S. naval blockade have not only reduced Iran’s exports; they have also throttled imports of much-needed capital and consumer goods. According to a July estimate by the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s GDP is set to contract 5.4 percent this year after shrinking by less than half that over the previous 12 months. Year-on-year inflation climbed from 52.6 percent in December 2025 to 88.6 percent by the start of the summer. The value of the country’s currency has hit a record low of over two million rials to the dollar. But even as the country’s economic situation is getting worse, Iran’s leadership remains better able to resist the coercive effects of sanctions than it might appear. The state of the economy is not yet impinging on Iran’s ability to wage war. Stockpiles of various goods remain deep, thanks to years of sanctions experience. And the Iranian state, with its powerful repressive tools, has figured out how to offload much of the economic pain onto ordinary Iranians while making sure its own needs are met. Trump’s approach, in other words, can certainly immiserate most of the country’s people. But it cannot successfully strangle the Islamic Republic itself. ANATOMY OF A CRISIS Iranian officials have acknowledged the country’s economic difficulties. “No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we will not endure,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran’s parliament and a key power broker, on August 21. (Bessent cited this quote as evidence that U.S. economic warfare was having its intended effect.) During a television interview last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian expressed frustration that some of his fellow political leaders continue to deny that sanctions are harming the country. “Some say sanctions have no effect at all; I really don’t know what to say to those people,” he remarked. The statements from Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian reflect genuine concern about Iran’s economic trajectory. The speaker and the president are understandably worried about deteriorating public opinion, given the inherent connections between general economic welfare and political legitimacy. But U.S. officials should be wary of overinterpreting these statements. Contrary to what it might seem, neither leader is suggesting that the country’s economy is on the brink of collapse. American assessments of the Iranian economy and the success of economic coercion fail to account for the ways in which sanctions have transformed Iran’s political economy, altering the distribution of economic resources in ways that reinforce its existing power structure. The Iranian leaders who are most vocal about the suffering of ordinary people are not worried about the country’s imminent economic collapse; they are dissenting against a political consensus that has long enabled Iranian elites to deliberately push the pressure of sanctions onto ordinary people. Ghalibaf and Pezeshkian are complaining about the social costs of a policy response that has worked largely as intended. Perhaps more important, U.S. assessments of the Iranian economy miss important dynamics. Typically, the effects of sanctions are described in terms of macroeconomic indicators, including rates of growth, inflation, and currency depreciation. But these measures mainly capture price levels: the value of goods and services. They provide, in other words, a financial—not a functional—view of the economy. To take a functional view, one must look at the dynamics at the firm and household level; they reveal why deteriorating figures in the headlines have not led to Iran’s capitulation. Iranian officials pushed the pain of sanctions onto households and firms. The fundamental dilemma for policymakers in any comprehensively sanctioned country is how to respond to balance-of-payments vulnerabilities, such as when a country runs out of the foreign currency it needs to pay for imports. There are, broadly speaking, two approaches. Policymakers can use expansionary monetary policy to fuel investment, restoring the trade surplus through a combination of higher exports and increased domestic production. Alternatively, policymakers can use monetary tightening and austerity measures to suppress import demand, restoring the trade surplus at similar export levels. When faced with major sanctions after invading Ukraine, Russian policymakers took the first approach. They increased fiscal stimulus, driving a rapid expansion in industrial activity and manufacturing employment that created a distinct war economy. This spending was necessary to increase military production, but it also had the effect of dramatically tightening the labor market, raising real wages for ordinary Russians. That, in turn, blunted the initial effects of sanctions-related inflation. This approach eventually reached its limits, and inflation is starting to bite, but the economic strategy allowed Russia to persist in its war aims despite U.S. sanctions pressure. Iranian officials, by contrast, chose the second course of action. When major financial and energy sanctions imposed by the Obama administration first pushed Iran into a recession in 2012, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called for Iran to adopt a “resistance economy,” focusing on domestic capacities to counteract the sanctions pressure. But Iranian economic policymakers never managed to implement a new industrial policy or set up a new welfare system. Instead, they tolerated inflation, effectively pushing the pain of the sanctions away from the government and onto households and firms. They ran austerity budgets and refused to rationalize production or consumption through direct administration, such as by instituting quotas or price controls. The worsening economic crisis led to weakness in the labor market, allowing employers to engage in wage repression and leading to further pressure on household incomes. At first, this may seem like a policy failure. But in reality, Iranian authorities appear perfectly content to see economic activity slow. Doing so, they believe, will give them staying power in their confrontation with the United States. GOOD TIMES, BAD TIMES Microeconomic data reveal the effects of U.S. pressure on economic activity at the firm and household level. A review of Purchasing Managers’ Index data compiled by Iran’s Chamber of Commerce makes clear how the country’s economic crisis has intensified. Between 2019 and 2023, Iran’s overall economy was in contraction for two-thirds of the period thanks to Trump’s initial maximum pressure sanctions, the COVID-19 pandemic, and disruptions related to the “Women, Life, Freedom” protests. But throughout this period, Iranian non-oil industries experienced modest growth. At the start of 2023, Iran even began to exit its long recession as the overall economy and the industrial sector grew in tandem. By March 2024, living standards were beginning to rise again, buoyed by a roughly 15 percent increase in real incomes. This recovery was derailed by the April 2024 Israeli airstrikes on Iran. Since then, the economic uncertainty associated with recurring military conflict has triggered a prolonged decline in industrial activity, pushing Iran into an even deeper recession. Industrial firms have reported deteriorating conditions for eight consecutive months. But that does not mean these firms are insolvent. Over the last two decades, Iranian companies have developed a practice of maintaining large inventories. This practice allows firms to mitigate the effects of sanctions on supply chains and helps shore balance sheets in a high-inflation environment in which cash loses its value but goods do not. According to filings made by companies listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange, the average “days inventory outstanding” level among Iranian industries is around three months. In sensitive sectors such as electrical machinery, which has been heavily targeted by U.S. restrictions, firms maintain inventories as high as 200 days. These large inventories have been a source of significant economic resilience during the war. Iranian supply chains came under strain as ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dwindled. A shift toward overland trade could not compensate for the loss of container traffic through Iran’s southern ports. But with an ample inventory of raw materials, semifinished goods, and finished products, Iranian producers could keep customers supplied—or at least customers with the means to pay. Tehran has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. Firms kept raising prices to protect their margins, passing higher input costs onto consumers. And as the war continued, these higher prices led to demand destruction. Iranian households, embattled by years of persistent inflation, began to consume less. When they did buy, they increasingly relied on consumer credit, including new buy-now-pay-later schemes and informal loans. Even in special categories such as food, Iranian retailers reported diminished sales volume. The sharp drop in household consumption is clear evidence that economic welfare in Iran is declining. It is why Iranian officials have been forced to acknowledge the pain felt by ordinary people. But even so, the government has thus far failed to intervene to control rising prices. Not only have officials failed to introduce price controls—a move that successfully blunted the economic pain associated with the Iran-Iraq War 40 years ago—they have also discussed the elimination of cash transfers and energy subsidies for large portions of the population. In this respect, demand destruction has acted as a form of rationing, providing a structured way for Iranian political and economic elites to push the costs of the war and sanctions onto ordinary people. Although the government continues to face significant fiscal pressure, it has accepted inflation as a necessary evil to maintain its own spending. With a monthly inflation rate of under ten percent, Iran is still a long way from the kind of hyperinflation—typified by monthly inflation of over 50 percent—that will make the government’s strategy untenable. Meanwhile, reduced economic activity has provided buffers for the real economy. In financial terms, the Iranian economy is in a worse position than at the outset of the war, but in functional terms, inventory levels are unchanged from December 2025, and supply and demand may find a new balance at a lower level of overall economic activity. Iran’s foremost vulnerability to sanctions and the blockade remains its persistent need for imports, which totaled $17 billion in the first five months of this Iranian calendar year beginning in March. That means imports will likely total around $40 billion by the end of the year, down significantly from $58 billion in the previous year and $72 billion in the year before that. The fall in import demand, driven by inflation and currency devaluation, is evidence of a deeper economic crisis. But in the near term, it will help Iranian policymakers forestall a wider economic collapse, possibly for several years. LOW POWER MODE When Bessent evoked the imagery of an “economic D-Day” in his August press conference, he failed to consider who is standing on the other side of his planned invasion. Although it may not seem like it, the success of Iranian authorities in transferring the costs of both sanctions and the war onto ordinary people represents a form of wartime mobilization. Ordinary Iranians may not wish to be mobilized in this way, but they do not have a choice. In a recent social media post, Trump asked, “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” But even if ordinary Iranians were to take to the streets again to protest the financial repression they are enduring, they would once again face the brutal violence of the Islamic Republic. With multiple repressive tools at their disposal, many Iranian leaders believe that the country’s population can be made to tolerate more pain, especially if it is necessary to defeat the United States militarily. To prevail in its economic war, the Trump administration will thus need to asphyxiate 25 million households and more than one million firms. But as breathing slows in parts of Iran’s economy, ample oxygen will remain for the country’s elite. item.title: The New Chinese Way of Cyberwar
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.65
Over the past year, the world’s attention has turned to economic chokepoints—with good reason. Iran has exercised its control over the Strait of Hormuz to gum up the global economy, and China has used its command over critical minerals to gain leverage in trade negotiations. Less consideration, however, has been paid to chokepoints in the digital domain, which could prove just as treacherous. Chinese hackers have gained and retained access to U.S. communications, energy, and transportation infrastructure. The goal of these intrusions is more than intelligence gathering; it is laying the groundwork for sabotage. Just as Iran’s closure of a vital waterway has been extremely disruptive and hard to get around, China’s penetration of critical networks could cause blackouts, make water unsafe to drink, or delay military mobilization. Indeed, the fragility of U.S. critical infrastructure was made clear this summer when Iranian hackers compromised water facilities across multiple U.S. states, causing one county to direct residents to boil water. U.S. allies are also vulnerable. China has breached hospitals in Taiwan, power grids in India, and telecommunications networks in Singapore. As I argued in an essay in Foreign Affairs last year, there is a fundamental asymmetry between China’s authoritarian approach to cyberdefense and the United States’ more democratic method. American laws and values preclude the U.S. government from monitoring private communications and critical national networks in the ways that the Chinese government does. Beijing, for its part, maintains a series of firewalls that—in addition to surveilling and censoring the Chinese people—protect Chinese networks from American offensive intrusions. And where critical infrastructure in China is centralized and controlled by the state, in the United States it is owned and operated by a diverse array of private actors with varying levels of cyberdefense. China, therefore, can use cyberweapons against the United States and its allies with greater confidence that it can withstand retaliation. Artificial intelligence is likely to exacerbate this asymmetry. Although the technology has revolutionized both offensive and defensive cyber-operations, it tends to benefit attackers more. Because AI could disproportionately benefit China, the United States has all the more reason to use the technology to improve its cyberdefenses. A year ago, using AI to defend critical infrastructure at scale was possible only in principle. Today, it is possible in practice, as advances in AI have brought down the costs of securing U.S. critical infrastructure. To root out Beijing’s digital chokepoints before they are weaponized, Washington, AI labs, and infrastructure operators need to proactively stress-test critical systems, such as plants and grids serving big cities or military bases, against cutting-edge AI models. Doing so would reveal decades of accumulated American vulnerabilities and offer a guide to how to fix them. Without such an understanding, the United States will continue to lose the cyberwar to China. A NEW FRONTIER Economies and militaries often run on digital infrastructure that wasn’t built for the tasks they carry out today, making them attractive and accessible targets for sabotage. That is, in part, why wars of the future will likely play out in the cyber-domain. The United States’ infrastructure is particularly vulnerable. Its power plants and pipelines run on decades-old hardware that was designed for physical reliability, not digital defense. They often lack the logging, encryption, or patching capabilities that create layers of protection. As American utilities modernized, their legacy equipment was wired into computer networks and cloud services for remote monitoring. This created a wealth of opportunities for hackers. Before the advent of the Internet, a saboteur might have had to plant explosives to destroy a gas pipeline. Today, a vandal might be able to shut one off by hacking into a poorly secured router sitting in a in a corporate office. To make matters worse, until recently U.S. utility companies had few incentives or requirements to shore up security. Before the advancement of AI, determining systemic risk required manual, expensive engineering analysis. And before 2021, there were few, if any, cybersecurity regulations for critical infrastructure. The Biden administration established baseline standards for pipelines, ports, airports, and water systems, such as requiring operators to implement multifactor authentication and endpoint monitoring. The United States’ infrastructure is particularly vulnerable. As AI has advanced, cyberattacks have become more dangerous. In fact, OpenAI and Anthropic admitted this summer that their models have already hacked other companies without human direction. Rogue AI could make deterring a state-sponsored cyberattack harder because it offers the aggressor plausible deniability. If a victimized country isn’t certain that a strike was directed by an adversary, or even intentional at all, it may be more hesitant to retaliate. Moreover, the United States needs to protect itself from the possibility that AI from an American company, on its own accord, attacks U.S. infrastructure. But just as AI can enhance cyberattacks, it can also make it easier to mount a cyberdefense. The technology is advanced enough to synthesize a massive amount of data to model infrastructure systems and the threats against them. A utility company could use AI to create a virtual replica of its physical systems, known as a digital twin, that uses sensors and data to mirror the behavior and performance of its real-world counterpart. A digital twin eventually learns what a system’s normal operations look like. It can pinpoint weaknesses and flag any unusual activity, potentially spotting malware. Today’s AI models have the capability to generate digital twins with varied accuracy and sophistication. Much as Waymo’s approach to testing its autonomous systems relies on millions of simulations at increasing detail and cost, a utility company building a digital twin can refine its granularity over time. If tensions heighten with an adversary, for example, the United States could model potential attacks on its own grid to figure out which vulnerabilities, if exploited, would wreak the most havoc. When the United States tried to prepare for the possibility of Russian sabotage in 2022, it could not easily determine which of its weaknesses could be used to disrupt a power grid or water facility for more than 24 hours or which investments in cybersecurity would be most effective at preventing chaos. Today, with the help of digital twins, it is possible to figure out those flaws and prioritize fixes. CARBON COPY Washington now has the technology to protect its critical systems, but it must overcome the obstacles to deploying it, including the decentralized nature of American infrastructure, the way legal liability is assigned, and the high cost of upgrading cybersecurity, which has suffered from decades of underinvestment. Throughout the United States, there are more than 4,500 public water systems, 3,000 electric utilities, and thousands of independent pipeline and telecom operators. And the private corporations and municipalities that operate most of these entities are hesitant to find and share details about their networks because revealing a flaw or unpatched vulnerability can expose them to government fines or lawsuits claiming negligence. But without such data, digital twins cannot operate accurately. The U.S. government must adopt a coordinated, national approach to building digital twins for the most critical of U.S. infrastructure systems—such as those serving ports, large populations, or military bases—and ensure those proxies are a faithful replica. The approach should change the way government and the private sector work together, leveraging the incentives that both frontier AI labs and infrastructure firms have to invest in digital twins. Over the last year, as frontier AI labs have released more powerful models, it has become increasingly difficult to generate puzzles complex enough to measure advancing AI capabilities. Digital twins of real-world infrastructure can provide a more effective testing environment for frontier models—acting as a new cyber gym. AI companies, therefore, have a reason to subsidize the building and maintenance of digital twins as they can be used to evaluate the safety of unreleased models against real systems. Infrastructure owners, in turn, would benefit by seeing their network defenses probed by state-of-the-art technology, at minimal cost. The United States needs a safe space to run such simulations. The Department of Energy, along with the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce, could partner with AI companies to establish a secure, air-gapped national enclave for the continuous testing of critical infrastructure. Utility owners and operators across the country could upload digital twins of their networks into this enclave and the enclave’s AI agents would constantly stress-test utility systems and offer recommendations for the highest priority cybersecurity fixes. Any unearthed bugs could inform Gold Eagle, an initiative the White House established this summer to coordinate finding and fixing vulnerabilities in U.S. networks. Patches could also be shared with allies to built trust in the American AI ecosystem and incentivize allies to use U.S. models. Rogue AI could make deterring a state-sponsored cyberattack harder. To entice utility owners and operators to participate, Congress should provide them legal safe harbor—including protections from lawsuits by the companies or people they serve—for finding weaknesses or evidence of misuse as a result of feeding data into authorized national defense AI platforms. Congress should also help cover the cost of fixing flaws or eliminating foreign footholds that are discovered by establishing a pool of money, modeled on the EPA’s funds, that would issue grants to patch immediate high-risk flaws, alongside long-term, zero-interest loans for larger utilities to undertake deep overhauls. In addition, nonprofit or private-sector programs, such as OpenAI’s Daybreak, could consider issuing grants to cover the costs. The federal government must also change how it conducts oversight. Today, it judges utility companies based on their compliance with legal standards that often lag behind advancements in hacking. A better way would be to assess utility operators on the amount of time it takes them to contain a cyberattack. Over time, these operators, for example, should be required to show, via a simulation with a digital twin, that they can isolate an attack within a reasonable time frame. Although such government efforts are worthwhile, they will take time to come to fruition. In the meantime, industries that are most at risk from the weaponization of digital chokepoints, such as hospitals and banks, should work together to press their most important suppliers to use AI to fix gaps in their cybersecurity. By coordinating through information-sharing analysis centers—organizations that act as a neighborhood watch for a particular industry and offer certain legal protections—companies can press for action through contractual means. Advancements in AI offer the United States and its allies their first real opportunity in many years to catch up to China on the cyber front. The technology to map and defend critical U.S. and allied systems is arriving faster than expected. The ultimate measure of U.S. resilience in the face of digital Chinese chokepoints will not be the raw capability of AI models but the willingness of U.S. institutions to use them—before an adversary causes a major disruption to American lives. item.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.41
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished. In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda. Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether. Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased. For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). In the case of core al-Qaeda, although decapitation and military repression played important roles, the group ended primarily through strategic failure—just as bin Laden feared it would. A MOVING TARGET In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, the U.S. campaign should have been focused on destroying the perpetrators. But the United States failed to clearly define the threat. The Authorization for the Use of Military Force that Congress passed on September 14, 2001, did not mention al-Qaeda at all, instead vaguely identifying Washington’s enemies as “those nations, organizations or persons [the president] determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” A few days later, President George W. Bush echoed that framing. “Our war on al-Qaeda begins with al-Qaeda but it does not end there,” he declared. “It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.” With that, the United States declared war on a tactic, one that had shaped political violence in the modern world since anarchist terrorism swept through Europe before World War I. Washington had set itself a task it could never accomplish. Making the enemy “terrorism” meant its efforts would lack clarity and drag on endlessly. What followed was an ill-focused campaign in Afghanistan (which removed the Taliban from power in Kabul but allowed bin Laden and his cronies to escape) and then the war in Iraq, where al-Qaeda had not even operated until an affiliate emerged after the U.S. military occupation had been in place for a year. The invasion of Iraq did more to prolong the life of al-Qaeda than any other single event, drawing fresh recruits from Sunni populations all over the world, and eventually creating the conditions for the emergence of the Islamic State organization. Still, in the 25 years that followed, sometimes almost despite itself, the United States along with its allies did defeat bin Laden’s al-Qaeda—often with inadvertent help from the group itself. An important factor was the May 2011 killing of Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, an event that undermined al-Qaeda’s coherence. U.S. forces stormed bin Laden’s compound, killed him, and then helicoptered his body to an aircraft carrier and buried it at sea, leaving no possibility for a memorial or focal point for his followers. The documents recovered in that raid were just as valuable to U.S. counterterrorism as bin Laden’s death, offering compelling evidence that he had not been centrally directing the group’s operations for some time. His death did not end al-Qaeda, but it was justice served, and it undercut the ability of his fans to rally around him. By September 2011, U.S. officials were claiming that the number of surviving people directly connected to carrying out the 9/11 attacks was no more than a couple of dozen. But instead of declaring victory over the group at that point and moving on, the U.S. drone campaign, which had begun in 2002 under Bush and accelerated in the early Obama administration, expanded its scope and target set. Instead of so-called personality attacks (which target known leaders), the campaign shifted to “signature strikes,” targeting unidentified individuals or groups who fit a particular profile, not just in Afghanistan and Pakistan but also in Somalia and Yemen. The drone campaign degraded al-Qaeda’s ranks and avenged attempted attacks—for example, by eliminating members of al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate who trained and equipped Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the would-be “underwear bomber” who tried to bring down a civilian airliner in 2009. But drone attacks also catalyzed terrorism: according to declassified FBI interviews, the 2013 Boston Marathon bomber, Tamerlan Tsarnaev (likewise inspired by al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate), told a friend that his killing of an eight-year-old in that attack was justified because children in Afghanistan and Pakistan had been killed by U.S. drones. The drone campaign had a strategic impact on U.S. allies: public attitudes in France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom hardened against Washington’s “global war on terrorism.” Drones were tactically important and probably saved lives, but they did not end al-Qaeda. More critical to that success was intelligence and law-enforcement collaboration among U.S. allies, which remains the bedrock of American counterterrorism. New measures to curb terrorist financing, biometric screening and databases, and new ways of sharing intelligence among allies helped Washington monitor threats beyond American shores. In 2006, for example, close cooperation between U.S. and British intelligence services thwarted an al-Qaeda-linked plot to smuggle the explosive TATP in beverage containers and take down U.S.-bound civilian aircraft over the Atlantic. THINGS FALL APART But much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. A key driver was a backlash against terrorist attacks that hurt Muslim civilians and a resulting loss of support among communities al-Qaeda supposedly represented. Bin Laden knew this was a weakness, and his frustration shows in the communications discovered in the Abbottabad compound. A May 2010 letter he wrote to one of his deputies warns, “This is when we lose the perception of the Muslims towards us, which is that we are the ones defending the Muslims and fighting their biggest enemy, the Crusader Zionist alliance…[and instead] killing those that the general public consider Muslims.” Al-Qaeda started building global franchises in 2004, but they typically emerged out of existing organizations, and their operational ties to core al-Qaeda could be hazy. According to bin Laden’s own assessment, rogue affiliates hurt al-Qaeda’s cause more than they helped it, since most victims of their violence were Muslim civilians, whose families and communities then blamed al-Qaeda. According to the Pew Global Attitudes project, between 2003 and 2011, support for bin Laden personally had dropped in Indonesia from 59 percent to 26 percent, in Jordan from 56 percent to 13 percent, and in the Palestinian territories from 72 percent to 34 percent. In Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding, support for him plunged from 46 percent in 2003 to 18 percent in 2010. A decade after 9/11, bin Laden’s dream of a vanguard uniting Muslims had evaporated. Internal divisions also played a role in al-Qaeda’s demise. The most dramatic split was with the Islamic State, or ISIS, which had started out as an al-Qaeda affiliate before rebranding. In 2014, ISIS conquered major parts of Iraq and Syria, drawing some 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries to join its self-declared caliphate. This was a huge challenge to the original group: al-Qaeda had ideas, but ISIS had territory. ISIS’s trajectory reflected the core problem of dealing with affiliates who did not share (or necessarily even grasp) bin Laden’s strategy. In 2005, bin Laden’s chief deputy, Ayman al-Zawahiri, wrote to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi—the leader of what was then known as al-Qaeda in Iraq and would eventually become ISIS—advising him to stop killing Shiite civilians and beheading hostages in grotesque videos. “Among the things which the feelings of the Muslim populace who love and support you will never find palatable … are the scenes of slaughtering the hostages,” Zawahiri wrote. “We don’t need this.” Zarqawi ignored him. In 2006, a U.S. airstrike killed Zarqawi. But for the next decade, global jihadism shifted firmly in his direction, and against the comparatively more cautious approach of al-Qaeda. Much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. Even as ISIS swamped al-Qaeda, however, the limits of its approach became clear, vindicating Zawahiri’s warning. The first mistake ISIS made was to gather forces and materiel in a concentrated space, becoming a perfect target for conventional military force. Its second error was to enthusiastically embrace gruesome forms of brutality and sadism, antagonizing virtually everyone who did not belong to the group; by 2016, almost the entire world had united against it. Working with Iraqi, Kurdish, and Syrian forces, a global coalition to defeat ISIS had by 2019 recaptured the territory the group had seized and destroyed the caliphate. But for al-Qaeda, the damage had been done: it had lost its foothold in Iraq and split its recruitment base with a younger, flashier brand. Zawahiri’s response was to decentralize and focus on groups in South Asia and North Africa, such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which primarily sought to overthrow local governments. In July 2022, nearly a year after the American withdrawal from Afghanistan, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed Zawahiri. The muted response to his death confirmed the weakness of core al-Qaeda. Today, the apparent head of al-Qaeda is Said al-Adel, who lives in Iran, a Shiite-majority country where, for a decade after 9/11, he and other al-Qaeda leaders and their families spent years living under a form of house arrest, and where his room to maneuver remains strictly limited. He has not even declared himself the group’s leader, perhaps because he fears assassination—but perhaps because there is, in reality, nothing for him to lead. Although the group could one day reinvent itself or carry out attacks sponsored or abetted by Iran, the al-Qaeda that attacked the United States 25 years ago has ended. The United States sometimes accelerated and sometimes slowed the group’s demise. But ultimately, al-Qaeda failed.
