item.title: Putin Will Not Yield
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.19
The war in Ukraine is causing undeniable harm across Russia. Ukraine’s deep strikes into Russian territory have added to the war’s civilian death toll; disrupted online commerce, a significant sector in a country as large as Russia; and prompted gasoline shortages. Burdened by a massive war, the Russian economy is delivering low growth rates and high inflation. In May, the prominent Russian banker Andrey Klepach offered a frank assessment in a speech published online: Russia is “falling behind. We are losing the [global] technological and economic competition.” In some respects, he added, “we are losing it to Ukraine.” In August, the state-controlled development bank where he worked fired him for this expression of disloyalty. Meanwhile, capital is quietly finding its way out of the country and deposits are being spirited away from bank accounts. None of this is good news for Russian President Vladimir Putin. After over four and a half years, Russia has been unable to convert its immense military sacrifices in Ukraine into meaningful military gains. But although Putin has no victories to present to the Russian people, he is not facing any real political precarity. One interpretation of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent visit to Moscow was that he went, in part, to convince Putin that continuing the war is futile. If Ratcliffe thought he could get Putin to desist, he was indulging in wishful thinking. Rather than inching toward a conclusion, the war is escalating. It is not forcing Putin into a dead end either politically or militarily, and to expect Russian concessions or a negotiated settlement in the near to medium term would be folly. The war, which Putin launched expecting a quick and complete victory, was not an accident. The decision to invade emanated from within the political order Putin has fashioned, a system that has been hardened by the war more than it has been transformed. The upcoming parliamentary elections that begin September 18 will certainly give the appearance of lockstep support for Putin. The reality is, of course, more complicated. But for outside observers, the key to understanding Putinism is its inner coherence, not the distance between stage-managed appearances and the actualities of public opinion. Day-to-day shifts on the frontlines in Ukraine and rhetorical expressions of domestic discontent are not among Putin’s major concerns. Despite its many costs, the war has bolstered Putinism and has been woven into the fabric of Russian statehood. SOLID STATE Analysts of Russia are understandably preoccupied by possible changes in the country’s internal trajectory—a burst of dissent, an election, a particularly destructive Ukrainian strike. Since the war began, the United States and Europe have expected its mounting costs to weigh down and even imperil Putin. Yet throughout the war, calm has reigned within Russia. A few weeks of panic directly followed the invasion of Ukraine, but after that, Russians withdrew into acceptance of the war. The 2023 mutiny by Yevgeny Prigozhin, the chief of the Wagner paramilitary company, led not to revolution but to his own untimely death. To the extent that polling can be trusted in Russia, Putin is vastly more popular than German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, or President Donald Trump are in their respective countries. Ahead of the parliamentary elections, the Kremlin has barred the antiwar political party Yabloko from participating just as it was gaining support, and it has sentenced Lev Shlosberg, an antiwar political figure, to an 11-year prison term. Such repressive moves are routine in Putin’s Russia, the default operations of a governing system that long ago neutralized contests between political visions or clashes of rival parties. Not only have party politics vanished from Russia without much visible objection, there is no antiwar movement at all. Many Russians may not regard Putin’s regime as solicitous of the public good, which could explain the withdrawal of capital from the country, but the regime is also accepted as a given, a distant presence impervious to outside influence. Before the war, Putin had spent decades disabling the channels of political opposition and of political action independent from the state. Two intersecting trends have marked his quarter century in power: the steady consolidation of his rule and the increasing militarization of Russia. The Putin who became Russia’s president in 2000 could seem to be many things at once: a modernizer, a reformer, and a strongman. But no matter how he framed his leadership, his instinct for power was acute—and power, for him, was always synonymous with control. From the start, he steadily expanded his control over the state, the media, and business. By 2012, when he was elected Russia’s president for the third time, he had the controlling stake in all three sectors. Throughout the Ukraine war, calm has reigned within Russia. Putin tied his ascent to the elimination of resistance. His progress toward dominance over Russia was gradual and linear: he took over the national television networks, disempowered regions that might have had friction with Moscow, forced oligarchs to give up their political ambitions, and turned all political parties into empty vessels. Deprived of their political clout, oligarchs were reduced to his monied vassals. A drawn-out struggle against the most prominent critic of his rule, the opposition figure Alexei Navalny, culminated in Navalny’s 2024 death in detention. After 2022, most of Russia’s remaining independent media outlets, along with hundreds of thousands of antiwar citizens, fled into exile; any critics who remained in Russia faced the threat of persecution. By now, the absence of meaningful dissent is simply the status quo. Putin used his power to militarize the state and society, a trend that, in turn, augmented his hold on power. He invested heavily in defense. He made the commemoration of the World War II victory foundational to the country’s identity and encouraged the militarization of the Russian Orthodox Church. By the time he invaded Ukraine in 2022, the operation was vocally supported by Patriarch Kirill and most of the church’s clergy. Before then, Putin had launched many wars and military operations—in Chechnya, in Georgia, in Ukraine eight years earlier, and in Syria. He had avoided putting Russia on a wartime footing while making war itself a constant. And so, to Russians, war became familiar but not intrusive. From the beginning of his presidency, Putin had defined Russia in heroic terms, glorifying himself as the leader who restored it to its proper status as a respected great power. After 2022, this heroic depiction of Russia acquired a much more openly militaristic tenor. The gradual accumulation of wars that could be depicted as at least partially successful—and which did not trouble Russians’ standard of living or sense of security—contributed to Russians’ toleration of a war in Ukraine that has lasted far longer than anyone initially expected. For the past four years, the Kremlin’s mission has been to convince Russians that the war is anything but an emergency. It is a necessary state of affairs, given Russia’s many enemies, and proper, given Russia’s mission and power. STRENGTH IN HOLLOWNESS Russian politics is not an edifice without cracks. Discontent with the war is gathering beneath the frozen surface. According to polls conducted on August 9 by the Levada Institute, many Russians would prefer peace talks to an ongoing war. Some business owners and workers, especially in small and medium-sized enterprises, are frustrated by sharp tax increases. Should the economy worsen and the war cast a darker shadow on daily life, this discontent could deepen. So far, the cracks remain small. Klepach’s criticism was a modest gesture of public dissent against an edifice of power that remains more than formidable. Putin has the institutional and practical means to do what he wishes. What he wishes, most of all, is to wage war. At the center of Putin’s governing intent is subjugating Ukraine and forcing the West to accept that outcome. “Sooner or later, Ukraine will lose [its] western territories,” Putin predicted in his July speech to the navy. This was not a throwaway line. He meant that Russia is destined to control eastern Ukraine, while Poland, Hungary, and Romania will absorb the country’s west; in time, Ukraine will cease to exist. Ukraine’s nonexistence was the thesis of an essay he published seven months before the invasion. He has not moderated or mellowed over the past four years. If anything, Putinism has become more radical over time as it has become more secure; the war is a paradoxical source of the system’s self-confidence. Unable to conceive of losing, Putin feels little pressure to make concessions. He has not run out of military options and may truly believe he can win. Russia’s sizable military has enough manpower to sustain a war of attrition and enough productive capacity to generate massive amounts of missiles and drones. The country has survived being severed, via sanctions and the difficulties of cross-border travel, from Europe and the United States. The Russian economy has suffered as a result of its warped relations with the outside world, particularly its broken relationship to Europe, its natural trading partner, but Russians have no political instruments with which to act on their grievances. They are observers to decision-making that cannot be publicly scrutinized. Inside the Kremlin, Russia’s considerable wealth is an unrestricted asset for Putin. It affords him the means to reward friends, indoctrinate Russian youth, and wage war in perpetuity. Indeed, Putin might prefer an unending war, miserable as the prospect might sound, to the compromises entailed in a negotiated settlement that does not equal Ukraine’s surrender. In his July meeting with naval soldiers, he sounded as if he cannot see beyond the enormity of the war: “We should think together about how to preserve this [spirit of wartime struggle] for the future,” he observed. It would be madness for Russia to initiate a full-scale conventional war with European countries, but Moscow is intensifying its undeclared unconventional war through acts of sabotage in Europe. The war’s extension to Russian soil may even bolster support for Putin, stoking a defensive patriotism, especially among Russians who loathe “the West.” For years, Putin has inculcated the idea that “the collective West” is bent on harming Russia. Now he can claim to be vindicated. The Kremlin can present demonstrations of military power, even without a victory, as proof of Russian independence in international affairs—sovereignty, in Putin’s parlance. Europe and the United States cannot tell Russia what to do. They cannot expel Russia’s armies from Ukraine or change the Kremlin’s calculus through economic pressure. Boris Yeltsin’s Russia had struggled to avoid NATO enlargement. Putin, who regards Yeltsin and Mikhail Gorbachev before him as weak leaders, has pushed for militarization as a means of ensuring Russia’s ability to say no to Europe and the United States. His emphasis on Russia’s autonomy is not a personal whim. It undergirds his domestic popularity. Despite his place at the helm of a lavishly funded military-industrial complex, Putin is not especially skilled at strategy. There is a hollowness to his foreign policy: he has difficulty coordinating coercion with persuasion and great difficulty building relationships that have long-term legitimacy. The fall of Nicolás Maduro left Russia with little influence in Venezuela. The ouster of the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad led Damascus to curtail Russia’s military presence on the eastern Mediterranean. Russian power is ebbing in Central Asia, in Moldova, in Azerbaijan, and, lately, in Armenia (although not in Georgia), and Russia has won independence from Europe and the United States at the price of increased dependence on China—a risky bet. Nowhere is the hollowness of Russian foreign policy more visible than in Ukraine. Russia is impossibly far from the victory Putin imagined in February 2022—controlling the country’s whole territory and populace. Putin can wreak havoc in Ukraine and may be able to establish a cease-fire he can accept, but he cannot conquer Ukraine. And an unconquered Ukraine will, by fighting or by remembering the horrors of Russia’s invasion, pose an enduring strategic challenge for Russia. Putin likely assumes that Europe will tire of supporting Ukraine. But for four and a half years, the trend has clearly gone the other way. The more suffering Russia inflicts on Ukrainian civilians, the more Europe invests in Ukraine’s defense and its own. Yet all these challenges are not unmanageable for Putin. Whether Russia makes mistakes or serves Russians’ quotidian interests is secondary to his project of strengthening state power in and of itself. The conundrum of Putinism is that strategic mediocrity can enhance the regime’s durability—if not forever, then for quite a while. The more Russia is said to inhabit a hostile world, the more it finds itself wedded to an autocrat enamored of force. FOREVER WAR Contemplating the solidity of Putin’s regime, analysts sometimes entertain fantasies of a more docile successor. The Kremlin, which surely has succession plans, cannot guarantee that they will be followed in the event of Putin’s death or departure from power. Yet Putinism is relatively well positioned to survive the career of its founder. Opposition movements and revolutions demand organization. (Organization was one of Vladimir Lenin’s greatest skills, which helped him lead the only successful revolution from below in Russian history.) Inchoate discontent must contend with the vast security services that Putin and his fellow travelers have at their disposal. A successor to Putin who could retain these tools would be difficult to unseat, even if the Putin mystique is nontransferable. Policymakers in the United States and Europe must accept that Putin will persist in his war effort. A stymied economy and public skepticism are distractions from the essential story: that by now, the conditions that have made for an already long war are an organic part of Russia’s relationship to Europe, a shaping presence that will be exceptionally difficult, if not impossible, to eradicate. Putin has survived many crises: the wars in Chechnya in the late 1990s and first decade of this century; the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine (which made him look incompetent and helpless); multiple major terrorist attacks; the 2007–8 financial crash; and Prigozhin’s mutiny, among others. Arguably, most Russian elites have not obeyed the Kremlin out of deep loyalty or ideological alignment throughout Putin’s long reign. They have done so out of opportunism, and increasingly they obey out of fear. Putin is prepared to prosecute this war for years to come, not because his advisers are promising him a quick victory, although they may be. The war is embedded in Putinism, just as Putinism is embedded in the war. His governing system gives him the freedom to do what he wants, and his legacy and the war are now inseparable. Both he and Russia are in it for the long haul. item.title: What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 5.58
What’s Behind Nigeria’s Military Spending Spree Ahead of January elections, Bola Tinubu is pulling out all the stops to stem insecurity. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief. The highlights this week: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu presses on with military reforms ahead of 2027 elections, Africa’s richest man launches the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Spending Spree Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has appointed Maj. Gen. Ibikunle Ajose as the new top army commander for the northeast, the epicenter of the country’s Islamist insurgency, after the previous leader spent less than two years in the role. The move is the latest in a series of military reforms ahead of January’s general elections, in which insecurity will be high on the list of voters’ concerns. Ajose’s appointment was part of a bigger reshuffling last week that involved 15 top generals. These redeployments, along with a major hike in military spending, are key to the government’s wider plan to stabilize bellwether regions before Nigerians head to the polls. Tinubu is seeking a second term as the candidate for the All Progressives Congress party and will face the same main challengers he came up against in 2023: former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, who is running under the African Democratic Congress (ADC), and former Anambra state Gov. Peter Obi, with the Nigeria Democratic Congress. This year, Abubakar and Obi initially joined forces to unseat Tinubu under an ADC-led opposition coalition, but the alliance fractured due to their competing ambitions. Observers are looking to see whether Obi in particular, who came in third in 2023, can translate the unprecedented backing he garnered from young Nigerian urbanites in the last election into rural support. Importantly, the public is paying close attention to how candidates intend to address widespread violence and kidnappings for ransom. A mass kidnapping of schoolchildren in Tinubu’s political heartland in the southwestern state of Oyo in May magnified the issue. More than 7,800 people were kidnapped in Nigeria between July 2025 and June 2026—a 66 percent increase from the previous year, according to a new report from risk advisory firm SBM Intelligence. Over that period, kidnappers received some $5.8 million in ransom money, three times that of the previous year. Boko Haram collected 90 percent of those payments, mainly from mass abductions. The insecurity has ripple effects across the country. For instance, many farmers have been unable to access their lands due to the threat of kidnappings, leading to food shortages and hunger, especially in the north. The “security question in Nigeria is closely connected to the economic one: An attack that closes a road, displaces farmers, or shuts a market very quickly becomes an issue of household income and food prices,” said Sekinat Ojeniyi of Africa Practice, a global risk advisory firm. On the campaign trail, Abubakar has pledged to end insecurity within one year if elected. His plan centers on cross-border military collaboration with Sahel nations and providing jobs for young people drawn to extremism. Obi has also promised to fix insecurity in one term through youth poverty alleviation and education. “You cannot create widespread poverty and expect peace,” Obi told Nigerian broadcaster Channels Television. Tinubu’s government, meanwhile, is injecting unprecedented amounts of money into defense in an attempt to address the issue. According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Nigeria’s military expenditure surged 55 percent year-on-year to $2.1 billion in 2025. That figure is expected to double this year. With this money, Tinubu approved salary increases for members of the military last month. The massive investment also supports the largest expansion of the Nigerian military since the country’s civil war in the late 1960s. In July, Tinubu approved the creation of four new army divisions with a planned recruitment of 28,000 additional personnel by December. A new bill passed by Nigeria’s National Assembly in June would also allow states to establish their own police forces, putting less pressure on the federal police to secure dense forested communities that have become hideouts for extremists. “The government’s emphasis on manpower and personnel welfare makes sense, but more personnel and better pay do not automatically translate into greater security,” Ojeniyi said. “Kidnapping networks are highly adaptive and operate across state and local government boundaries, while the police, military, and intelligence agencies do not always have the same visibility or operational reach.” Meanwhile, many Nigerian and U.S. political observers have commended Tinubu for his handling of tensions with Washington, which has transformed the Trump administration’s divisive rhetoric about supposed Christian persecution in Nigeria into security cooperation. Beginning late last year, the United States deployed troops to assist with counterterrorism operations. (Most U.S. troops withdrew in July.) Although U.S. strikes in northeastern Nigeria in May killed a senior Islamic State leader, the mass abductions have continued. More than 600 people were taken from Nigeria’s north-central Niger state last month in an attack on a mosque. Although many Nigerians welcome his new security reforms, Tinubu will likely be judged on whether these last-gasp efforts a few months ahead of elections can stem the violence. The Week Ahead Wednesday, Sept. 16: The U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee holds a nomination hearing on ambassadors to Benin, Gabon, Kenya, and Togo. Wednesday, Sept. 16, to Thursday, Sept. 17: Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo meet in Geneva to discuss monitoring their cease-fire. Wednesday, Sept. 23: Morocco holds general elections. What We’re Watching Historic IPO. Africa’s richest person, Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote, launched the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering on Monday, floating 4.1 billion shares in his $20 billion oil refinery on the outskirts of Lagos on the Nigerian Exchange. The rush to buy shares briefly crashed many Nigerian investment apps. The move is expected to raise about $1.6 billion, which will fund Dangote’s expansion projects across Africa. Dangote Industries said it will use the investment to double production capacity, deliver refined products across the continent, and build another refinery in Kenya. The public offer closes on Oct. 13, and Dangote is reportedly eyeing a secondary New York listing in the future. Sahrawi citizenship. The Spanish parliament’s lower house approved a bill granting citizenship to Sahrawis born before 1977, when Madrid administered Western Sahara. The legislation will now go to Spain’s Senate. It marks the latest escalation of tensions with Morocco after thousands of migrants entered Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta from Morocco in late July. Rabat claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Western Sahara, and it has occupied about 80 percent of the latter’s territory since the 1970s. More than 170,000 Sahrawi refugees live in camps in Algeria, which hosts the Polisario Front, a group fighting for Sahrawi independence. U.S. tech bid. The United States will lend nearly $100 million to Africell, the only mainstream U.S.-owned mobile network operator in Africa, as part of broader strategic investments to counter China in the region. Africell operates in Angola, Congo, Gambia, and Sierra Leone. The loan from the U.S. Export-Import Bank is part of Washington’s efforts to counter the expansion of China’s Huawei company in Africa. But the United States has a long way to go: Chinese firms are now baked into the continent’s tech infrastructure. For example, the three major smartphone brands in Africa—Tecno, Itel, and Infinix—are manufactured by China’s Transsion and have dominated the market for nearly two decades. Congo-Israel ties. Congo has revived plans to move its embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem following President Felix Tshisekedi’s visit to the country earlier this month. Analysts consider the move an attempt to both court Israeli security support and get the United States to exert more pressure on Rwanda to stop backing the M23 rebel group in eastern Congo. Tshisekedi previously told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2023 that Congo would move the embassy, three years after Tshisekedi announced that he would appoint its first ambassador to Israel in more than two decades. Meanwhile, Tshisekedi faces mounting calls in Congo to resign over his attempts to implement constitutional reforms that could pave the way for a third term in office. This Week in Health The United States has announced that it will no longer fund Namibia’s HIV program after a final $45 million disbursement for the 2027 fiscal year, ending more than two decades of aid through the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, which has provided around $1.1 billion to Namibia since it was launched under President George W. Bush in 2003. The withdrawal follows Namibia’s refusal to give the United States unrestricted access to genetic data and pathogens, which it could then share with private companies and organizations without oversight from the Namibian government as part of Trump’s America First Global Health Strategy. Namibian officials cited concerns over sovereignty, national law, and patient privacy. Since pulling out of the World Health Organization in January, the Trump administration has pursued deals that would provide commercial access to African nations’ health data. So far, Ghana, Zambia, and Zimbabwe have rejected such deals, while at least 19 nations, including Nigeria and Ethiopia, have agreed to them. “We need to reserve our data, and no one has the right to get a sovereign state to be used for other things, except for the World Health Organization cabinet,” former Namibian Health Minister Richard Kamwi said in August. FP’s Most Read This Week - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan What We’re Reading Al-Shabab’s win. In Foreign Policy, Mohamed Gabobe reports from Mogadishu on how the U.S. withdrawal of support for the African Union peacekeeping mission in the country has severely jeopardized the remaining forces’ capacity to counter the Islamist group al-Shabab. The two-decade military intervention’s failure to quash al-Shabab—which has “has retaken nearly all the territory that it lost in a 2022-2023 Somali army campaign,” Gabobe writes—partly informed Washington’s decision. There “is no one other nation that can fill the United States’ void,” he adds. What’s in a map? On Sept. 4, the United Nations General Assembly voted to adopt a Togo-sponsored resolution to replace the traditional Mercator map with one that better represents Africa’s true size. Only the United States voted against it. In Foreign Policy, Howard W. French argues that this is just the latest example of the West being behind in understanding not just Africa’s geographic size but also its demographic weight. “Just as drawing up maps in ways that graphically diminish Africa does nothing to reduce Africa’s true dimensions, actively shunning African migrants will do nothing to change the hard demographic realities that will radically shape our collective future,” he writes. Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. item.title: The EU’s 28th State?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.82
The EU’s 28th State? European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floats making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca. The EU Looks Across the Pond Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca. The EU Looks Across the Pond Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member. “We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seated on her left, von der Leyen outlined what such a future might look like, starting with an expansion of their existing free-trade agreement. Carney has been pitching such an arrangement to European officials for months. A Canadian official told The Associated Press last week that the two sides are discussing potential ties that stop just short of full membership. This could include allowing Canadian citizens to live and work in EU member states without needing a visa. An expanded partnership might also bolster collaboration in defense production, critical minerals procurement, economic security, and the development of artificial intelligence, among others. Canada wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc, Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said on Wednesday, adding that further discussions are expected to take place at the Canada-EU summit in October. Under EU regulations, the bloc requires unanimous approval to welcome new members. Although von der Leyen insisted on Wednesday that the Canada proposal is “not a partnership against anyone else,” the gesture comes at a time when both Canada’s and Europe’s relations with the United States under President Donald Trump are greatly strained. Last month, the White House imposed sweeping tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting “dollar for dollar” retaliatory duties on around 700 U.S. products. This was in spite of Canada being one of the United States’ largest trading partners; bilateral trade accounted for around $872.3 billion in 2025. Alongside a recent war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford as well as the U.S. president’s repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state, Ottawa has begun to prioritize its relationship with the EU over what it once considered its closest partner. But not everyone in Europe appears thrilled with von der Leyen’s proposal. “Of all the third countries, Canada is one of the few that we all want to get closer to right now,” an EU diplomat told the Financial Times. “But even with them, we all know we have to be careful when you start talking about trade access and preferential treatment.” Notably, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify the bloc’s 2017 free-trade deal with Canada, citing several provisions that they argue favor Canadian investors. Whether the idea ever materializes, the fact that it’s being talked about at such high levels is a sign of what Carney called the “rupture in the world order.” The Canadian premier will take the stage on Thursday to address the European Parliament. Today’s Most Read - Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree - Why My Kyiv Visit Worried Me So Much by Ravi Agrawal - Only China, India, and Russia Can End the Iran War by Amir Handjani What We’re Following Guilty of war crimes. Former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Wednesday after being found guilty of orchestrating war crimes during the country’s brutal fight for independence against Serbia in the late 1990s. He continues to deny any wrongdoing and is expected to appeal the ruling. The sentence was handed down by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a special tribunal at The Hague. According to the tribunal, Thaci oversaw the murder, torture, arbitrary detention, and abuse of alleged opponents, including ethnic minorities and perceived collaborators, while serving as the top commander of the since-disbanded Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA). “The vast majority of them were innocent civilians,” the tribunal said of Thaci’s victims. Thaci was sentenced alongside three other senior members of the ethnic Albanian KLA. Wednesday’s ruling is expected to heighten divisions between Serbians and Kosovar Albanians, the latter of whom often regard Thaci as a hero for his contribution to Kosovo’s independence. Clashes broke out between Thaci supporters and security at The Hague when protesters tried to walk to the tribunal. Incumbent Kosovar Prime Minister Albin Kurti condemned Wednesday’s ruling, saying, “While the verdict may have been formally pronounced in the name of the people of Kosovo, this hollow formula must not be conflated with the will of the people.” Mecca is under fire. Saudi forces claimed on Wednesday local time to have intercepted a Houthi drone targeting the holy Muslim city of Mecca the day before. According to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, the attempted attack crossed a “red line,” as it was “intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims.” The Organization of Islamic Cooperation similarly denounced the operation as a “heinous” assault. This is the first alleged Houthi strike aimed at Mecca since fighting erupted between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in July. The Houthis denied Riyadh’s allegations, with rebel spokesperson Hazem al-Assad saying, “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.” Both sides have escalated their assaults in recent days. On Wednesday, Saudi warplanes struck Yemeni territory, and Houthi troops attacked Red Sea port cities and Saudi military bases. Such assaults have exacerbated the already tenuous global energy crisis and injected further insecurity into the war-embroiled Middle East. Seeking peace. Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo resumed peace talks in Geneva on Wednesday, alongside mediators from Qatar, Togo, and the United States. The two-day session—the seventh meeting since the two countries signed a U.S.-brokered peace accord last year—aims to address continued fighting in eastern Congo between Congolese forces and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels. Less than a year ago, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame signed an agreement in Washington to end the deadly conflict. However, without M23 representatives in attendance—and Kigali maintaining that it does not support the rebel group despite U.N. evidence to the contrary—Trump’s self-proclaimed “historic” peace deal did little to actually quell the fighting; just days after the December 2025 signing, around 200,000 people fled renewed violence in the region. Since then, the situation in eastern Congo has continued to deteriorate despite repeated cease-fire attempts. During this week’s talks, Kigali is expected to seek assurances that armed groups will not be allowed to operate in Congolese territory, while Kinshasa asserts that foreign security forces have no right to Congolese soil. Odds and Ends A Paris court awarded Kim Kardashian 1 euro (or $1.15) on Tuesday as compensation for being the victim of an armed robbery in 2016. Kardashian was at the Hôtel de Pourtalès for Paris Fashion Week when a gang of eight thieves, six of whom are currently in their 60s or 70s, bound the media personality with zip ties and stole more than $6 million in jewelry; the so-called grandpa robbers were found guilty of armed robbery and kidnapping, among other charges, last year. Kardashian has since described the incident as “the most terrifying experience of my life” but only requested a symbolic 1 euro in restitution. item.title: Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.79
Modi and Xi’s Meeting Caps a Detente Despite the thaw, India-China rivalry remains inevitable. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet on the sidelines of the BRICS summit, Bangladesh faces the world’s worst measles outbreak as the death toll passes 1,000, and thousands of people remain missing after Nepal’s deadly floods. Modi, Xi Meet on BRICS Sideline Over the weekend, Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to India for the first time in seven years. Xi was in New Delhi for 24 hours to attend this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, where he held a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. An Indian Foreign Ministry statement said the two leaders pledged to strengthen commercial and cultural cooperation. A more striking readout came from Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who said that the bilateral meeting covered long-term, strategic issues and that Modi and Xi reached “the most important consensus” to be partners, not rivals. Beijing hopes the meeting will advance bilateral ties “without stagnation or backsliding,” Wang added. These are positive words for a relationship between major competitors—and one that was plunged into deep crisis after a deadly 2020 border clash in the Ladakh region. But an India-China rapprochement has been playing out for nearly two years. Xi’s visit marked the culmination, not the commencement, of India-China detente. Still, the extent of the thaw shouldn’t be overstated. Historically, India-China ties have had their moments, with ample heady talk and good optics. Invariably, fresh tensions have spoiled them; the two are destined to remain rivals by history, geography, and geopolitics. In October 2024, the post-Ladakh tensions began to ease with the inking of a new border agreement. India and China subsequently made pledges to resume direct air flights and bolster commercial cooperation. In March 2025, Modi said on a podcast that cooperation with China was “essential” for global stability. Contrary to some commentary, the detente began before U.S. President Donald Trump was elected to a second term and wasn’t sparked by his policies. But Trump’s tariffs, which have hit both India and China hard, and concerns about access to U.S. markets gave both sides a strong incentive to accelerate their rapprochement and especially to deepen trade ties. However, the reality is that continued India-China rivalry is all but inevitable. Both countries are both proud civilizational states and dispute claims to around 15,000 square miles of territory—equal to the size of Greece—along their shared border. They disagree on many other major issues, from Taiwan and Tibet to surveillance. Perhaps most significantly, China is a close ally of India’s bitter rival Pakistan. Last year, the Pakistani military used Chinese weaponry in air combat operations against India for the first time. Such challenges may seem surmountable, given what the India-China relationship has going for it. This includes their rock-solid trade partnership, shared interests, and considerable cooperation in global forums (including BRICS, but also the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.) Not surprisingly, India-China ties have often enjoyed periods of warmth—but ultimately a trigger, often a border provocation, has shattered that calm. In 2017, a few years after Xi and Modi were photographed smiling on a swing together, a 73-day military standoff on the Doklam Plateau plunged relations into crisis. The Ladakh clash came just months after another Modi-Xi summit in India. Though border tensions have subsided, territorial disputes still fester and occasionally flare. To be sure, there are plenty of reasons for New Delhi and Beijing to bury the hatchet. They want to ease tensions along their fraught border, create space for deeper commercial cooperation, hedge against Trump’s unpredictability, and remove a diplomatic headache from the BRICS grouping, which both capitals badly want to succeed. Ultimately, however, so many divergences and sources of lingering mistrust preempt the possibility of full-on rapprochement. Though an extended period of cooperation is possible, it’s likely only a matter of time before the very “stagnation and backsliding” that Beijing says it wants to avoid. What We’re Following Bangladesh passes 1,000 measles deaths. More than 1,000 people in Bangladesh have now died from the measles virus since March 15, according to the latest government figures, released on Sept. 9. The country is suffering the world’s worst measles outbreak; it has logged thousands of new cases this year, including nearly 60,000 between January and June alone. Nearly 20 million children have been vaccinated in Bangladesh since a new national inoculation campaign was launched in April. Health experts attribute the ongoing crisis to underestimations of how many children needed to be vaccinated—the target figure was 18 million, but experts say that a more accurate estimate is 22.6 million. The number of measles vaccinations in Bangladesh—both first and second doses—fell between 2019 and 2023, and this year’s national campaign was the first since one from December 2020 to January 2021, during the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. A sudden change of government in August 2024 caused further vaccine interruptions. The current government, which took office in February, is working hard to ease the crisis. But it must grapple with not only the large number of children who still need to be vaccinated, but also economic stress and energy shortages that further complicate inoculation efforts. Thousands still missing in Nepal. Three weeks after a glacial collapse precipitated catastrophic floods in Nepal, more than 5,000 people remain missing. Authorities say they continue to search and are trying to provide information to families as soon as possible. But massive destruction—including 2.2 million tons of—has made search and rescue difficult. Authorities are now transitioning from search and rescue to relief and reconstruction efforts, with an eye toward the large number of people who lost their homes. The disaster leveled entire villages, submerged tunnels, and swept away hydropower facilities. Damage to roads and bridges has created additional complications. Nepal’s government said that the total estimated cost for reconstruction efforts will be $4.8 billion—around one-tenth of the country’s total nominal GDP. Sri Lanka signs labor accords with Thailand. This week, Sri Lanka and Thailand signed agreements to enable 10,000 Sri Lankans to work in the Southeast Asian country, with a focus on young workers and sectors including information technology and tourism. The Sri Lankan workers will receive equal rights and protections under Thai labor laws. The agreements address a key need for both countries: Thailand has a labor shortage, and Sri Lanka is looking to tap into a wider array of foreign labor markets. But the deal goes against a common pattern in Sri Lanka—and elsewhere in South Asia—in which young people go to the Middle East, Europe, or the United States for work. There appears to be a cultural factor at play. The Sri Lankan government believes cultural similarities between Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia will make for a smoother adjustment process—putting them in a strong position to be productive and send home remittances that are critical for the Sri Lankan economy. FP’s Most Read This Week How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan Under the Radar Last week, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said that it was not contemplating the use of military force against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Middle East. The statement came in response to speculation, fueled by a Turkish news report, that Pakistan was considering invoking the Mecca Agreement—the new mutual defense pact among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey—and joining a military operation with the Saudis against the Houthis. Houthi attacks against Saudi targets have escalated in recent days. Pakistan’s statement gives ammunition to critics of the Mecca Agreement—as well as a similar bilateral deal between Islamabad and Riyadh—who dismiss the accord as a paper tiger. In the last year, Taliban military operations have hit Pakistan has been hit multiple times; Saudi Arabia has been assaulted by the Houthis as well as direct Iranian strikes. At no time has Pakistan or Saudi Arabia intervened militarily to assist the other, though Pakistan has sent some arms and troops to Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Still, the two mutual defense pacts are mainly meant to focus on deterrence, which the signatories say the United States cannot provide sufficiently in the Middle East. In Pakistan’s case, the accords are meant to help advance key foreign-policy priorities, including playing a larger role in the security architecture of the region. Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. item.title: What the BRICS Summit Meant for Brazil
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.84
What the BRICS Summit Meant for Brazil One year after hosting the event, is the country still shaping the bloc? Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Brazil sends its foreign minister to a BRICS summit in New Delhi, Guatemalans protest fuel price hikes, and Chile remembers a renowned documentarian. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Brazil sends its foreign minister to a BRICS summit in New Delhi, Guatemalans protest fuel price hikes, and Chile remembers a renowned documentarian. Brazil’s Balancing Acts at BRICS The BRICS leaders’ summit in New Delhi last weekend underscored how as the global order unravels, cooperation among the grouping deepens. Many long-standing BRICS demands, such as expanding the United Nations Security Council, haven’t materialized. But the bloc has steadily increased economic ties, including by launching its own development bank. BRICS members have long sought to reform the Western-dominated order, making their joint positions particularly relevant today. This year, the warring parties of Iran and the United Arab Emirates sent their president and crown prince of Abu Dhabi, respectively—marking the furthest international trip for Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian since the Iran war began in February. Brazil, a founding member of BRICS and the host of last year’s summit, has had a more difficult time steering the grouping’s priorities since it expanded from five to nine members in 2024. (Indonesia, the newest member, joined in 2025.) Brazil opposed the expansion, fearing a loss of cohesion with the addition of avowedly anti-West Iran. Like India, Brazil wants BRICS to be reformist, not revolutionary. Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira attended in place of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is in the midst of a reelection campaign. Last week, Vieira said Brazil believes “a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.” In other words, Brazil wants a system of rules—not rule by the strongest. Brazil managed to keep some of its priorities alive in this year’s summit declaration. Notably, in the joint statement BRICS reaffirmed its support for the U.N. system and the Paris climate agreement—going further than the G-7, whose most recent declarations did not mention the climate pact. The summit’s endorsements are words, not actions, and some of the group’s members—most notably Russia—have flagrantly violated the U.N. Charter in recent years. But words still matter when both the U.N. system and climate action are under attack—and when the leadership of the U.N. itself is up for grabs. Russia may have only begrudgingly endorsed U.N. principles, but the fact that it agreed to acknowledge the legitimacy of the U.N. system at the BRICS summit bodes better for the world body’s future functioning than if Russia had blocked any mention of it. Brazil’s window to continue shaping BRICS in this direction may be closing as its general elections approach on Oct. 4. Far-right Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro—whose political camp has a record of U.N.-bashing and climate change denialism—has as strong a chance of winning as Lula, polls say. Upcoming Events Saturday, Sept. 19: Chile marks its Independence Day with a military parade. Sunday, Oct. 4: Brazil holds presidential and legislative elections. What We’re Following Support for democracy on the rise. In its latest polling, AmericasBarometer at Vanderbilt University has found increased public support for democracy in Latin America. The share of respondents across the region who agreed that “democracy may have problems, but it is better than any other form of government” rose to 65 percent, up from 59 percent in 2023. The report attributed this rebound in part to “positive changes in individuals’ lived experiences with crime, corruption, and economic well-being.” Support for democracy was higher among respondents who said their household income had risen in the last two years, who had not run out of food recently, and who had not been victims of crime. The survey also touched on geopolitics, echoing a recent Pew Research Center survey in finding that views of China in the region are improving relative to the United States. Washington has historically cast itself as Latin America’s partner in democracy. But under U.S. President Donald Trump, democracy promotion has largely fallen off the agenda. Panama Canal restrictions. A drought worsened by El Niño has Panamanian authorities planning to again reduce the number of daily ship transits through the Panama Canal. Starting in October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed each day, down 18 percent from August, according to a draft plan submitted to the legislature. Transit prices through the canal, meanwhile, are climbing to record highs. Prices shift with demand, and some Asian energy importers that typically source supplies from the Persian Gulf are now buying from the U.S. Gulf Coast instead, amid the Iran war—and those shipments must pass through Panama. Star filmmaker remembered. One of Latin America’s most celebrated documentary filmmakers, Chile’s Patricio Guzmán, died on Tuesday at 85. His three-part series The Battle of Chile chronicled the 1973 coup against Salvador Allende’s government and won international acclaim. Guzmán was already filming in Santiago when the coup occurred, having originally set out to document the implementation of socialism through the ballot box. His cameras captured the range of opinions on the street about that process—and the military intervention that brought it to a halt. Guzmán fled Chile immediately after the coup and managed to smuggle the film negatives abroad for processing, but the film’s cinematographer, Jorge Müller, was detained and disappeared during the dictatorship. Guzmán eventually settled in Paris, where he died, though he returned to Chile over the years to make several more films. “A country that does not have documentary films is like a family without a photo album,” he once said. Question of the Week Panama’s government is planning to create a new reservoir to ensure higher water levels in the canal. What is its estimated completion date? FP’s Most Read This Week - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree In Focus: Unrest in Guatemala Guatemala has joined the ranks of countries where economic fallout from the Iran war has spilled into political unrest. For more than a week, demonstrators angry over high gasoline prices have blocked highways across the country. Some gas prices topped $6 per gallon this week, Bloomberg Línea reported. Guatemalan President Bernardo Arévalo has tried to cap gas prices by decree, but the measure—which requires congressional approval—has been blocked by an opposition lawmaker. Arévalo says organized crime groups are encouraging demonstrations and has sent security forces to clear some roads. The protests are only the latest governance challenge for Arévalo, who was elected in 2023 on an anti-corruption platform but lacks majority support in Congress. Reformers had high hopes that Arévalo could reshape the political environment this year, when a complex process to elect a new attorney general and judges came due. But Guatemala’s moneyed establishment lobbied Trump to oppose Arévalo’s anti-corruption agenda and achieved some success. The Trump administration has worked to boost the candidacies of some would-be judges in Guatemala who had themselves been accused of corruption, the Washington Post reported in June. A U.S. State Department spokesperson denied meddling, saying U.S. policy is to respect “Guatemalan sovereignty.” After the election this year of a top judge who Arévalo has publicly said “lacks integrity” and amid the ongoing fuel price protests, public opinion of Arévalo has nosedived. He had the lowest approval rating among Latin American leaders in a regional CB Global Data poll taken last week. Correction, Sept. 18, 2026: A previous version of this newsletter misstated the rank of the official leading the Emirati delegation to the BRICS summit. item.title: How Americanness Overcomes Islamophobia
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.79
How Americanness Overcomes Islamophobia In Rozina Ali’s new book, four families grapple with the post-9/11 shift. In 1965, as the United States began to ramp up its war in Vietnam, President Lyndon B. Johnson authorized a massive increase of draft numbers. Ron Amen, the son of Lebanese immigrants in Dearborn, Michigan, was one of the young men called up to serve that year. When he received his dog tags before being deployed, he was surprised to find that, even though he had spelled out “Islam” for the bemused official in the recruitment office, his religion was listed as “none.” Amen’s dog tags offer an early glimpse of what would grow into the widespread anti-Muslim sentiment that journalist Rozina Ali traces in her new book, Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. For generations, Muslims occupied a small and largely overlooked place in U.S. life, even if the country rarely accepted or acknowledged their identity. But after 9/11, a small group of politicians and activists seized on the tragedy to scrutinize Muslims and openly question whether they should be in the United States at all. In 1965, as the United States began to ramp up its war in Vietnam, President Lyndon B. Johnson authorized a massive increase of draft numbers. Ron Amen, the son of Lebanese immigrants in Dearborn, Michigan, was one of the young men called up to serve that year. When he received his dog tags before being deployed, he was surprised to find that, even though he had spelled out “Islam” for the bemused official in the recruitment office, his religion was listed as “none.” Amen’s dog tags offer an early glimpse of what would grow into the widespread anti-Muslim sentiment that journalist Rozina Ali traces in her new book, Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. For generations, Muslims occupied a small and largely overlooked place in U.S. life, even if the country rarely accepted or acknowledged their identity. But after 9/11, a small group of politicians and activists seized on the tragedy to scrutinize Muslims and openly question whether they should be in the United States at all. Ali’s book documents that shift, illuminating the policies and practices that shaped Americans’ suspicion of Muslims decades both before and after 9/11. Unlike much of the literature on the attacks and their aftermath, Ali does not ask whether the so-called war on terror succeeded or failed. Instead, she examines what it did to Muslims in the United States—and, in turn, to the country itself—through the stories of four families, all of whom experienced Islamophobia in different ways yet refused to relinquish their claims to American life. Seasons of Fury begins with Abdeen Jabara, an attorney whose parents emigrated to the Midwest in the early 20th century from what was then called Greater Syria. Jabara recounts one striking moment in 1967, when he was watching the race riots that rocked Detroit from the city’s Cadillac Tower. He was there for a gathering of the local chapter of the National Lawyers Guild. Yet rather than focusing on the chaos taking place just below, the chapter’s leader called for the condemnation of the Soviet Union for arming Arab states against Israel, which had recently captured more territory in the Six-Day War, leading to its occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza. Jabara pushed back, saying that the situation was more complicated—to no avail. Soon after the guild meeting, a friend who was a professor called Jabara to invite him to a dinner with fellow Arabs to discuss how to better inform Americans about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. There, along with other attendees, Jabara formed the Association of Arab American University Graduates, an organization that sought, in Ali’s words, to “win over American minds.” For a time, the group’s vice president was Columbia University scholar Edward Said. In doing so, Jabara caught the attention of the FBI, which admitted in 1974 that it had been monitoring him since 1967 and sharing his information with Zionist organizations and foreign governments. Under J. Edgar Hoover in 1956, the FBI had launched a covert surveillance program called COINTELPRO to monitor “radical” groups—or at least what the agency deemed radical. It initially targeted communists but expanded to civil rights leaders and anti-war activists. Organizing around Palestine—and against Israel—eventually landed on its radar, even as the government’s own intelligence assessments found “little evidence that Arab groups were plotting attacks against the United States,” Ali notes. Jabara’s experience was not isolated. By the 1970s, Arabs in the United States increasingly came under surveillance, including by the National Security Agency, which Ali writes was “then a little-known part of the Defense Department.” Two decades later, laws helped institutionalize government suspicion and surveillance. President Bill Clinton approved two pieces of legislation in 1996 that, as Ali describes, “would forever shape the country’s criminal and immigration landscape.” One was the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, which “gave the government power to deport more immigrants, by expanding the list of deportable offenses.” The other, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act, stretched the definition of who could be implicated in terrorism under a new “Foreign Terrorist Organization” list. Anyone providing “material support” to any of the listed groups, including Hamas and Hezbollah, could be found guilty of abetting terrorism. Furthermore, the government could offer classified evidence in court that the defendant could not see. Ali notes that “Congressman David Bonior, from Michigan, called it ‘one of the most pernicious laws I’ve seen in my 28-year profession.’” He would see just how pernicious shortly after 9/11, when Congress passed the Patriot Act, which broadened the definition of “material support” to include those who offered “advice or assistance” to a supposed terrorist, effectively allowing the government to investigate and prosecute anyone it deemed vaguely suspicious. The law sparked widespread fear that Muslims would become targets, not just of the government but of an angry public eager for revenge. Indeed, in the aftermath of 9/11, Ali’s own father told her not to tell anyone that she is Muslim. “If a stranger asked, we were Hindu,” she recalls him saying. For good reason. The FBI reported that anti-Islamic incidents grew by more than 1,600 percent between 2000 and 2001. Official suspicion validated public fear, and public fear enabled aggressive government action. Ali gives a human face to these statistics through Jabara and three other families, whose stories before and after 9/11 are the heart of Seasons of Fury. Like a descent into Dante’s inferno, each family history reveals a particular layer of Islamophobia. In an effort to separate the terrorists from Muslims, six days after the attacks, President George W. Bush visited the Islamic Center in Washington, where he spoke about how Islam was a religion of peace. That gave Mohammad “Ali” Chaudry—a Pakistani immigrant who was elected to New Jersey’s Bernards Township council in 2001—hope. His election to mayor in 2004—which made him the first Pakistani-born Muslim mayor in the United States—seemed to indicate to Chaudry that despite 9/11, Americans were heeding the president’s call for tolerance. But the Bush administration’s actions spoke louder than his words. In an effort to identify threats, whether credible or not, the White House shifted counterterrorism efforts into overdrive. By the end of 2002, it had championed the Patriot Act, which expanded mass surveillance and curtailed civil liberties; formed the Department of Homeland Security; and rolled out both a “no fly list” and the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System, more commonly known as the Muslim registry, which required visa holders from specific countries—almost all of which were predominantly Muslim—to register with law enforcement. All of this ensured that the mood in the country locked into vigilance, something Chaudry witnessed a decade later when he moved to build a mosque in Basking Ridge. His neighbors subjected the proposal to years of review and 39 public hearings, repeatedly invoking zoning and planning objections to block the project. (Construction of the mosque was eventually allowed to move forward in 2017.) While Chaudry’s neighbors did not want a mosque in their midst, the Omars—a pseudonym Ali uses for a family of five due to concerns over their safety—came across a neighbor who did not want them, period. Shortly after 9/11, they moved to an unnamed U.S. suburb, where a neighbor began a relentless campaign of harassment: stalking, vandalism, and intimidation. He placed nails on the Omars’ walkway and a lawn ornament of a pig between his house and theirs. When the family sought help, with a meticulously documented record of incidents, local authorities repeatedly dismissed the harassment as an ordinary dispute between neighbors—not a sustained campaign directed at a Muslim family. Racial bias, authorities told the Omars, requires proof beyond a few claims. It took many years for the family to get a protective order in place. As Ali documents, that is the exact opposite problem that the Siraj family encountered from a national-security apparatus determined to find a threat from Muslims. Shahawar Matin Siraj, a 20-something Pakistani American, became entangled with a government informant who encouraged him to follow through with the idea of bombing a subway station—a bombing that never took place. He went to trial, believing that he would be found innocent, but was sentenced in 2007 to 30 years in prison. A day later, U.S. immigration officials detained his mother, father, and sister, who were later released. Siraj’s mother continues to maintain her son’s innocence. If authorities were reluctant to recognize the menace facing the Omars, in Siraj’s case they were willing to go extraordinary lengths to identify, cultivate, and prosecute a potential danger—even if they had to manufacture it themselves. Manufacturing fear against Muslims was not only ideological, but profitable. Tens of millions of dollars went into endeavors claiming to educate Americans about the supposedly dangerous nature of Islam. The Clarion Fund, which helped distribute Raphael Shore’s 2005 documentary Obsession: Radical Islam’s War Against the West, received $17 million from a single donor in 2008 alone. Right-wing commentator David Horowitz received more than $8 million for his eponymous Freedom Center, which housed Robert Spencer’s Jihad Watch blog and hosted Islamofascism Awareness Week on college campuses. Other conservative donors joined in. Banking and oil-fortune heir Richard Mellon Scaife was among several who put more than $42 million into anti-Muslim efforts in the years following 9/11. By the end of the Bush administration in 2008, Islamophobia no longer needed a terrorist attack to sustain it. Individuals and institutions with a financial interest in anti-Muslim sentiment kept it alive. Perhaps that, along with the massive bureaucracy that sustained Islamophobia, is what made it difficult for Bush’s successor to fight it. Ali points out that although President Barack Obama spoke about civilization’s debt to Islam in a 2009 speech in Cairo in an attempt to reset relations between the United States and the Muslim world, his administration did little to correct Bush’s overreach. In fact, she writes, during the first two years of his presidency, “the number of Islamic terrorism-related prosecutions ticked upward.” A Democratic president may speak more acceptingly of Islam, but anti-Muslim bias had already become ingrained in U.S. politics. Despite the racism and fearmongering on display in Seasons of Fury, Ali’s subjects do not reject the United States or the institutions that have failed to protect them. They turned to courts, free speech, activism, and public service to insist on the rights the United States promises its citizens. As Ali notes, the country may not deem Islam compatible with it, but Muslims have shown that their faith in the American experiment is unwavering. By the time she finished writing her book, Zohran Mamdani was elected New York’s first Muslim mayor. The night of the vote, Ali writes in the epilogue, “felt electric with possibility, charged by the promise that the American experiment was not yet worth giving up on.” Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: What’s the Matter With Eastern Germany?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.68
What’s the Matter With Eastern Germany? German far-right populism traces back to reunification—but historians disagree about why. There’s a widespread consensus in Germany that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a xenophobic far-right party that threatens the republic’s postwar political order. But there’s no accord on remedies—and, relatedly, no agreement about the sources of the scourge. What seems clear is that the AfD’s variety of national populism is most heavily anchored in eastern Germany and traces back to the country’s Cold War division, the terms of its eventual unification, and East-West relations since 1990. But that surface-level agreement about recent history masks deeper disagreements about what exactly happened during those periods. There’s a widespread consensus in Germany that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is a xenophobic far-right party that threatens the republic’s postwar political order. But there’s no accord on remedies—and, relatedly, no agreement about the sources of the scourge. What seems clear is that the AfD’s variety of national populism is most heavily anchored in eastern Germany and traces back to the country’s Cold War division, the terms of its eventual unification, and East-West relations since 1990. But that surface-level agreement about recent history masks deeper disagreements about what exactly happened during those periods. The AfD is not solely an eastern German phenomenon: Parties like it exist across the European Union, in the United Kingdom, and in the United States, too. In western Germany, the AfD breaks into double digits everywhere and even tops 20 percent in places. But its popularity is twice as high across eastern Germany—where polled rates of xenophobic sentiment are also much higher. The record result of 44 percent in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections on Sept. 6 is conceivable only in an eastern state, at least for now. One school of German historians explains the eastern mentality through the prism of the German Democratic Republic’s (GDR) fundamentally totalitarian character. Its clearest proponent is Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk, a historian affiliated with the Stasi Records Archive, the repository of the GDR’s secret police files. Kowalczuk hails from a GDR family that was closely tied to the regime, a story he tells in his book Freiheitsschock (Freedom Shock), but broke with his family and cast off the system’s Marxist-Leninist straitjacket, which cost him the opportunity to attend university. (After unification, he studied history at Humboldt University.) At 22, he joined the countrywide demonstrations that eventually chased out GDR hardliners and caused the Berlin Wall to fall. Kowalczuk emphasizes the all-encompassing totality of a state that dictated every facet of life to its subjects: “from cradle to grave,” indoctrinating and controlling through schools, party, mass organizations, and the workplace. Most historians who argue along Kowalczuk’s lines hold that the Stasi itself, through informant networks and an all-knowing, all-powerful apparatus, kept the GDR’s population of 16 million in line. Kowalczuk, however, argues that the Stasi itself was not as powerful as claimed or thought (or as portrayed in The Lives of Others): Much of its power of intimidation stemmed from its reputation, not its actual reach. In other words, eastern Germans, argues Kowalczuk, could have acted more independently and even defiantly had they had the gumption—but they didn’t. Kowalczuk argues that East Germans passively allowed themselves to be subjugated, browbeaten, restricted, and instructed by the regime. They were obedient pupils internalizing its narrow-minded, racist, authoritarian character and reproducing it in families, schools, and society. He casts eastern Germans essentially as sheep who relinquished freedom in exchange for certainty and security. In his view, the so-called peaceful revolution of 1989 wasn’t instigated by these cowed masses but by a tiny minority of dissidents and rebels—like himself. The public took to the streets only once the regime was on the run, and then portrayed themselves as freedom fighters—and victims. The newly liberated East Germans had no conception of an alternative state or society beyond that which then-West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the “reunification chancellor,” dangled before their eyes. Today’s eastern Germans, Kowalczuk says—even those born in a unified Germany—have undertaken too little to emancipate themselves from the GDR’s totalitarian mindset. They refuse to take responsibility for their own condition, demand the state provide for them, and express the same intolerance toward other cultures that the regime once did. The uncertainties that freedom presents are so unnerving that they retreat into nostalgia for the GDR—beyond even that in Goodbye, Lenin!—that idealizes its old ties to the Soviet Union and sympathizes with a dictator as ruthless as Vladimir Putin. Kowalczuk’s most direct foil is Katja Hoyer, also a GDR-born historian, though she was only 4 years old when the peaceful revolution broke out. She’s known to English-language readers through her UK bestseller Beyond the Wall: East Germany, 1949 – 1990, which argues that life in the GDR was more textured than Kowalczuk acknowledges. East Germans lived and loved, had birthday parties and weddings, and enjoyed vacations and families. They weren’t passive, she argues, despite the formidable security apparatus. The GDR’s film industry—during periods of liberalization—even produced quality films like the 1973 cult classic Die Legende von Paul und Paula (The Legend of Paul and Paula). Hoyer also credits GDR socialism with genuine achievements, such as women’s rights, affordable housing, and hands-on workplace participation. If unglamorous, just about everyone had a two-room apartment and, of course, a job. Rents were subsidized, healthcare free, and there was childcare for all families. Hoyer treats the relative material equality of the self-described “workers’ and farmers’ state” as a humane alternative to capitalism’s wealth gaps. “Many East Germans were proud of their achievements as social mobility provided unprecedented opportunities for the working classes,” she argues. Although Beyond the Wall stops in 1990, elsewhere Hoyer argues that eastern Germans’ lives and achievements were dismissed in the united Germany as worthless “ballast.” West German condescension and the “sink or swim” into which eastern Germans were thrown in the 1990s caused resentment to fester, and snowball, and be passed on to subsequent generations. The problem today in Germany’s eastern states, she argues, isn’t that citizens are undemocratic but that the system is less democratic than they had expected. Materially, the easterners lag behind their western brethren not least because they had no assets when communism collapsed. She has sympathy for the hardships that economic union imposed. Seen this way, the AfD vote is explicable. This party alone avoids demonizing the GDR, thus offering eastern Germans respect that none of the other parties do. The AfD may be German, Hoyer argues, but versions of it exist everywhere in Europe, including England, where she currently works. Eastern Germans’ “behaviors and characteristics have lazily been written off as a deviation from the west German norm, fostering a defiant us-against-them mentality,” she argued in 2024 in the Guardian. “This east German identity, combined with the feeling of being othered and marginalised, is a powerful thing for the AFD to exploit.” As for the racism and xenophobia, she attributes them to economic anxiety and condescension. The way to win back the easterners is to take their concerns seriously, including migration, and treat them with respect. A third prominent commentator is Dirk Oschmann, a literature professor at Leipzig University. His take in Der Osten: eine westdeutsche Erfindung (The East: A West German Invention), a 2023 work widely discussed in Germany, is close to Hoyer’s but not identical. He contends that the western Germans’ derogatory labeling of easterners as lazy, dim-witted, bigoted complaining losers is a means to deflect legitimate criticism that the West itself flubbed unification. He argues that the lock-stock-and-barrel incorporation of eastern Germany into the Federal Republic constituted a one-sided takeover. There was, for example, no constitutional convention to create the unified Germany anew. East Germany’s economy was put on equal footing with West Germany’s overnight, causing it to implode—while western companies swooped into pick up the business. The East’s factories and firms were sold off to Western buyers, who made out like bandits. West German elites stepped into leadership posts across the East: in universities, police forces, hospitals—just about everywhere. Oschmann considers Kowalczuk a proponent of this tendency by tracing everything back to the GDR itself, rather than the humiliation of unification and the travails of decades since. He explains the AfD and the power of the migration issue much as Hoyer does: as a response to grievances and disrespect. As for the East’s cultural racism, he admits its presence but calls the West’s pejorative treatment of the East a form of xenophobia or “othering.” This surfeit of analysis begs the question of whether any response from the mainstream German parties can win AfD voters to their side. Certainly, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz thinks so. His remedy is to double down on restricting migration, the top reason for AfD voting. This was Merz’s answer before the Saxony-Anhalt vote and, while asylum applications have fallen by nearly half under Merz, there’s been no political payoff. Rather than vote for the copy act, 44 percent of Saxony-Anhalt’s voters cast their ballots for the original, the AfD, whose jingoism Merz chases after, while the CDU was rewarded with less than half of its previous vote share. The Social Democrats think better social safety nets will do the trick, even though AfD voters are not poor. Germany’s political establishment is clueless how to handle the AfD’s surge—and the country’s historians, sadly, offer no concrete answers either. Paul Hockenos is a Berlin-based journalist. His recent book is Berlin Calling: A Story of Anarchy, Music, the Wall, and the Birth of the New Berlin. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription.
