item.title: By Nearly Every Metric, the U.S. Is Losing the Iran War
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.21
By Nearly Every Metric, the U.S. Is Losing the Iran War “It’s irrefutable that the U.S. failed in its main strategic goals,” one expert said. In early March, U.S. President Donald Trump said that the United States had already “won” the war against Iran but still had to “finish the job.” Months later, as fighting escalates across the region and diplomacy is stalled, the “job” remains unfinished with no end in sight. Trump on Wednesday said that “hopefully we are toward the end of the war” and suggested that Iran wants to make a deal. But that optimism is belied by what’s happening on the ground—and there’s little evidence that Tehran is eager for an agreement. In early March, U.S. President Donald Trump said that the United States had already “won” the war against Iran but still had to “finish the job.” Months later, as fighting escalates across the region and diplomacy is stalled, the “job” remains unfinished with no end in sight. Trump on Wednesday said that “hopefully we are toward the end of the war” and suggested that Iran wants to make a deal. But that optimism is belied by what’s happening on the ground—and there’s little evidence that Tehran is eager for an agreement. The United States has had military successes in the war, but, overall, the conflict has been a strategic disaster for Washington. The fighting has exposed serious vulnerabilities for the U.S. military and left its forces spread thin, cost the United States an estimated $38.1 billion so far, and caused a global energy crisis. The war is extremely unpopular with American voters, and a growing number of Republicans in Congress are voting in favor of ending the conflict; one GOP congressman has even moved to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war. But for all of those costs, the United States has achieved very little in Iran—and in some cases, things have gotten worse. By nearly every metric—from Iran’s ability to project power in the region through its proxies, to its military capabilities, to the strength of its regime, to the status of its nuclear program—the United States is losing the war. What’s more, Tehran has now proved that it can shut down the Strait of Hormuz long term, an ability it long boasted of having but had never actually demonstrated. “If you wind the clock back to February and take a look at what the U.S. stated it was trying to do, it’s irrefutable that the U.S. failed in its main strategic goals,” Gregory Brew, an Iran expert and senior analyst at Eurasia Group, told Foreign Policy. Proxies When Trump announced the onset of major combat operations against Iran in late February, he said that the United States was going to ensure that “terrorist proxies can no longer destabilize the region or the world and attack our forces.” Similarly, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine in early March said that the United States was aiming to dismantle “Iran’s ability to project power outside of its borders, both today and in the future.” In a primetime speech to the nation a month into the war, Trump also said the United States was “systematically dismantling the [Iranian] regime’s ability to threaten America or project power outside of their borders.” But there’s no evidence to suggest that the United States has accomplished this. The fact that the conflict has for months been centered on a fight for control of the Strait of Hormuz—a waterway that was open when the war began—is indicative of Tehran’s enduring capacity to influence the course of events both in the Middle East and wider world (more on that below). Tehran’s proxies also remain a major threat months into the war and are increasingly contributing to both regional chaos and rising oil prices. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen made major territorial gains along the country’s Red Sea coast this month, including seizing the port city of Mocha and strategic islands like Perim, in a blistering offensive against Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. As a result, the group has taken effective control over another critical waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and separates the Arabian Peninsula from Africa. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait was already a key shipping lane before the war but became even more important amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran and the Houthis for months warned that the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could be closed if the United States continued the war, and they are now in a position to make good on that threat. Meanwhile, the Houthis and Saudi Arabia are exchanging fire, reigniting long-running tensions tied to a civil war that began in 2014 but were largely on pause following a 2022 truce. There are now growing concerns that Yemen is on the verge of returning to full-blown civil war. Saudi Arabia also temporarily shut down its 750-mile East-West oil pipeline last week after it was damaged in a drone attack that Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed militants in Iraq, and it’s unclear when it will be operational again. The pipeline transports crude oil from the kingdom’s east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and its temporary closure impacts roughly 4 percent of the world’s oil supply. It’s true that other Iranian proxies like Hamas and Hezbollah—long considered Tehran’s most powerful ally in the region—are now far weaker than they were a few years ago, but this is almost entirely due to Israeli actions in Gaza and Lebanon. Ballistic missiles and drones The Trump administration also launched the war with the objective of destroying Iran’s ballistic missile and drone capabilities. In April, Hegseth said Iran’s missile program was functionally destroyed and that the country could “no longer build missiles.” Trump has also claimed that Iran’s military has been “totally destroyed.” Iran’s military has certainly been significantly affected by the war. A number of top Iranian military and intelligence leaders have been killed since the bombs started falling, its industrial capacity has been diminished, and its conventional navy has largely been destroyed. But Tehran’s continued ability to launch attacks on targets across the region with both missiles and drones shows that this goal remains elusive and that the Trump administration has greatly embellished its military successes. Intelligence assessments also contradict the Trump administration’s public claims about the extent to which Iran’s military has been degraded. Iran has reportedly resumed ballistic missile production in underground facilities, even after thousands of U.S. strikes targeted its missile facilities and launch sites in the early days of the war. It was also always going to be difficult to completely destroy Iran’s drone capability given how cheap and easy they are to produce. Regime change While the Trump administration has fluctuated on whether bringing down the Iranian regime is a central objective, when the war began it was clear that toppling Iran’s leadership was among the White House’s key goals. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump said on Feb. 28. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take. This will be probably your only chance for generations.” Though top Iranian leaders, including former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, have been killed, the regime remains very much intact and, in many ways, has only calcified. “Insofar as regime change was a goal, U.S. action has been almost entirely counterproductive. The regime is now more entrenched. It is more confident of its position inside Iran. It is more emboldened. It’s dominated now by military security leadership that, while pragmatic, are almost uniformly hostile toward the West and not interested in any kind of broader accommodation with the U.S. or the West in general,” Brew said. Nuclear program More than any other issue, Trump has repeatedly returned to Iran’s nuclear program as the primary objective of the war. The president has also misleadingly claimed that the United States “obliterated” Iran’s program, even as he justifies continuing the war for the sake of preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. There’s no doubt that U.S. strikes have set Iran’s nuclear program back by destroying infrastructure and killing important figures within Iran (including top scientists), but the country still has a roughly 440-kilogram (970 pounds) stockpile of highly enriched uranium (HEU). Experts have repeatedly emphasized that as long as Iran has access to this stockpile—the precise location of which remains unknown—its nuclear program remains a threat and cannot be considered neutralized. International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director-General Rafael Grossi this week lamented that the agency’s oversight of Iran’s nuclear program “deteriorated” this year. “We have not conducted any in-field verification activities in Iran for more than six months,” Grossi said, while emphasizing that it’s been “well over a year” since the IAEA “lost continuity of knowledge” regarding Iran’s uranium stockpile. “The Agency’s lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern and needs to be addressed with the utmost urgency,” Grossi said. Trump has flip-flopped on whether the United States needs to retrieve the country’s HEU stockpile—suggesting it’s buried under rubble and inaccessible due to previous U.S. strikes. “We will get it. We don’t need it, we don’t want it. We’ll probably destroy it after we get it, but we’re not going to let them have it,” Trump said in May. Satellite imagery has also shown a “surge” in construction activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site, in 2026, according to a recent analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Last week, Trump suggested the United States could take action based on the reports of construction activity at Pickaxe Mountain. “We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe,” Trump said. “I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard.” Despite such rhetoric, the Trump administration’s actions increasingly indicate that Iran’s nuclear program has been bumped down the White House’s list of priorities. Amid the lack of progress on the nuclear issue and the failure to achieve its initial goals in the war more broadly, the Trump administration has shifted its attention to other objectives. The administration has moved to strangle Iran economically, via both a naval blockade and a financial campaign—dubbed Operation Economic Outcast—to further isolate Tehran via sanctions and other actions. “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said as he announced the effort in late August. But Iran’s leadership has withstood economic pressure from the United States for decades, raising doubts as to whether this approach will actually move the needle and see Tehran make concessions in any future talks. Control of Hormuz The war is now fundamentally a fight over oil and shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz. While around 4 million to 5 million barrels of oil were flowing through the strait daily in early August, that number is now approaching around 10 million, Brew said. This is positive for the United States and also comes as its naval blockade appears to be working given Iranian oil exports have ground to a halt. But traffic through the strait is roughly a fifth of what was seen before the war, Brew said, underscoring that the situation is also being “managed through a pretty considerable outlay of resources.” The process involves the U.S. Navy and air assets providing defense for tankers moving through the strait in small convoys. This system has steadily increased the flow of oil through the strait over the last month, and while it’s helping to delay a “general crisis” in energy markets, Brew said, it’s “not removing the risk.” The price of Brent crude—the global benchmark for oil—sat around $104 on Thursday. Just before the war began in February, the price of Brent crude was roughly $72 a barrel. In response to a request for comment on whether Trump believes the war will end on a positive note for the United States, a White House official on background told Foreign Policy that “Iran is calling constantly and is desperate for a deal,” but the president is “only open to making a good deal with Iran, whereby they permanently renounce their desire for a nuclear weapon.” The official also said that while Trump is open to talks under the “right circumstances,” he has “no need to negotiate with the Iranians.” “Unlike previous presidents, President Trump will not be played by the Iranian regime. The President is satisfied letting the inevitable Iranian collapse play out,” the official said. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: The Houthi Advance Is About More Than Just Iran
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.15
The Houthi Advance Is About More Than Just Iran The Saudi-Emirati rivalry is driving moves across the region. On Sept. 8, the Houthis launched a major offensive against Saudi-backed forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, seizing key points across the country’s west coast and suddenly establishing a commanding position on the Bab el-Mandeb. That same week, Algeria declared that it was severing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates and subsequently closed its airspace to Emirati planes. These two events, in countries almost as geographically distant as possible within the bounds of the Middle East and with dramatically different geopolitical stakes, may seem to have little in common. But developments in Yemen and Algeria are bound together by three powerful processes shaping regional order at this moment: the failure of the United States to defeat Iran or protect its Arab allies, the Saudi-Emirati conflict, and the rapid erosion of the artificial divides between the Middle East and Africa. The escalation in Yemen has received the most attention, for good reason. The Houthi seizure of the port town of Mokha, most of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, and several key islands in the Red Sea allow the group to disrupt and deny shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb. That entryway to the Red Sea has always been one of the most important maritime chokepoints for global trade, with transit through the Suez Canal connecting Asia to the West (with associated toll revenues keeping the Egyptian economy afloat). It took on even greater importance after Saudi Arabia sought to circumvent Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz by redirecting oil shipments through its East-West pipeline to its Red Sea outlet. The Houthi offensive, combined with drone strikes on the pipeline attributed to Iraqi militias, has suddenly and dramatically closed that outlet, putting unprecedented pressure on Saudi Arabia and the global economy. On Sept. 8, the Houthis launched a major offensive against Saudi-backed forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, seizing key points across the country’s west coast and suddenly establishing a commanding position on the Bab el-Mandeb. That same week, Algeria declared that it was severing diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates and subsequently closed its airspace to Emirati planes. These two events, in countries almost as geographically distant as possible within the bounds of the Middle East and with dramatically different geopolitical stakes, may seem to have little in common. But developments in Yemen and Algeria are bound together by three powerful processes shaping regional order at this moment: the failure of the United States to defeat Iran or protect its Arab allies, the Saudi-Emirati conflict, and the rapid erosion of the artificial divides between the Middle East and Africa. The escalation in Yemen has received the most attention, for good reason. The Houthi seizure of the port town of Mokha, most of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, and several key islands in the Red Sea allow the group to disrupt and deny shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb. That entryway to the Red Sea has always been one of the most important maritime chokepoints for global trade, with transit through the Suez Canal connecting Asia to the West (with associated toll revenues keeping the Egyptian economy afloat). It took on even greater importance after Saudi Arabia sought to circumvent Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz by redirecting oil shipments through its East-West pipeline to its Red Sea outlet. The Houthi offensive, combined with drone strikes on the pipeline attributed to Iraqi militias, has suddenly and dramatically closed that outlet, putting unprecedented pressure on Saudi Arabia and the global economy. While the impact of the Houthi offensive has been felt most profoundly on the Iran front, Yemen’s war has its own dynamics. Saudi Arabia triggered the most recent round of fighting in July by bombing Sanaa’s airport, and fighting had escalated for several months. But as with everything in the Middle East these days, there was a Saudi-Emirati angle as well. Last December, Saudi forces suddenly and unceremoniously drove Emirati-aligned forces out of Yemen, pushing back against a Southern independence movement that it viewed as part of a broader Emirati campaign to promote secessionist groups across the region. It had been particularly concerned about potential Emirati support for Israel’s recognition of the breakaway Somali province of Somaliland. The prospect of Israel gaining a strategic foothold on the other side of the Bab el-Mandeb, particularly if that facilitated Emirati encirclement of Saudi Arabia, struck Riyadh as a major strategic threat. Riyadh followed its Yemen moves with a bid to assemble a regional coalition, including states such as Turkey, Egypt, and Qatar, that would become a third pole competing with Iran’s Axis of Resistance and the Emirati-Israeli-led Abraham Accords project. Pushing the UAE out of Yemen was the easy part, though. The quick defeat of the UAE’s allies left the Saudis responsible for supporting and leading the remaining forces defending the territories under the control of the internationally recognized government. While Riyadh made a show of pouring support and reorganizing those forces and pledging air cover (while reportedly quietly paying off the Houthis), much of that aid proved short-lived. Saudi strategy did not seem much improved from decades of previous failures and underperformance, with the influx of cash, episodic airstrikes, continued blockade, and ample propaganda failing to substitute for the absence of human capacity or strategic competence on the ground. Reporting suggests that as many as 80 percent of the Saudi-backed forces were ghost fighters, drawing salaries and little else. Saudi communications seem to have been thoroughly compromised by the Houthis, while promised air cover largely failed to materialize. In the fever swamps of Arab social media, rumors run rampant about the UAE covertly activating its former allies to undermine the government forces—payback for Riyadh’s December humiliation and in support of Israel’s concerns about the new Saudi-led coalition. Houthi motivations therefore cannot be reduced solely to Iranian grand strategy or even to the opportunity to strike a decisive blow in the ongoing war with Saudi Arabia. Their advance also responded to the potential transregionalization of the conflict. Israel’s recognition of Somaliland, and rumored covert deployments on the ground, could potentially bring Israeli, Emirati, and even U.S. forces directly to the other side of the strait to contest control and serve as a base for counterstrikes into Yemen. That could, in turn, turbocharge Houthi ties with the Somalia-based al-Shabab terrorist group, which has been organically growing for several years, raising the risks of a transregional expansion of the war across the Horn of Africa. No doubt these East African concerns were on the mind of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman dropped in for an unusual visit to Cairo this week. Egypt took Riyadh’s side in the December crisis but has thus far declined to join the Saudi-led Mecca Pact with Pakistan and Turkey. The economic impact of the potential closure of the Bab el-Mandeb on the Suez Canal on top of the effects of the Iran war would be devastating to an Egyptian regime already struggling with profound economic problems. The expansion of the Yemen conflict into the Horn of Africa also intensifies the pressure on Egypt, which is locked in an ongoing struggle with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Egypt seems no likelier to be willing to join a ground war against the Houthis than it was when Mohammed bin Salman asked a decade ago, but in many ways the stakes are now higher and the choices more fraught. In a region defined by a fierce struggle between Saudi Arabia and the UAE, Cairo can no longer count on financial support from both, since choosing either side could cost it dearly with the other. Saudi Arabia, frustrated by the refusal of the United States to intervene against the Houthis on its behalf, had hoped to get assistance from its new alliance partners, Pakistan and Turkey. But both countries seem content to offer moral support and stay out of the Yemeni quagmire. Pakistan quickly clarified that its alliance commitments only extended to new conflicts. But such a stance may be untenable as Saudi options rapidly narrow. Pakistani intervention in Yemen in support of Saudi Arabia, though not currently in the cards, would represent a new frontier for transregional security competition and for the necessity of thinking beyond the Middle East. Which brings us to Algeria. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s decision to sever diplomatic relations was a response to the surge of Emirati activities across the Sahel and especially its support for Moroccan claims to the Western Sahara. Algeria’s problems with the UAE center on its support for Morocco as part of the Abraham Accords, which manifests in the Western Sahara as well as across the Sahel, where Rabat has sought to increase its influence at Algeria’s expense—with Emirati backing. Algiers accused the UAE of expanding its influence in Chad, Mali, and Niger and perpetuating destabilizing and bloody wars through support for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan and Khalifa Haftar’s Libyan National Army in Libya. Algerian pro-regime media also accuse the UAE of attempting to manipulate the country’s own 2019 presidential election, though evidence is thus far scarce. Like Riyadh, Algeria sees the UAE’s ambitions in part through the lens of the Emirati alliance with Israel and blames it for the acceleration of Morocco’s diplomatic ties with Israel and American recognition of its sovereignty in Western Sahara. All this points to a Middle East map that is bigger than the one U.S. policymakers tend to hold in their heads, with countries across North and East Africa advancing their own alliances and interests in ways that stubbornly refuse to follow the traditional lines of Middle Eastern politics. A few days after Algeria’s diplomatic moves, Eritrea accused the UAE of “port imperialism” in collaboration with Israel. Like the Houthis, Eritrea has watched Emirati expansion in the Horn of Africa and Israeli support for Somaliland with concern while keeping an eye on Ethiopian military preparations warily. And all of this unfolds amid growing international and regional condemnation of the UAE’s support for the brutal RSF, credibly accused of massive war crimes. Houthi gains in Yemen may prove ephemeral. There is a long history of sudden surges and reversals in Yemen’s long internal war, and a new status quo may eventually emerge that avoids the worst-case scenarios. But the bigger lesson is that regional politics today are not a bipolar struggle between Iran and a U.S.-led coalition. The Saudi-Emirati conflict, which is in turn a proxy for a regional argument over Israel’s place in the order, has now entrenched a three-way competition unfolding across regional boundaries. Marc Lynch is a professor of political science and international affairs at the George Washington University and the director of the Project on Middle East Political Science. His most recent book is America’s Middle East: The Ruination of a Region. X: @abuaardvark Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Emily Wilson Chooses Her Words Carefully
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.88
Emily Wilson Chooses Her Words Carefully The Homeric scholar’s new book on translation is bitingly smart. Is there a scholar better at promoting a book launch than Emily Wilson? Almost a decade ago she revolutionized the promotion of literary translation after the release of her first Odyssey translation. While literary media outlets were breathlessly heralding the arrival of the first-ever translation of the Odyssey into English by a woman, Wilson took to Twitter and showed everyone in granular detail how a translator works, with lengthy threads (still available here, even though Wilson has since deleted her Twitter account) detailing how the choices she’d made differed from earlier renditions. The threads combined transparency, accessibility, and humor, and they were hugely popular. Whether you came to them as a trained classicist trying to figure out which translation you wanted to teach, or as a newcomer to Homer wondering why another translation was needed at all, Wilson had something to teach you. Is there a scholar better at promoting a book launch than Emily Wilson? Almost a decade ago she revolutionized the promotion of literary translation after the release of her first Odyssey translation. While literary media outlets were breathlessly heralding the arrival of the first-ever translation of the Odyssey into English by a woman, Wilson took to Twitter and showed everyone in granular detail how a translator works, with lengthy threads (still available here, even though Wilson has since deleted her Twitter account) detailing how the choices she’d made differed from earlier renditions. The threads combined transparency, accessibility, and humor, and they were hugely popular. Whether you came to them as a trained classicist trying to figure out which translation you wanted to teach, or as a newcomer to Homer wondering why another translation was needed at all, Wilson had something to teach you. Those threads form the basis of the final, largest essay in Wilson’s essay collection, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea: Journeys Through Ancient Literature, released earlier this month. It’s a wide-ranging and compulsively readable book, comprising mostly revised and reworked review essays that she’s previously published but to which she added substantial new material. And once again, Wilson’s promotion strategy has been impeccable, intentionally or not, with her scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of the Odyssey, which begins by calling the movie “an entertaining way to hide from the high temperatures for a few hours” at which “[m]y teenagers had a good time.” That perhaps was the nicest thing she had to say. Wilson’s review briefly crashed the London Review of Books website and sparked a debate about whether she had been overly or inappropriately harsh with the film. Joyce Carol Oates may not have approved, but if you enjoy Wilson’s shade, you’re in for a treat, because that reviewer voice is the one that you hear in Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea. Readers might expect a book from one of our most prominent public intellectuals to sound like one of those large, endowed lectures universities host to show their commitment to educating the broader public—edifying, learned, entertaining, occasionally funny. Wilson’s book reads more like the kind of jokes scholars make to each other over mediocre wine at the reception after such events. You’ll learn a great deal about ancient literature from this book, and even more about the complexity of translation. But you’ll also learn a whole lot about what academics sound like when the (polite, erudite) knives come out with surgical precision. Wilson’s harshest critiques are reserved for translators who embellish or expand on the original text without adding anything useful or interesting, and she’s especially tough on those whose translations add length without bothering to sound like actual English. The most illustrative example, perhaps, is Wilson’s assessment of the opening of Daniel Mendelsohn’s 2025 translation of the Odyssey. Her analysis of Richmond Lattimore’s opening—“Tell me, Muse, of the man of many ways, who was driven far journeys”—is absolutely withering; by comparison, when she shifts gears to Mendelsohn, she is relatively brief and neutral. Mendelsohn’s Odyssey has many well-deserved fans, but two Odyssey translations coming so close together are bound to jostle for space like kids in the backseat of a car. Wilson ends her book with a set of 20 rules that guide her translation practice, and her second is that a retranslation (that is, a translation of a book that’s already been translated) is “fundamentally pointless” if it doesn’t bring something new to the text. It seems to be in this spirit that she chides Mendelsohn: “Fourteen words in Greek have become twenty-four in English, through the addition of words and phrases that correspond to nothing specific in the Greek, though they often draw on the phrasing of earlier English translations: ‘the tale’ is an addition also found in the 1929 translation by Herbert Bates; ‘off course’ is a nautical phrase, not corresponding to anything in the Greek but also found in Robert Fagles’ version.” She concludes with the most damning of praise, saying that Mendelsohn is “[f]ollowing Lattimore in his courageous defiance of contemporary English idiom.” Ouch, but you can’t say she doesn’t have the receipts. Whether or not you agree with her, Wilson is consistent and has a clear point of view, necessary ingredients for a critic (as I suspect Mendelsohn, a fine critic himself, would cede). Wilson’s rule no. 16 is, “Don’t try to please everyone. If nobody objects to any choice you make, your choices are too timid.” Nobody could claim that Wilson doesn’t live by that rule in any of her writing, including here. In the first essay of the book, “Tongue Breaks,” about the translation and reception of Sappho, Wilson is perhaps especially harsh on women writers whose only connection with Sappho is a shared gender. In the margins of a paragraph where Wilson wrote, Mary “Robinson aspires to sublimity, but, sadly, her writing sounds like this,” I scribbled to myself, “Is EW best when bitchy?” But I could almost hear Wilson’s own voice in my ear, scolding me, because that isn’t the right word. Wilson herself points out the dangers of importing entirely unnecessary misogyny into our interpretations, as generations of translators did with editorializing editions calling the 12 slave girls executed by Telemachus for sleeping with the suitors “sluts” or “whores”—a judgmental gloss completely missing in the original. So when I revisited my note, I considered crossing out my word choice and replacing it with something like “tart”—but no, that’s too archaic. Her critique is often too direct to be rightly called shade; saying her teenagers enjoyed a film is shade, but calling someone’s writing “turgid” is not. So what, exactly, should I call this voice? As I considered, I realized just how much reading this book had conditioned my eye to look for careful word choice—which, actually, feels like the bigger project of Wine-Dark Sea. Wilson sometimes seems to long for a slightly higher caliber of critics and readers of her translations. The seemingly most-quoted and argued-about part of her review of Nolan’s Odyssey is her claim that she “would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.” Harsh, yes, but consider what came right before it: “In at least one interview, he cited my version of the first line of the poem, ‘Tell me about a complicated man.’” My sense, reading this, was that Wilson was especially aggrieved by how an offhand comment by the director got twisted in the media to make it sound like Nolan had substantially based his script on Wilson’s translation. One can only imagine how infuriating it would feel for a translator as careful and considered as Wilson to have her name incorrectly attached to a film she thought was merely entertaining. If only the broader public had a better understanding of what goes into producing a translation and what makes different translations distinct! The answer to this lack of education is to read this volume. Throughout the essays in Wine-Dark Sea, Wilson walks the reader through the infinite number of tiny choices translators must make to try to produce a text that transmits not only the original’s meaning but also its tone, its pace, and its poetic effects into something that will mean something to readers. In her final essay, “Translating the Odyssey,” she delves into minute grammar questions, like the effect of replacing a Greek purpose clause with a participle. Elsewhere she goes further into broader questions of translating texts into very different cultures, especially in back-to-back essays about the challenges of translating ancient comedy, “Punishment by Radish” (a reference to the often-threatened ancient Greek punishment of sodomizing criminals with root vegetables) and “Ave, Jeeves.” In the first, she argues that the spirit of Aristophanes’ comedy is best expressed by the obscene lyrical fluidity of Cardi B and Megan Thee Stallion’s “WAP.” But some tropes may be harder or even impossible to bring to contemporary readers, like the brilliant slaves of Roman comedy, of whom Wodehouse’s Jeeves was the last accessible avatar. Wilson is entirely unafraid of a modern comparison—in one of my favorite passages in the book, she writes approvingly of the resonance between her “complicated man” and Avril Lavigne’s “Complicated.” Other modern parallels didn’t work as well for me. Several of the essays veer, in their final paragraph, into the briefest possible parable for modern times. In an essay about Demosthenes’ rhetoric against Philip, she concludes with a gesture toward Brexit and the election of Donald Trump to show how voters can still be swayed by an “enticing lie,” and an essay about Aeschylus’ Oresteia ends with a claim that it has something to teach us “[a]s we turn our attention to the angry voices of those who feel themselves marginalised in modern life.” Sure, but to my eye the continued relevance of Wilson’s analysis in our world was obvious without making such explicit nods. I wondered if she didn’t entirely trust the reader to get the point, which felt at odds with the confidence she displays elsewhere. But this minor quibble doesn’t detract overall from how much Wilson teaches readers about how to be educated readers of translations—lessons that, one hopes, some will absorb before Wilson’s newly announced retranslation of the Odyssey is released. It is difficult to overstate what an unprecedented literary event this is: Wilson has decided to retranslate from the ground up her bestselling 2017 translation, further iterating on her work along the guidelines she sets for herself in those final 20 rules. Wine-Dark Sea holds some clues for what that new translation might broadly look like; she notes that the translations she uses in the final essay don’t quite match her 2017 text. But it seems she’s also motivated by a desire for more nuance than she originally felt was possible. Her spare 2017 text matches Homer line for line but cuts Homer’s dactylic hexameter into English iambic pentameter, which often meant turning a 17-syllable line into a 10-syllable one, a choice that keeps that translation lean and swift. The new one, she says, will be longer, which will give more room to explore the ancient world. Wilson told the Associated Press that she feels she overused “slave” as a general term—including in the passage I mentioned earlier, the hanging of the slave girls—where she could have given more specificity that would shed light on the broad array of social roles held by slaves in the epic. Ironic, considering that nearly a decade ago her original translation was much-lauded for its willingness to call a slave a slave, where even other recent translations used euphemisms like servant. As always, Wilson is pushing us to be better readers of Homer—and of her. Donna Zuckerberg is the author of Not All Dead White Men: Classics and Misogyny in the Digital Age and the forthcoming memoir Antiquated. She founded and ran the award-winning online publication Eidolon from 2015 to 2020. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: Will Russia Ever Be ‘Normal’?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.07
Will Russia Ever Be ‘Normal’? Empires inevitably decline, and Putin’s project will be no exception. When asked “how’s it going,” average Russians usually respond with one word—normalno. Life is normal when you’re doing neither exceptionally well nor exceptionally poorly. The English-language equivalent might be somewhere between “hanging in there” and “I’m OK.” Normalnost—or the condition of normalcy—is obviously a relative notion. What is normalno for a Russian pensioner eking out an existence is not normalno for President Vladimir Putin and his minions. Even so, most Russians would probably agree that life is normalno when you’re getting by financially, your kids don’t hate you excessively, your spouse drinks too much only occasionally, and the authorities mostly ignore you. When asked “how’s it going,” average Russians usually respond with one word—normalno. Life is normal when you’re doing neither exceptionally well nor exceptionally poorly. The English-language equivalent might be somewhere between “hanging in there” and “I’m OK.” Normalnost—or the condition of normalcy—is obviously a relative notion. What is normalno for a Russian pensioner eking out an existence is not normalno for President Vladimir Putin and his minions. Even so, most Russians would probably agree that life is normalno when you’re getting by financially, your kids don’t hate you excessively, your spouse drinks too much only occasionally, and the authorities mostly ignore you. Putin’s fascist regime has put normalnost to the test. Life was fine for your average Russian—and for Russian elites—before Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Now, four and a half years into a bloody war that is killing or wounding around 1,100 Russian soldiers per day while pushing the country’s militarized economy to the brink of collapse, life is anything but normalno for Russians living outside the protected bubbles of Moscow and St. Petersburg. Now, even the residents of these two cities have begun experiencing first-hand what seemed for so long to be a faraway, fantasy conflict. At a minimum, a return to normalnost presupposes the end of the war. That, in turn, more or less presupposes the end of Putin. Although Putin’s removal in a coup is possible even as the war continues, it cannot end as long as Putin remains committed to it for the sake of his own personal and political survival. But the relationship between normalnost and war goes deeper than Putin and his determination to destroy Ukraine. Unfortunately for Russia and its neighbors, normalnost will always be susceptible to breakdown—and Russian aggression will always be possible—as long as two structural factors remain in place. The first is Russia’s political culture and sense of national identity. Central to Russians’ self-perception is the culturally sanctioned, deeply ingrained belief that their country is uniquely predisposed to greatness with a quasi-right to dominate others. Russia’s world-historical mission is thus the very opposite of normalno: Its mission is not to rest on its laurels and enjoy life within its borders, but to fulfill its historical destiny and spread Russian civilization—a messianic concept that is deeply rooted in Russian Orthodoxy but largely devoid of any religious content today. Variants of these views were held by imperial Russian officials and cultural figures (such as Fyodor Dostoevsky), as well as anti-communist dissidents (including Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn). These same views are currently held by Putin; Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox church and reputed former KGB agent; Putin’s propaganda attack dog Dmitry Medvedev (known for his eagerness to incinerate European capitals with nuclear weapons); the crackpot philosopher Aleksandr Dugin; the rabid television personality Vladimir Solovyov, and scores of other propagandists. Most Russians espouse them as well—if not explicitly, then as part of the cultural waters in which they swim. The fact that these views have been dominant in Russian discourse over decades and even centuries suggests that we’re dealing with a deeper structure—a stable political-cultural norm, not a set of transient views. Given this tenacious political culture, the many Russians who strive for normalnost in their everyday lives are hard-pressed to resist that culture’s claims about the greatness of their nation. In the final analysis, this undermines Russians’ desire for quotidian normalnost. Could these cultural mindsets change? Other nations with megalomaniacal views of themselves were able to abandon them and focus their attention on daily life only after suffering humiliating military defeats. Britain and France lost empires; the once-aggressive Germans and Japanese were bombed into pacifism during World War II and afterward refocused on domestic prosperity. The United States may be getting its comeuppance today. These examples suggest that Russia can finally embrace normalnost if and only if it suffers a clear defeat by Ukraine. A mere ceasefire won’t do. Neither will Putin’s departure. Defeat would have to be of such a magnitude as to get even the most vociferous supporters of greatness to question their assumptions. Right now, it is difficult to imagine that anything short of a spectacular collapse would finally enable Russians to do what the Germans did after 1945: Accept responsibility for their leader’s crimes and become average citizens of the world. The second factor standing in the way of Russia becoming a normal nation is the Russian state—not the type of regime, whether imperial, Soviet, fascist, or something else, but the size and complexity of a political entity that spans 11 time zones and is populated by a plethora of nations with different cultures, religions, histories, and identities. Such a state is structurally imperial, with defined metropoles and outlying colonies whose residents have the choice of being voiceless subjects, de facto collaborators, or persecuted oppositionists. Tsarist Russia was openly imperial; the Soviet Union, with its hyper-centralized political and economic systems, was arguably the apotheosis of empire; and Putin’s Russia certainly remains an empire both domestically and in terms of its grand ambitions in its region and beyond. All three empires adopted repressive policies toward their non-Russian subjects, ranging from cultural repression to imprisonment to deportation to genocidal war. With just a few exceptions, the ethnic Russian majority appears to be perfectly happy with the imperial state. How many protested Putin’s Chechen wars or invasion of Georgia? How many managed to restrain their glee at Crimea’s becoming “ours” in 2014? How many Russians truly believe that Ukraine is an independent state entitled to go its own way? How many are refusing to fight in a genocidal war that is killing them at an extraordinarily high clip? (Surely arrest for draft evasion is not worse than death within an estimated 30 minutes of being sent into battle.) The supposedly liberal oppositionist Alexey Navalny supported Russia’s invasions of Georgia in 2008 and Ukraine in 2014, spouting various nationalist and openly racist views toward non-Russians before reevaluating only in 2022. Ukrainians are fond of pointing out: Scratch a Russian liberal and find a Russian imperialist. That doesn’t apply to everyone, but it does address an unfortunately common Russian trait. Empires inevitably decline, and Putin’s project will be no exception. The reasons for decline are many, but central is the dynamic between the imperial nation that vies for greatness and the colonized nations who invariably question that claim upon attaining some degree of identity. It was the Soviet revolutionary Vladimir Lenin, after all, who said that Russian chauvinism gave rise to non-Russian nationalism and separatism. But how are Russians committed to their nation’s greatness supposed to respond to non-Russian demands for greater autonomy and cultural identity that threaten the unity and size of the mighty imperial state and the political culture that sustains it? As the tsars, communists, and now Putin have consistently done, greatness demands that non-Russians be silenced. (That some of these leaders—such as Joseph Stalin—were non-Russians themselves does not invalidate the structure of their rule.) Ironically, Russians are trapped in a vicious circle of their own making. Abandoning the political culture of greatness and imperialism would pave the road to normalnost, but it would also upend a key source of affective empowerment and national pride. Dismantling or at least slimming the imperial state would go a long way to making more normalnost possible, but that too would require either a massive Ukrainian victory that undermines the current state’s integrity or a Gorbachev-style perestroika that loosens the internal bonds of empire. Normalnost isn’t just a desirable goal for Russia. It’s also of great importance to Russia’s neighbors. Although neither the culture of greatness nor the imperial state are necessary or sufficient for Moscow to start wars, both facilitate war-mongering and make aggression much easier to sell to Russian elites and the public. They thus make war more likely. Imagine a counterfactual: Would a normal Russia bereft of its imperial culture and all-powerful, centralized state have embarked on a genocidal war against Ukraine? Possibly, but not likely. The sad but inescapable truth is that Russia will be an existential threat to its many neighbors, especially Ukraine, as long as its infatuation with greatness persists—as long as normalnost is only a quotidian aspiration, not a political goal. A modern-day Cato, echoing his Roman predecessor’s insistence that “Carthago delenda est,” might be right in saying that “Russia must be destroyed.” But who, besides the Ukrainians, Balts, and Poles, would agree? The Trump administration appears committed to Russia’s revival as a great power. The Europeans are only just beginning to realize that Russia has already declared “hybrid war”—or, more honestly, war without a mitigating adjective—on them. Much of the rest of the world sees the United States as more of a threat today than Putin’s Russia. That’s the bad news. The good news is that, while Putin may be killing Ukrainian civilians in greater numbers, Ukraine’s determination to achieve victory remains undiminished, as does its ability to kill Russian soldiers faster than Putin can recruit them. The even better news is that Putin is putting into practice Cato’s demand by continuing a war that is undermining the economy, exterminating Russian soldiers in staggering numbers, demoralizing and angering his population, and demonstrating to the world that Russia is a has-been great power. Putin is destroying Russia. Putin promised to make Russia great again. Instead, he’s making it weak—so weak that its disintegration due to his self-destructive policies becomes more likely each day. Russians may take heart: Once they let go of the conviction that their country and state have a special destiny of imperial greatness, they will finally be able to enjoy the normalnost to which they aspire. Alexander J. Motyl is a professor of political science at Rutgers University-Newark. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription.
