But the coming up with the idea in the first place, that strikes me as much more like coming up with a poem. It’s an act of imagination. Now I wanna talk about something you’ve thought and written a lot about, which is the relationship between science and the humanities. And probably viewers and listeners have heard the phrase “the two cultures.” And I’m just gonna give a one-minute history of what that phrase comes from. So after World War II, there’s this guy named C. P. Snow who was trained as a physicist, so he’s trained as a scientist, and he becomes a novelist, and he becomes a very good novelist, and he delivers a paper saying we’ve broken down into two cultures. One of them is the culture of the humanities, and these idiots don’t know what the second law of thermodynamics are. And then there’s the culture of the scientists, and these idiots can’t read Dickens. They are too different. And so it has a lot of resonance with people. It turns into a big discussion thing. And what Snow had said, in addition to the separation, was that the people of science, not his novelist buddies, but the people in science—they were building the future. They were contributing to society, and the humanists were just failing and just being passive. Do you think that “two cultures” applies to our society now, and what has been your experience in bridging this chasm between these two? Natarajan: C. P. Snow’s characterization of the two cultures is of a time. So it was at that particular time, the project of modernity, of science and technology changing the world—this was when the world was starting to get decolonized. There were big problems in vast tranches of societies and cultures. It was poverty. You needed machines. You need—it was in that context that he framed that two-culture debate. And you’re right. It had enormous salience. So I think that what has happened—it’s very unfortunate that the structure, academic structures, the ways in which universities and colleges are set up by virtue of departments and this kind of specialization, sort of hyper-specialization, and this idea of expertise being characterized by hyper-specialization, right? I think that has led to silos of knowledge. And I think what is really damaging is that it’s increasingly becoming very clear that all the global problems, any problem that we as a society face, cannot benefit from just one point of view or one kind of intervention. It requires the combined knowledge across disciplines, a truly multidisciplinary approach to the problem, because the problem itself is multifaceted and has a human part, has a technical part. At MIT, I also had this real pang of—I come from a family with a lot of public service and people devoted to India. And I felt that I was being quite self-indulgent So I saw this curious article about the World Bank having designed some hand pumps for water. And the result is they had installed them in many, many villages in South India. And they are drought-ridden sort of regions of the country. And the report said that these are not being used. There’s drought, but these hand pumps are not being used. So I said, “I wanna look into this.” So I went to India. It was my first encounter. Actually, I was an urban child. My family’s from South India, although I grew up in Delhi. So I went to this rural university and talked to them about appropriate technologies, and I went to a village to see this hand pump. And I had thought, This is going to be a fluid mechanics problem. There probably isn’t enough water coming in, and I will figure out, I’ll draw the force diagram. I’ll figure out what’s not working, right? So I get up there, and in five seconds I know why it’s not being used. So I pumped it; lots of water came out. So not a technical problem. It’s just the way you had to stand. In India, it’s women who do the bringing water, and they wear saris. And so it was very unbecoming to put your two feet askance like this and then press it out. So no woman wanted to be seen that way. It was sort of an obscene posture. And so I was like, “Oh, that’s what’s happened. That’s why it’s not being used.” Everything is, it’s all mixed up, right? And you can’t say this is purely a scientific issue, that the best computers are gonna solve this. This is going to be a human. And we didn’t even go into AI yet, right? So I mean, all of the big problems—be they intellectual, be they real-world—that we are facing need a flexible mental frame. So we operate, right? We build models as humans with mental frames. We have these frameworks that we carry around in our heads, and each discipline offers you—and this is the way I think about science and the humanities—they offer you different superstructures to sort of view the world, or different lenses to basically view the world. At the end, you need to put all the lenses together. And that’s what gives you not just a richer view of the world itself, but also a richer set of tools and ways to intervene with the world, interact with the world. Brooks: I think it was Ludwig Wittgenstein who said, “When all the problems of science have been solved, the elemental questions of human life will have remained untouched.” And so I think what he meant by that was that questions like “What’s the purpose of my life?” cannot be solved scientifically. But maybe the scientific frame can inform— Natarajan: Yeah. Brooks: Maybe the distinction isn’t as stark as that sentence seems to imply. Natarajan: Scientists are in two camps in terms of this idea, and I fall in the camp where we believe that science can answer certain kinds of questions. There are questions that are within the purview of science. Are there things that are outside the purview of science? Absolutely. And what do we need to think about them? We need other frames, other ways of thinking; that’s how I feel. But then I have scientist friends, very close friends, with whom I have lots of arguments. So for example, the debates really are—so the emotion anger: Something angers me, something completely different angers you. The question is, will we know, will we ever be able to figure out, what is the precise firing of all the neurons that are needed to create anger in Priya, right? Will we decode that? So I have scientist friends who think, Oh, it’s just a matter of time. We will figure it all out. I don’t necessarily think that, because I think that there may be—in this process of figuring out what triggers anger also sits the definition of anger, and it may not be a universal definition. You’re used to universals in science. And so there’s a lot of, to me, there’s a lot of complexity, and not every aspect of that could be answerable in scientific terms. So I think there are many of us scientists, and often it’s people who really try to bridge different ways of thinking and engaging with the world, who feel that, yeah, science does have its limits. There are certain kinds of questions that science can answer, and there’s some that science cannot answer. That’s not a criticism of science. It’s a way of thinking. It’s a way of seeing the world. And, yes, it is incredibly powerful. There’s no question about it. And, and I think I have to say that now because, we are living at a time where the sort of disbelief and mistrust in science is so rampant. Yeah. That is scary. It’s totally unwarranted, and it’s dangerous. Brooks: So I have two random questions that I’m gonna ask you. The first is Elon Musk calls you up and says, “Priya, you’re really into space. I’m sending all these rockets into space. Do you wanna get on one?” What would you say? Natarajan: I don’t think I wanna get on one. Okay, let me preface. That’s not from a lack of adventurousness, okay? It comes from rooted scientific reality. One of the fundamental problems that we have not yet solved is the impact of radiation on human beings. Okay? So even in the International Space Station, which is not far, which is really nearby—and I don’t know if you saw that study with Scott Kelly, the twins? So the twin who was in space, his chromosomes got—the telomeres got altered. And that radiation exposure is a problem that we have not yet solved. And to say that, oh, we can make a colony there or whatever, til we solve that fundamental problem. So my kind of caution of not really wanting to go anywhere, it’s not safe yet. But I think there’s a big—this is the big fundamental problem, and I am interested in this problem and I am gonna spend some time thinking about it, scientifically and intellectually. But I think that you can escape from this mess that you have made and somehow the future of our species is elsewhere. I don’t know. I’m much more optimistic about what we can do here. What more we can do here, and that we can mitigate a lot of the damage that we have already done. Yeah. Brooks: I don’t like cramped spaces, so the idea of living on some little— Natarajan: No, although I mean if— Brooks: —plastic dome on Mars is— Natarajan: You know, if Elon calls me up and says, “Hey, do you want more money to do your basic scientific research?” I will not refuse him. Brooks: Now the final question is what’s your favorite space movie? Natarajan: Interstellar. Brooks: I’m glad you said that, because that’s the only acceptable answer. Natarajan: Are you serious? Brooks: Yeah. Natarajan: I love it. And not just because—I mean, I am a Christopher Nolan fan, as it turns out, but also because one of my friends and colleagues—he incidentally won a Nobel Prize as well—Kip Thorne, was a scientific adviser to that film. Brooks: He wrote a book about the science in the movie. Natarajan: Exactly. And so no physical laws were broken with all of that. But another remarkable thing happened with that, right? So there were calculations that they did in that movie about the ways in which light is warped by black holes. Double Negative, the company that did the visuals, they actually wrote a scientific paper. Talk about the two silos mixing, right? When have you seen a Hollywood studio and a Nobel laureate co-author a paper? They actually found something, because they did the mathematics of all the ray tracing and the light bending. They found an effect that had not yet been scientifically noted before. So they published a peer-reviewed scientific paper. And so for me, that is like the ultimate sort of dream team thing, right? Brooks: Priya, I’ve learned so much from this conversation. Thank you for coming on The Permanent Questions and expanding our minds. Thanks. Natarajan: Thank you so much for inviting me. This was a lot of fun. Brooks: So I just feel like I had a graduate education in astrophysics, and I loved it. And I want to focus especially on one question I asked her: Does all the vastness of space make you think human life is insignificant? And I have to say, having hung around with Priya for the last little while, I feel sort of the opposite. What she does and what humans do in exploring space, in venturing into space, creating maps of space—it makes the case for human significance, to me, almost irrefutable. And so I don’t feel depressed by the fact that there’s all that vastness out there. And I’m sort of mimicking Psalm 8. If you know your Psalms, King David writes this psalm, and he says, God, you put the stars above us. The work of—consider the heavens. There’s all this stuff out there. And then he says, “And you have made us a little lower than the angels.” And I sort of like that sentiment. We’re not quite at angel level for sure, but we’re still kind of impressive. And I leave this conversation filled with gratitude for that. Thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Priya Natarajan. This podcast is produced by The Atlantic and made possible by support from Yale University. New episodes of The Permanent Questions come out on Sundays. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube page, Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you wanna support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. See you next week. This episode of The Permanent Questions was produced by Rebecca Davis, edited by Christopher Beha, and engineered by Rob Smierciak. Our theme is by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

item.title: The Wisdom of Uncertainty
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 4.06
This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. How comfortable are you with saying, “I don’t know”? Most of us spend our lives trying to know more. We look things up, seek expert advice, and gather information before making decisions. In many cases when we disagree with someone, we assume that if we could just establish the facts, one of us would turn out to be right. We accumulate knowledge until, we hope, the uncertainty disappears. But what if uncertainty never fully goes away? In a recent Atlantic essay, the physicist Carlo Rovelli argues that modern science complicates the idea that we can ever arrive at a completely objective description of reality. Even physics suggests that what we see can depend on the relationship between the observer and what they’re looking at. We are not standing outside the world looking in, Rovelli writes. We are part of the world we are trying to understand. That doesn’t mean that facts don’t exist or that knowledge is useless. Rovelli points out that we make decisions without absolute certainty all the time, and science works much the same way: It can give us extraordinarily reliable knowledge without perfect certainty. The same idea can be freeing in everyday life: We can hold convictions without assuming that our understanding is complete, and approach other perspectives with curiosity rather than immediately dismissing them. Today’s newsletter explores the value of leaving room for uncertainty. On Valuing Uncertainty The Myth of Perfect Knowledge By Carlo Rovelli Science will never be able to give a completely objective description of the world. That should make us humbler—and wiser. How to Have a ‘Don’t-Know Mind’ By Michael Pollan My quest to understand consciousness took me to a cave in New Mexico and then deep into the cosmos. The Truth Physics Can No Longer Ignore By Adam Frank The fundamental nature of living things challenges assumptions that physicists have held for centuries. (From 2025) Still Curious? - You don’t know yourself as well as you think you do. And that’s okay, Julie Beck wrote last year. - How to think, not what to think: College is not just about transmitting knowledge—it’s also about learning and practicing the skills that connect us to one another, Sian Leah Beilock wrote last year. Other Diversions PS My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. Nick G. shared a photo from “the volcanic blast zone of Mount St. Helens in Washington State during a summer sunrise.” We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. — Rafaela

item.title: The Data-Center Debate Is Divorced From the Facts
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 4.04
As the build-out of AI data centers has accelerated, the public has tended to focus on every possible downside of these industrial projects. Some wariness—about the developments and the companies behind them—is sensible. As with almost any new industrial development, and depending on where they are built and how they are powered and cooled, data centers pose risks of excessive carbon-dioxide emissions and noise pollution. But the panic about the harms of these projects has well outpaced the evidence. In my years researching and reporting on AI and the environment, with support from a grant from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), I’ve noticed that misconceptions abound. This panic, moreover, is leading communities to forgo massive amounts of tax revenue—largely because of threats that are inflated, confused, and sometimes nonexistent. The trade-offs are real. In June, a Massachusetts city near where I grew up blocked a data center, in large part out of concern over the amount of water the development would use and pollute. Data centers do need a lot of water to cool their equipment, and—as with most industrial building projects—constructing these developments can introduce chemical additives into the local wastewater. But there are no confirmed cases of this data-center pollution harming people, and this city specifically has abundant fresh water. Most of the fear about water seems to be the product of misunderstood details from news reports, spread like a game of telephone. The New York Times published a story last year about a Georgia couple whose water taps at home went dry after Meta broke ground on a $750 million data center nearby. The couple suggested that Meta’s construction created a buildup of sediment in the water, which caused water-pressure problems and damaged their well (many homes in the area use well water). Whether the construction actually caused these problems remains unclear, but the story is often read as evidence of the harms of data centers. Yet sediment buildup in groundwater is a standard construction risk, and most places don’t ban large buildings over it. Almost all stories about the harms of data centers cite such construction-related problems. As for the concern that data centers add toxic “forever chemicals,” known as PFAS, to local water sources, this seems to involve some confusion over how centers use water to cool the machinery. Some systems use fluorinated fluids classified as PFAS to help cool servers and prevent fires, but these are designed as closed loops that stay contained in equipment. There’s always the threat of a leak, but contaminating local waterways is a risk of any major industrial project. One known exception in which a data center was linked to a water-pollution problem was in Oregon, where Amazon data centers used groundwater that was already contaminated from decades of local agriculture and food processing. Because much of the water used to cool equipment ends up evaporating during the process, the wastewater that left the data center had a higher concentration of nitrates, which exacerbated the contamination problem in the local groundwater. Amazon agreed to settle the matter for $20.5 million without admitting guilt. The company accurately noted that the area had been suffering from polluted water for decades, even if the data center made it worse. The data-center debate includes plenty of dauntingly large numbers without context, such as that they consume millions of gallons of water a day. This is a significant amount, but also comparable to the water use of other industries. The data center with the highest known water consumption, Google’s development in Council Bluffs, Iowa, consumes about 1.3 billion gallons a year. That sounds massive, but so is the amount of water used to irrigate Iowa’s corn crops. If Google had bought a cornfield four to six times as large as the data center’s plot, or about eight square miles (roughly 0.04 percent of the total area Iowa uses for corn), the company would consume the same amount of water irrigating it. All American data centers together will consume about 1 percent of the water that America uses to irrigate corn. This is not nothing, but hardly horrifying in context. Another misconception is that data centers consistently raise local electricity prices. There is no clear positive relationship or broad pattern between data centers and household electricity prices, but people are happy to spread misleading claims on the subject. A common statistic that critics bandy about is that electricity costs near data centers have skyrocketed by as much as 267 percent in five years. Senator Elizabeth Warren cited this number in an op-ed earlier this year. But the figure comes from a Bloomberg analysis of wholesale electricity prices at specific nodes on the grid, not the prices that households pay. Although wholesale prices influence residential prices over time, residential prices are largely insulated from wholesale spikes and drops, and American-household bills have not risen anywhere near 267 percent during the data-center build-out. When price hikes have been linked to data centers, the amount looks more like 10 percent. Perhaps the most pernicious misunderstanding of the facts involves the claim that data centers don’t pay taxes. Early reports about the sales-tax exemptions on machinery and equipment that data centers enjoy in most states have somehow morphed into a sweeping assumption that data centers are actually depriving states and municipalities of tax revenues. The reality is that data centers are a reliable and lucrative source of tax revenue wherever they are built. Real-estate and personal-property taxes ensure that the tax burden on these developments is high, regardless of sales taxes. For example, Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the country, collects $1.3 billion a year in county taxes from these centers—about $2,800 per resident. This represents nearly half of all local tax funding for county government and public schools, despite Virginia’s waiver of sales taxes on related machinery and equipment. Local opposition to new data centers has come to Loudoun too, but residents are unlikely to forgo hundreds of millions of dollars a year to shut down the data centers in operation. Another common concern is that data centers will “take up all the land” because these facilities consume a lot of space. Yet my own rough estimate puts the combined footprint of all data-center buildings in America at about 25 square miles by 2028—a little over half the size of Disney World and spread across the country. These projects also buy land around the buildings and for future expansion, but the combined landholdings of all new and existing data centers would cover about 1,400 square miles, a little more than three times the land used to grow Christmas trees in the United States. For a sense of scale, again consider Loudoun County. Data centers take up 3 percent of Loudoun’s land, even as they generate nearly 40 percent of the county’s general-fund revenue. Despite concerns that these centers depress local land values, a 2025 study of home sales in Northern Virginia, including Loudoun, found that homes closer to data centers sold for higher prices, perhaps because the infrastructure that’s valuable for data centers is also valuable for homeowners. Then there are the conspiracy theories, such as the idea that data centers emit harmful, inaudible low-frequency sounds, known as infrasounds. Such claims sometimes misrepresent the studies they cite. No infrasounds at the levels the data centers emit have been found to be harmful. This is not to say that data centers don’t cause some noise pollution, but the idea that imperceptible infrasounds have some mystical ability to make people unwell is not borne out by the evidence. As for the underlying anxieties about AI that may be motivating the data-center backlash, slowing down the construction of data centers is not the same as slowing down the capabilities of AI. Yet banning data centers has become shorthand for political candidates who wish to seem tough on AI, when this is a distraction: The wiser and tougher move is to heavily regulate the industry. No data center is a harmless boon for locals, but the real question is whether their downsides outweigh their benefits. Given the status-quo bias at play—whereby change seems inherently costlier than keeping things the same—I’ve discovered a simple trick to make the trade-off clear. I now ask people, “Would we spend as much tax revenue as the data center will bring in to avoid its downsides?” For example, would the residents of Loudoun County each pay $2,800 a year to reduce some of the county’s air pollution and water use, lower electricity bills by about $6 a month, and make about 3 percent of the county’s land available for something else? Since this is the actual question before communities, I find that spelling it out is handy. In Loudon, and in other jurisdictions around the country, many voters seem, on balance, to prefer the data centers.

item.title: Emily Wilson Can’t Let The Odyssey Go
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.51
Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics. Her 2017 The Odyssey, the first major translation of the poem into English by a woman, has sold more than 1 million copies. (Her Iliad translation came in 2023.) And this summer, she found herself right at the center of cultural discourse after she drew her sword and published a scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of the ancient work. She didn’t anticipate that she would become part of a pop-culture controversy, and she was reluctant to revisit the episode when we sat down for an interview at this year’s Atlantic Festival. “I really wanted to like the film,” she said, but “it seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth.” Her strong convictions animate a new book of essays, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea, which dissects translations of ancient work with unsparing rigor. Wilson, who is now working on a second translation of The Odyssey, entertained the idea that there might be something “compulsive” in her art and her approach. Her new essays reveal a translator’s difficult balancing act—between fidelity and originality, and between accessibility and strangeness. In the course of our wide-ranging conversation about the pleasures and blind spots of translation—and, yes, the backlash to her now-notorious movie review—she spoke about the imperative she feels to get that balance exactly right. The following conversation was condensed and edited for clarity. Gal Beckerman: You take a pretty hard line in this book about when a text should be retranslated, but you’re translating The Odyssey again. It’s interesting that you should want to go back in again. Have you learned something new about the text or come to see it in a new way that makes it exciting for you to tear it all up and start it from scratch? Emily Wilson: It’s not tearing it up to do a new one, right? Partly it’s that I’m kind of addicted; I can’t stop doing this. I have several other projects I’m supposed to be doing. I did The Odyssey really prioritizing pacing, because my students would very often show up to class saying, Oh, it was so boring. And I would be like, How can The Odyssey be boring? And then I would realize it’s because the translation was twice as long as the original. Then, with my Iliad translation, I was a little bit looser about not confining myself to the exact same number of lines as the original. I thought there were advantages to doing that. So as soon as I’d finished The Iliad, I wanted to go back to The Odyssey and start all over again to produce one that matches my Iliad. So it’s not that I think there’s anything wrong with my current translation, and I think that there will be readers who will like that one better. It will be snappier and all that. Beckerman: Do you think that translators have a kind of a compulsion to continue to play with the words, to work this Rubik’s Cube? Wilson: Yeah, I think it is compulsive, maybe that’s right, but I don’t think that’s just me. I think that is very common, especially for a very long project like this. You’re constantly thinking about, How might I be able to get closer to whatever the vision is? Beckerman: One of the things I love that you do in the book is demystify translation, and make us understand that these are human beings and that they have biases, that they’re in a specific cultural moment—a certain gender, a certain kind of life experience—and that it shows up in the word choices. When your translation of The Odyssey came out, a lot of the excitement about it was that you were the first woman who was translating The Odyssey in English. And I wonder if you feel like being a woman has affected your translation? Wilson: I think some of those headlines were kind of bogus, right? I mean, they were suggesting this really simplistic set of ideas about gender: And of course gender will be the only factor that will contribute to how someone writes. And of course all women write in iambic pentameter, just naturally, and all men don’t. Some of it was really silly, I thought. Beckerman: But do you feel like you understand the particular worldview that you’re bringing to it? None of us fully know the water we’re swimming in, of course, but when you’re translating, are you like, Oh, I think that I’m reading this way or I’m making these choices because I’m a woman of a certain age living in the 21st century in America? Wilson: You know, I honestly never think that. I mean, I think that when I’m talking to people like you. Well, I don’t mean “people like you”— Beckerman: Nosey journalist. Wilson: Exactly. It’s only very belatedly that I feel that I have to prepare an answer for things like this. When I’m actually wrestling with it, I do quite often think, Okay, I’m putting the stress on that, and that syllable and that name; is that because I’m British? To what extent is my approach to the passage informed by that critical study or this critical study? That kind of thing comes into my thinking all the time. But the question is about my lived experience, and do I have this particular relationship to this banquet scene because I don’t eat meat? No. Beckerman: Right. I mean, meter is important to you, that the sound of the poem or the text in another language have some relationship to the original. For translators 200 years ago, they wouldn’t necessarily care in the same way. Wilson: Yeah, this is a very old-fashioned choice on my part. I see myself as super retro. I see myself very much as taking a sort of mid-19th-century approach to translation. Beckerman: How do you think film adaptation is different or similar to literary translation? When you think about a director approaching a text like The Odyssey—wanting to adapt it and making very definite choices about the value system that is underlying the plot that he’s created—is that the same type of thinking through interpretation that a translator does when they approach a text? Wilson: I would say no. I think it’s a very different kind of thinking. What I’m trying to do as a translator is to get to something equivalent to the experience of the original. I think a good adaptation tries to do the opposite of that. Virgil was certainly doing that in rewriting The Odyssey as The Aeneid. It’s on some level the same story; it’s also the opposite story. So I think the more the adaptation pushes against it, in many cases the more successful it is artistically. Beckerman: There is this interesting sort of tension through a lot of these essays in your new book, where you want these ancient texts to be popular, to get out there, to have people engage with them and to make new things with them. But on the other hand, that often leads to a kind of a reductive quality. And I feel like it’s a tension that came out around Nolan’s movie. You wrote a very critical review of the film, and I had a moment as I read that when I wondered, Is she trying to distance herself from it as something that has reductive qualities, and is it popular in a way that doesn’t engage with the full texture of the text? Wilson: I wish I would have liked the film more. I went in hoping to like it and thinking I was going to like it. And it turns out I didn’t. It seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth. There’s another kind of responsibility: that you shouldn’t actually lie about your actual feelings and thoughts. And there’s also a question about: What does it mean to spread the word that everyone should read ancient literature? Everyone should take some kind of interest in history. Everyone should engage with long, difficult books. I really believe in those things, and I don’t believe that the best way to engage with history and to grapple with the essential questions of art and cinema and plays and music and literature is to sort of say, Yay, we love it all. Beckerman: But what lenses did you put on to critique the film? As a translation or as an adaptation? Wilson: No. I mean, I say at the start of the review that very often the best adaptations are the ones that are most resistant to the original. The ways that I was critiquing the film were in terms of pacing and characterization and narrative. A satisfying cinematic experience needs to follow through on its own premises. And so if you set us up to think this is going to be the kind of film where we’re supposed to care about the characters, then you need to follow through on that promise. Beckerman: What did you make of the response to your response—the backlash of sorts? I’m just curious what it told you about people’s relationship to these stories, because there was this real defensiveness about the film, about this effort to make a popular piece of art around The Odyssey. Were you surprised? Wilson: Yeah, I thought it was really weird. Many people reviewed this film, including other Odyssey translators, and there was no discourse about anyone except for me, which is really weird, I thought. So I’m not sure that I can really comment on what weird people thought. But I feel like this is taking us a bit far from the book? Because I don’t discuss the film in the book. I discuss theater and ancient literature. Beckerman: I know, I understand. It’s just that it was an interesting cultural moment. It is not every day that my Twitter feed is full of people wanting to debate the finer points of The Odyssey. So I can imagine, for somebody who’s as immersed in it as you are, that it must be unsettling but also exciting. Wilson: I think it’s wonderful insofar as it is actually substantially about either the film or about the poem, or some combination of the two. I felt that some of the discourse wasn’t about either of those things. I’m, on some level, interested in it because it’s a symptom of some kind of bad stuff in our culture, but I’m not that interested in it, and I’m not going to celebrate it. Beckerman: Right. So my last question: I’ve thought a lot about the limits to how much we can understand people’s lived experience so far in the past, and as a translator of these texts, you come the closest—you walk right up to that edge—and I’m curious for your thoughts about that. Is it never going to be possible for us to get at what it meant to be living in the time when The Iliad or The Odyssey were written? Or do you see a kind of universality that connects us to the people who wrote those texts? Wilson: That’s a great question and such a difficult one. I mean, part of my reason for focusing so much on literary form and poetic form is that even if we can’t get the lived, embodied experience of what it means to be going around in your chitons and eating your ancient Greek olives—I’m not sure that we can get to that through texts—I do think we can get quite close to something like the experience of being a fluent listener or reader. I don’t think that means universals, but I think it means we can get to a kind of multicultural imagination that includes going back in time as well as going to different places in space. And if we can do that, there’s a kind of magic in that in itself.

item.title: The Greenland Fiasco Stumbles to an End
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.04
Jesper Møller Sørensen, the Danish ambassador to Washington, projected an air of calm. He was serving hors d’oeuvres, including reindeer sausage and smoked salmon, at his residence, where American, Danish, and Greenlandic guests had gathered for a Wednesday event billed as “A Taste of the Arctic.” On the terrace, he told me that months-long discussions about the future of Greenland were heading in a good direction. But, he warned, the outcome would depend on whether one person could be swayed. It was obvious that he was talking about President Trump, who has long coveted Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark. Trump has claimed that the United States needs the island for national security, at times declining to rule out using force to acquire it. When his rhetoric became more threatening earlier this year, the Danish armed forces flew emergency blood supplies and explosives to the island to prepare for a potential U.S. attack. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, warned that a U.S. invasion would mean that “everything ends” for NATO—something of an understatement for a scenario in which one founding member of the alliance attacks another. At the World Economic Forum in Davos, in January, Trump stepped back from the brink, proclaiming the “framework of a future deal.” In the subsequent months, he returned to the topic in fits of pique, at one point arguing that Greenland “should be controlled by the United States, not Denmark.” Meanwhile, representatives from the United States, Denmark, and Greenland met to consider ways to bolster U.S. security interests on the island and fend off hostile powers in the Arctic region, namely Russia and China. Now the promised “future deal” appears to be here. It builds on a Cold War agreement between the U.S. and Denmark and includes no transfer of territory to the United States. Instead, it envisions the kind of expanded U.S.-military access and multilateral cooperation that leaders from Denmark and Greenland said was available all along, and doesn’t threaten to blow up the security architecture that the U.S. has helped maintain for nearly 80 years. Earlier tonight, Trump wrote on social media that Washington “will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.” He also said that U.S. adversaries will be barred from having bases on Greenland or making sensitive investments in the island, which is rich in minerals and other raw materials. A Cold War–era agreement signed by Denmark and the United States already gave Washington broad latitude to conduct military operations in the territory, and the U.S. Space Force currently has a base on the island’s northwest coast. The United States once stationed thousands of soldiers across multiple bases and radar sites, but it shrank its presence in the decades after the Cold War. Current and former U.S. officials told me that one area of concern in Washington was the possibility that Greenland, not party to that 1951 agreement, might vote for independence or otherwise alter its political allegiances, and then proceed to restrict U.S. infrastructure and access. The new agreement will also include Greenland and bind all three parties to a more permanent U.S. presence; the U.S. will, among other things, have the ability to build additional bases and use the island’s airspace. Trump wrote, “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many.” U.S. and European officials told me that the agreement will affirm the right of Greenland’s population to determine its own future. It is also expected to include language barring non-NATO bases as well as mechanisms for blocking Chinese and Russian investments. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose deputies played a leading role in the discussions, hailed the agreement. “This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland,” he said in a statement. Danish officials said that the three parties will sign the agreement at the United Nations General Assembly next week and that it will enter into force after necessary parliamentary procedures. Greenland’s premier, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said that the accord “recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation.” Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, said that the agreement is a boon for NATO and Europe as well. The statements were positive but restrained, reflecting the pain inflicted by this saga. Europeans found it difficult to decipher Trump’s motives—or to understand whether they were about to be attacked or simply trolled. One day, there was menacing rhetoric on Truth Social; the next, memes on X of penguins. It was already late at night in Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, when Trump announced the deal. But a reporter from Denmark’s public broadcaster observed politicians going in and out of the government building, reflecting fervent interest in the American president’s designs on their land. Washington may have achieved its security objectives. But it has lost something else: trust among its hosts. “Goodbye, U.S.A.,” one resident said.

item.title: The Artist Who Ripped Up the Rules of Drawing
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 3.81
Most retrospectives unfold like a stately procession. You buy your ticket and proceed through a choreographed sequence of galleries, scrutinizing first the juvenilia, then the promising early work. Next come the triumphal years, and finally (if the artist was lucky) a poignant late phase. An idea of timelessness prevails, enhanced by an enveloping atmosphere of climate control, security, and massive insurance coverage. The lighting is good; the frames are tasteful. Everything looks marvelous. There’s not a whiff of the urgency of the studio, no hint of the emotional or psychological state in which these objects were made. Lost is any suggestion of that feeling, deep inside the creator, of an improvised, inner necessity. “Willem de Kooning Drawing,” at the Art Institute of Chicago, is a classic retrospective—a decorous, deeply researched exhibition about a much-lauded artist at a major museum. In another, more robust sense, however, the show is a giant debauch. It’s frankly (and thrillingly) unseemly. I’ve never been to an art show that takes you so far inside the creative process. You start to wonder if you should even be permitted to get so close. “Art never seems to make me peaceful or pure,” De Kooning once said. “I always seem to be wrapped in the melodrama of vulgarity.” This show, more than any other De Kooning exhibit I’ve seen, delivers on the spirit of that oft-quoted statement. De Kooning, arguably the most widely revered of America’s 20th-century avant-garde artists, took the language of drawing, ripped it up, and rearranged it. Put that way, what he did sounds rebellious. It sounds punk. The exhibition, which will travel to the Rijksmuseum, in Amsterdam, in early October, embraces that spirit. But it has a more conservative purpose, which is to demonstrate that you can’t rip up art’s language effectively—or interestingly—without first really knowing it. De Kooning knew, from long study, how to draw contours. He knew how to create volume using gradations in tone or marks that move in certain ways, how to apply ink or paint with varying degrees of pressure and velocity, and how to employ color relations to suggest depth. Before you can throw all that technique up in the air and have it land again, you need to have the tools. De Kooning was both the best draftsman and the most lavishly gifted painter of the generation of postwar artists (among them Jackson Pollock, Lee Krasner, Mark Rothko, and Helen Frankenthaler) who helped move the art world’s center of gravity from Paris to New York. Born in the Netherlands in 1904, he trained, from the age of 13, as a commercial artist at the Rotterdam Academy of Visual Arts and Technical Sciences while apprenticing with a design firm. The show kicks off with a large drawing, Dish With Jugs, that De Kooning made at the academy. Working in charcoal and conté crayon two days a week for an entire year—600 hours—the young student achieved a remarkable level of photographic verisimilitude in the still life. As one of the exhibit’s curators, Kevin Salatino, writes of De Kooning’s trajectory in an introductory essay for the show’s catalog, the drawing became “the archetype of what he would forcibly reject while retaining the learned skills the work so brilliantly exemplifies, only now putting them to radically different purposes.” That De Kooning could draw like Ingres (or like Picasso during his Ingres-inspired period, from roughly 1917 to 1925) is amply demonstrated by other early works in the show, such as his adoring, fastidiously controlled pencil portrait of Elaine Fried, a fellow artist and his future wife. But, like a libertine desiring undiscovered pleasures, his appetite for new sensations only seemed to grow with time. Drawing has long been regarded as an intellectual activity, something generated, above all, by the mind, with its capacity for conceiving, imagining, and mandating. (You draw to design buildings and invent machines; you “draw up” battle plans and national borders.) “Drawing, as a way of thinking,” Salatino notes of De Kooning, “lay at the core of his practice, the root of everything.” But is it thought, as such, that we’re seeing in De Kooning’s drawings? The critic Peter Schjeldahl, who knew the artist, described him as “a hand with a man attached.” If you can attribute thought to a hand—and I’m willing to admit that you can, but it surely isn’t rational—then this show is indeed a record of thinking. But it may be better described as the record of some more mysterious melting of mind into body. De Kooning came to America as a stowaway in 1926. Residing first in Hoboken, New Jersey, for less than a year before settling in New York City, he remained without legal status for the next 35 years. During an extended period of hard graft as a house-and-sign painter, a window dresser, a show-card letterer, and an advertising-layout man, he encountered various avant-garde artists, including Arshile Gorky, who became a close friend. Under the Armenian American painter’s influence, he gradually shifted his focus from commercial art to modernist fine art, experimenting with different styles derived from Picasso, Miró, and Matisse. Even when ostensibly abstract, De Kooning’s work was populated by bobbling fragments of body parts. He conveyed these with his characteristic wobbling contours and flesh-textured paint. “Content is a glimpse of something, an encounter like a flash,” he once said. “It’s very tiny—very tiny, content.” He proceeded in the studio intuitively, precipitously, as if wanting to catch his subjects unawares. De Kooning had his first solo show in 1948. He broke through to widespread acclaim in 1950 with Excavation, a painting he labored over for many weeks, using a process of patient buildup and repeated erasure. At almost seven feet high and more than eight feet wide, Excavation was the largest canvas he’d ever worked on. (The following year, it was awarded a prize by the Art Institute of Chicago, which subsequently acquired it.) The work was initially inspired by scenes from an Italian movie, Bitter Rice, an art-house hit in Greenwich Village that year, showing young peasant women working in water-soaked fields. But over time, the bodies dissolved into their surroundings and the pictorial space flattened out into a scrim of fleetingly seen forms with hooked and curving contours that push forward from the surface or twist back into shallow space. If, in its genesis, the work recalled Picasso’s proto-cubist breakthrough, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon—the Spaniard’s 1907 painting of five naked women in a brothel—it also pointed the way to what would become a more explicit, and enduring, obsession for De Kooning: depictions of women, wobbly-edged, many of them leering or aggressive, disintegrating before our eyes into a welter of ambient marks. Inspired by prehistoric figurines of such powerful female divinities as the Venus of Willendorf, and by depictions of women by Rubens and Picasso—and riffing, too, on female figures in contemporary cartoons, movies, and magazine advertisements—De Kooning’s women take up a hefty portion of the show. The critic Harold Rosenberg, an early champion of his work, admired the classical balance of Excavation, likening it to “a formula wrung out of testing explosives.” Observing De Kooning drawing, another critic, Thomas Hess, noted that the artist “made a few strokes, then almost instinctively, it seemed to me, turned the pencil around and began to go over the graphite marks with the eraser. Not to rub out the lines but to move them, push them across the paper.” De Kooning’s line, he concluded, “is always under attack.” This ethos of creative destruction remained a guiding principle for De Kooning. The artist’s methods, however, continued to change. His drawings appear to be in a state of constant becoming. Shapes swell and fall away. They coalesce and unravel. De Kooning’s reversals of figure and ground aren’t binary or static, as in classic cubism; they’re in flux, like water moving in water. The show’s emphasis on the muck and mess of the studio may explain why artists in the Chicago area have flocked to the exhibit—and keep on returning, according to Mel Becker Solomon (who organized the show with Salatino, Margaret Holben Ellis, and Charlotte Healy). Solomon recounted to me that she walked through the exhibition with an artist, who told her, “This is what students are missing in their current practice: the tenacity and rigor to keep pushing, experimenting, and searching for what comes next.” What the show demonstrates, in ways that aren’t always obvious with his paintings, is that De Kooning never lost touch with the vocational skills he acquired as a young man. As Rosenberg wrote in 1962, “There was not a trick of the painter’s trade that de Kooning did not have up his sleeve.” Ellis, a paper conservator who worked on the exhibit, lists those “tricks” in the catalog and explains how De Kooning adapted them to purposes for which they were never intended. She describes, for instance, his use of carbon-transfer paper and translucent vellum to copy motifs from one drawing to another. Such processes were typically used to duplicate technical drawings. But De Kooning would apply fragments of the reproductions to new compositions, often in different orientations. He also used frottage, or rubbing—another technique favored by commercial artists—to activate his lines. He would apply charcoal to thin vellum placed over corrugated cardboard or other textured surfaces to give the marks a stuttering look. “Frottage transformed stillness into speed,” Ellis writes of Reclining Nude, a 1963 drawing. This observation approaches the core of De Kooning’s art: More than any other artist I can think of, he gave painted marks and lines different velocities and trajectories. Co-existing in the same composition, those visible shifts in speed, thickness, and direction carved out three-dimensional spaces of ravishing complexity and urgency. Salatino suggests, in his catalog essay, that the artist’s use of frottage “functions, inescapably, as a metaphor for the masturbatory—making and meaning converging in an act dependent upon the probing, rubbing, exploring hand.” Salatino is a first-rate curator, but this sort of writing, to which his introduction is rather too prone, gives art writing a bad name. De Kooning didn’t traffic in metaphors. He wasn’t interested in meanings. There’s a reason Susan Sontag quoted him at the beginning of her essay “Against Interpretation.” Other techniques that De Kooning learned as a commercial artist included cutting out parts of images he found in magazines and inserting them into his compositions, or using masking tape and paper overlays to give his own marks abrupt, crisp boundaries. When drawing, De Kooning loved to use liner and sword brushes, which are favored by sign painters. Both have short handles and extended, bushy bristles. Loaded with ink and applied with control, they allow artists to make long, even lines. De Kooning had mastered their use as a younger man. (Ellis reports that the illustrator Gus Falk, who was taught by De Kooning at Black Mountain College, remembered him applying a perfectly even line to a spinning bicycle wheel by holding the brush steady. “He was in control,” Falk said. “He was interested in exactitude.”) But in his own drawing, De Kooning let rip with liner brushes, swishing them about all over the paper, achieving undulant lines that contract and expand like living creatures. Perhaps the most remarkable of De Kooning’s maladapted techniques was his use of fixatives. The word itself suggests De Kooning’s perversity. Fixatives are sprayed onto vulnerable media, such as charcoal and crayon, to stabilize drawn marks. But instead of spraying a fine, even mist from an appropriate distance, De Kooning aimed the fixative straight at his drawings from close range, creating puddles and rivulets that turned the paper gray, creating strange, smudgy marks and chemical textures. Later in his career, De Kooning tried drawing with his eyes closed or with both hands at once. Long plagued by alcoholism, he was often inebriated. “I’m in my element when I am a little bit out of this world,” he once said. “When I’m falling, I’m doing all right; when I’m slipping, I say, Hey, this is interesting!” The words could sound somewhat pathetic, like a drunk man’s sad, self-soothing rationalization. But the relationship between De Kooning’s virtuosity and the lengths to which he went just to get in his own way is intriguing to consider. Clement Greenberg, the most influential critic of the postwar period, framed the problem in a review of De Kooning’s first solo show. The artist’s “really great facility,” Greenberg argued, risked getting in the way of his ability to express authentic emotion with real originality. “Facility,” Greenberg argued, “has a stubbornness of its own and is loath to abandon easy satisfactions.” For Greenberg, “easy satisfactions” were always close to kitsch. But his assessment was reductive. De Kooning was an immigrant from Europe. His extensive training and virtuosic way with line connected him to an evolving tradition of European drawing that led from Tintoretto, Rubens, Delacroix, and Ingres to, in the modern era, Picasso and Matisse. He would never disown that tradition. But he was in America now. It was the 20th century. Young women were screaming in front of the Beatles. Crowds crammed into theaters to see Marilyn Monroe magnified on the screen. Betty Boop and Minnie Mouse bounced from frame to frame in the cartoons. De Kooning—neither calm nor pure and “wrapped,” as he had put it, “in the melodrama of vulgarity”—longed to incorporate all this impudent American energy into the authority of his European inheritance, and especially into his drawings and paintings of female figures. His efforts to interfere with his own facility were an expression both of his dividedness and of his deep hunger for freedom. Anyone who stands in front of De Kooning’s urgent, sensuously greedy drawings, with their writhing contours, cacophonous colors, and perverse processes, can feel the force of that craving.

item.title: An Ingredient That’s All Too Rare in Adult Life
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 3.46
Silliness, in general, is not hard for me to come by: I have a toddler who is, as she declares often, a “silly person.” Still, the very pleasure I take in being silly with my child and her friends reveals to me its rarity in adult public life. Few social situations encourage or even allow unadulterated loopiness. In general, art made for adults tends to abide by this taboo. We get satire, scatological jokes, imitations, and absurdity, but rarely do we get silliness. A new play, Bocking, reminds us that this is a mistake. A wild, sometimes surreal, and ultimately tenderhearted farce that premiered last month at Baltimore Center Stage, Bocking does not suggest at the outset that it will be silly. It does, however, seem interested in provocation. It begins with a pair of glamorously behatted ladies moving through the crowd, thanking theatergoers for “coming to church.” When the show’s action begins, some of it is, indeed, a church service—but as a pastor delivers at the center of the stage a sermon that turns more and more homophobic, two other characters, a cisgender man and his trans wife, begin to have raucous sex at stage right. It’s a good bit, and it drew uproarious laughs the night I saw the play. In most regards, the scene sets up the show’s concerns well, if rather transparently: Bocking’s author, the young playwright Preston Crowder, wants to teach his religious characters some lessons about acceptance and sex positivity. The show’s comedy tends to cater to a crowd that already agrees with its message. But Bocking has one scene that I found fairly transcendent—one that was not just dirty or gasp-inducing but was also silly to its very core. It’s also the best scene in the play. The moment builds on Bocking’s oddest plotline: One of the characters, an anxious school guidance counselor named Erickson, suffered an unusual childhood trauma. When he was 8, he and his mother caught his stepfather having sex with—stick with me here—a hen. (Animal-rights activists may object to the levity with which this is portrayed; other people may be reminded of the Swedish Chef.) Erickson’s grief-stricken mother then attempted to turn into a hen herself, an event that the play shows as a descent into madness rather than a true transformation. Still, years after her death, the adult Erickson communes with her by “bocking”—that is, speaking in chicken. For much of the play, he does so in private, which registers to the audience as an inexplicable subplot. But when the pastor’s wife, Tiana, visits him to express her marital woes, she winds up extracting the secret of his chicken talk from him—and then demands to give it a try. At first, Erickson is reluctant, but soon, the two begin bocking together. As dialogue, the exchange that follows is incomprehensible. As a moment of human connection, it’s undeniable. And as sheer silliness—not spectacle or satire like the rest of the play—it beats almost any recent piece of art I’ve heard, read, or seen. Crowder understands, clearly, that silliness is a vehicle for catharsis. By behaving ridiculously with each other, Tiana and Erickson get respite from their isolation and their troubles. In watching them behave ridiculously, the audience gets a break from the show’s moralizing and can, instead, connect directly to the characters’ emotions. As a result, the scene deepens the rest of the show. Sketch comedy is typically the most frequent source of silliness in art and culture: Saturday Night Live is often silly, and in my view no one has ever been sillier on camera than the comedians of the legendary British sketch group Monty Python. Plenty of the Pythons’ work is satirical—consider their send-ups of English sexual repression—but what sets their comedy apart for me is their willingness to be purely silly. In the beginning of their sketch “The Ministry of Silly Walks,” a bowler-hatted, briefcase-carrying John Cleese, his back beautifully straight, gavottes down a London street. Viewers don’t know why he’s moving so ludicrously; it doesn’t matter. His silly walk undermines not only his dignified wardrobe but also the very idea of a professional persona. Just by changing his gait to something ridiculous, Cleese gives his audience a moment of release from the entire world of work. But sketch comedy, even when it has recurring characters, cannot develop those characters in the way a full-length work can. Its silliness, therefore, cannot have the emotional impact of the chicken-talk scene in Bocking, or the hot-dogs-as-fingers segment in the movie Everything Everywhere All at Once. One of that film’s many interwoven strands involves an alternate universe in which the characters played by Michelle Yeoh and Jamie Lee Curtis move through their days, experiencing life and love, with frankfurters for fingers. It’s a ridiculous conceit, pointless except to force a visceral sense of frustration, followed by acceptance, into their scenes together—which it does quite well, just as Tiana and Erickson’s bocking creates a visceral sense of relief. Silliness, in both cases, circumvents cerebral experience. No other means of getting a laugh goes so directly to the heart. Real silliness—serious silliness, if you will—lands in a sweet spot between the intellectualism of satire and the visual heft of spectacle. It strips away layers of adult logic, convention, and pretense, delivering grown-ups to the instinctive knowledge that toddlers possess: Work clothes are just costumes. Maneuvering a body through the world is both annoying and a cosmic joke. And communication, as Bocking so well demonstrates, often isn’t really about what gets said. Reasonably, this is tough for many writers, verbal creatures that we are, to admit, but in times of real emotional duress, words are rarely what counts. What matters are the feelings that lie underneath.

item.title: A Diagnosis for Social Conflict That Gets Lost Along the Way
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.86
Weddings, famously, create conflict. Before I got married, my parents and I fought over the guest list. A friend of mine struggled with adding some of her husband’s Protestant traditions to their otherwise Jewish ceremony. Another friend had to decode, and then manage, complicated tensions among her future aunts- and uncles-in-law. All of these issues got resolved, and according to the conflict-resolution facilitator Priya Parker, the process of figuring them out made our weddings more successful expressions of our values. Parker explored the group creation of meaning in her 2018 best seller, The Art of Gathering. In her new book, The Art of Fighting, she writes that arguments are crucial to a group’s ability to do just that. What’s more, in American society—which Parker describes as both conflict averse and low on big rituals—high-stakes events such as weddings are among the “last remaining collective mechanisms to help us have the fights we need to have to figure out who we are now.” The Art of Fighting is predicated on Parker’s conviction that without confrontation, no group can work well. “Fighting,” she writes in her prologue, “is not the death of community. It is its lifeblood.” Parker considers Americans far too willing to focus on themselves rather than their communities, in large part due to a widespread fear of confrontation. A lot of loneliness, in her view, originates from the all-too-common decision to exit a challenging situation instead of dealing with its simmering disagreements. It’s a smart diagnosis, one that’s as relevant to small-bore social scenarios as it is to interactions within religious organizations, schools, and workplaces. The choice to hide from conflict is, to Parker, in many situations, a choice to be alone. Parker’s idea that conflict is inherently a social good is intriguing and counterintuitive. But The Art of Fighting is not nearly as communitarian a book as its setup would suggest. Although its more abstract passages describe healthy confrontation as helpful and worthy, its examples tell another story. Parker presents The Art of Fighting as a “group-help book” but tends to take a side in her case studies—and in most instances, her side wins. Her own life serves as illustration, too, and often provides the book’s most revealing moments. By way of arguing that everyone needs to get comfortable with disagreement, she mentions a clash she and her father had after the latter got upset that Parker hadn’t invited her stepbrother’s wife to her baby shower. As Parker relates it, their discussion of her reasoning—she and her stepsister-in-law just aren’t close—ends not with compromise or reconciliation but with the blunt lines: “He wasn’t getting it. And that was OK.” Such a one-sided resolution suggests a disinterest in compromise and an interpretation of fighting as an individualistic act. Facing conflict may very well be a social good—I believe it is—but her book more often seems to urge readers to wade into arguments to get what they want. The Art of Fighting is full of stories of conflict. Some appear only once, and some are threaded throughout the book. The quarreling groups that Parker features, many of which she worked with in her role as a facilitator, range in size from an extended family to a percussion ensemble to a large architecture firm. Parker uses every case to ask a variation of her central question: “How do you fight with those to whom you want to belong?” In the book’s most moving example, she writes about a church that, in the mid-1990s, deliberated about and then voted on whether it would perform and recognize gay marriages. Its pastor, Martin Copenhaver, understood that they couldn’t make a decision that might lead to division if his church were to survive. “In the political arena,” he tells Parker, “if you win by one vote, you win. In this arena, you win by one vote, you don’t win.” Hoping to forge meaningful consensus, he hosted four meetings to discuss the subject; only those who attended were allowed to vote. After the election—the church decided, not unanimously but with “no great division,” to allow gay marriage—he asked everyone to reconcile in person with someone who voted differently. In essence, Copenhaver organized the entire conflict to prioritize congregants’ investment in the church, not to lead them toward a certain outcome. I wanted to learn more about how other sorts of disputes, especially less orchestrated ones, might bolster a sense of community. But Parker is surprisingly blurry about the variety of incentives for confronting or ignoring tension that exist in one setting or another. Some strategies for managing conflict—waiting to engage until no one has steam pouring from their ears; ensuring that the arguing parties’ grievances and goals are clear; creating the right conditions for a tough conversation—may apply to all kinds of groups. But the book doesn’t do enough to acknowledge that different sorts of conflicts have different stakes. Starting a fight for the good of the group may be wise among relatives but foolish if doing so could also mean losing your job. And a values-based argument may not be worthwhile in a corporate context where the overall goal is to maximize profit. One of Parker’s recurring examples is a debate that took place within a law firm about whether the TV in its common space should show World Cup games played in Qatar. It begins with an intern objecting, on Slack, to the “human rights abuses of workers in the lead up to the World Cup and the horrific status of rights for LGBTQ people and women in Qatar.” The managing partners invited employees to what Parker characterizes as a too-wide conversation about the World Cup. It was, she writes, “the wrong fight with the wrong assemblage of people in the wrong room.” Parker uses this argument to underscore good and bad ways to navigate conflicts, especially ones that arise online—certainly an important issue in our screen-heavy times. But missing from this analysis is any real engagement on Parker’s part with the substance of the conflict itself. Readers never learn how the issue was resolved: Did the World Cup get shown or not? Was there ever a meaningful discussion about the objections the intern had raised? The book uses this example to describe strategies for handling internal dissent, focusing on how the managing partners could best have reestablished peace among their employees. It becomes a story about conflict management rather than conflict as a potential social good. Some of Parker’s personal anecdotes more vividly illustrate her not-quite-communitarian approach to fighting. In one, she describes enrolling her children and their cousin in a small soccer camp one summer. Initially, the kids report hating camp and getting bullied by their counselors. Parker speaks with the camp director, who talks with his employees and establishes that Parker’s children and niece, who started on the eighth week of camp, are unfamiliar with both the established cohort’s “teasing culture” and the basic rules of soccer. Parker suggests that the camp’s coaches “give our kids a Week One experience, orient them, do the things you did with all the other kids when they were new.” They comply, and the camp—which Parker needs for child care—works out. Parker’s reaction to the situation is entirely reasonable; what parent wouldn’t try to help a kid who’s being picked on, or scramble to rescue a child-care setup that seems about to fail? It is not, however, an illustration of confrontation as community service. She shows herself engaging in conflict to get her kids special treatment rather than nudging the kids to advocate for themselves or asking how the camp might better help them settle in despite their latecomer status. Another way to put this is that no compromise is on offer here, and we get no sense of a group working together. Parker, as the customer, gets to be right. Throughout The Art of Fighting, individuals prevail in this way. A woman named Rebekah, exhausted by attending her family’s Passover seders—too much cooking, too much disruption to routine, too much airtime for her right-wing uncle—gives them up. But Parker never writes about what Rebekah’s parents, siblings, or children might lose when she and her nuclear family stop coming, or how her continued, if conflicted, attendance might have led her relatives to create more sustainable traditions. Just as some therapists prioritize clients over the other people in their lives, Parker prioritizes the subjects of her anecdotes over those with whom they fight. What these stories add up to, ultimately, is a much less surprising take on conflict than the book tries to lay out. Parker provides a useful guide to having arguments in good faith without hurting anyone’s feelings unnecessarily or creating a corporate crisis. But arguments can be so much more than that. Alone in the book, the story of Copenhaver’s church demonstrates that even enduring and loaded disagreements can, if handled with enough care and respect, strengthen the bonds between parties—in other words, they can be productive, not just nondestructive. Many readers will have experienced this in intimate relationships. I, for one, have grown closer to some friends after air-clearing arguments and have drifted from others who weren’t willing or able to talk through issues when they arose. But as Parker points out, public life in the United States isn’t set up for healthy conflict. Meaningful group fights are rare experiences. Aside from my wedding planning, I haven’t been part of one. I believe, in theory, that such a dispute could be transformational for both a community and its individual members. But in order for Parker’s book to have taught me how to navigate one, she would have had to truly let go of the old idea that the reason to fight is to win. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: What Comes After America
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.64
Emily St. John Mandel writes science fiction, with the accent firmly on fiction. Imagination, not technical verisimilitude, is her strength; she wisely disregards the scientific in favor of the human. Her indifference to plausibility is a measure of her confidence as a storyteller, and helps snare readers like me, who have a mild allergic reaction to postapocalyptic settings and outer-space odysseys. Her previous novel featured time travel, interplanetary travel, and a cosmic glitch; now, in her challenging new novel, Exit Party, we have accidental teleportation between parallel universes. The underlying theme, though, is irresistible: how shockingly little humanity understands about the sudden swerves and reversals that shape a life—or end it. The new book also offers a prescient invitation to consider the human toll that a world of chaos or repression can exact. Exit Party’s stunning first sentence leaps ahead to 2031 and peeks into a woman’s soul: “In the first spring after the collapse of the United States, the blossoming of the jacaranda trees felt to Ari like grace.” Newly released after 18 years in prison, 48-year-old Ari Waker is just getting used to a Los Angeles that has seen vicious internecine violence. Although international peacekeeping troops have been withdrawn and the city’s curfew has been lifted, nothing like normalcy prevails. Ari walks with her roommate from their apartment in Echo Park (note the locale) to a party in Silver Lake. There, the incomprehensible happens: Two people from a parallel world materialize at the party, and another person (the host) is teleported in the opposite direction—all by accident. The inexplicable appearances and disappearances are as disorienting for the reader as they are for Ari, who wonders whether she has a brain tumor or is having a stroke. For the three teleported individuals, the experience is a disaster: instant, complete, and irreversible dislocation. In the alternate universe, we soon learn, the “United State” has become a fortress, “closed like a fist,” where the national doctrine is “Harmony at any cost.” There we encounter, among other characters, Ibari, an enforcer of the brutally repressive social order. Abrupt cataclysm is a signature of Mandel’s recent work. Before Exit Party came Sea of Tranquility (2022), The Glass Hotel (2020), and Station Eleven (2014)—all of them ingeniously splintered narratives involving many protagonists, zigzagging timelines, and some kind of shattering event. It’s never clear until the end that the shards of narrative can be assembled to form a coherent story. The big picture that at last emerges in Exit Party features paired life stories of doppelgängers, genetically identical sets of characters who have made decisions in their divergent worlds that move them along radically different paths. Ari and Ibari are the principal “twins.” Though at first they seem utterly dissimilar, they are, as Ibari recognizes late in the novel, “two sides of the same coin.” Repeatedly drawn to criminality (which she associates with freedom), Ari has had more than her share of “hinge moments,” the term she prefers for dramatic, world- and life-changing twists. She launched one criminal enterprise—selling luxury goods bought with stolen credit-card numbers—as a teenager, while living in Brooklyn with an aunt and uncle who dealt in stolen antiques. Soon enough, helped out by her cousin, she was selling U.S. passports. When the Russian Mafia lured her into smuggling people, her cousin, beset by moral qualms, balked. So she hired an assassin to kill him. That’s how she landed in prison. Sprung from jail and hoping to find her footing, Ari drifts instead. She works as a dishwasher and in warehouses, and then becomes, in dizzying succession, a gunrunner, a trophy wife, a philanthropist, an art collector. Arriving in Paris in a car with bulletproof windows (another hinge moment), she wonders, “How many completely separate lives am I going to get to live before I run out of chances.” Mandel makes this resilient character—a serial transgressor with a pragmatic code of ethics, uncannily accurate premonitions, and a touching capacity for regret—sympathetic and compelling. Her last name, Waker, is a clue to her essence: She’s awake, aware. She will always notice the jacarandas. A meticulous observer by profession, Ibari is 79 when we meet her, and has risen to a high rank in the Internal Security Service. She’s as frank about her complicity in the disappearance of rule-breaking fellow citizens as Ari is about her weakness for criminality. Ibari has nonetheless imagined a scenario in which, instead of running surveillance operations for the State, she became a criminal; like her twin, she felt there would be “freedom in that.” The door that swings open at the party remains thereafter obdurately shut. Appalled, puzzled, fascinated, Ari and Ibari (in their parallel worlds) try their best to comprehend what has happened. They investigate, quizzing the accidentally teleported. Eventually, they (and the befuddled reader) learn enough about each other and the different worlds they inhabit to have some thoughts about “entanglement”—about how doubles in their respective universes intersect. Which they do, eerily. Even before she knows anything about Ibari and her career in the secret police, Ari wonders why she herself hadn’t “just become a detective, instead of turning to crime.” She can see the appeal of a life played out in the ranks of the NYPD. She yearns for a homeland where she would be spared the “permanent unease” of encroaching anarchy, where armed fighters aren’t forever shooting at one another on the edge of town. In Exit Party, those who diverge nearly converge, and every echo resonates. When they were young girls, Ari and Ibari each read the same children’s detective novel and both latched on to the same sentence: “True diligence means following the improbable path.” While in prison, Ari had TRUE DILIGENCE tattooed on her left wrist; to judge from the improbable path that Ari and Ibari’s creator has followed, it’s Mandel’s motto too. After growing up in western Canada, mostly homeschooled, Mandel graduated in 2000 from the School of Toronto Dance Theatre. Nine years later, at 30, having abandoned her dream of dancing professionally, she published her debut novel. Like her next two books, it was a noir thriller; all three slipped by more or less unnoticed. Her fourth, Station Eleven, about a flu pandemic “that exploded like a neutron bomb over the surface of the earth,” killing almost every human, won prizes and much-deserved critical praise, and sold remarkably well—before getting a big bump six years later during COVID. Sales of the book passed the 1 million mark shortly after the first episode of an HBO adaptation aired, in late 2021. Station Eleven was Mandel’s own hinge moment. In addition to introducing what has since become her fiction’s hallmark fracturing of time and lives, the novel displayed her calm authority and her easy way with ambitious imaginative gambits—one world erased, another fighting to be born—carried off with barely a trace of writerly flourish: “The caravans had once been pickup trucks, but now they were pulled by teams of horses on wheels of steel and wood.” In Mandel’s work, unadorned realism is at the service of baroque invention, and everything, including the prose, is subordinate to the story. Like all the best stories, hers are character-driven. In Station Eleven, Kirsten Raymonde, a child actor before the pandemic and afterward a skilled warrior, is canny and resourceful in the face of catastrophe. Eight years old when her familiar world ended, and a semi-feral teenager when she hooked up with a ragtag troupe that stages Shakespeare plays and orchestral concerts, Kirsten is permanently traumatized, ferocious when necessary, and somehow still capable of tenderness. She’s a sturdy hook for the reader. Mandel holds tight to some of her characters: She teleports a few between the parallel worlds of her novels. Ari made her debut in The Singer’s Gun (2010), where she was already mercilessly pragmatic and minimally sentimental.
